children.translated_text: 'This servant with joined hands entreats you for this matter: sleep with me as if wearied from the exertion of love-play — please, do not [refuse], do not [act] thus.'

'O Lord, when you had descended into the demon's cave for the benefit of the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, and the company of friends had set out in search of you, I too, wandering the earth, on the bank of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> outside <s>Campā</s>, learned from some gathering of people conversing that "there is a certain great sage named <s>Marīci</s>, possessed of divine sight born from the power of <s>tapas</s> (austerity)." Wishing to learn from him the whereabouts of my friend who had gone away on some errand, I went to that place. In that hermitage, in the shade of a certain young mango tree, I found some ascetic of troubled countenance. Having been received by him as a guest and having rested a moment, I said: "Where is the venerable <s>Marīci</s>? I wish to learn from him the fate of a friend who has gone away on business, for that great sage is renowned to me as one possessing marvelous knowledge." Then that one, sighing deeply and warmly, related: "There was indeed such a sage in this hermitage. One day, a young courtesan named <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, who held the position of ornament of the city of <s>Aṅga</s>, her breasts starred with tear-drops, approached him with dejection, and with her peacock-feather [fan] scattered on the ground that she had spread, she bowed down. At that very moment, her trusted circle led by her mother, having compassionately followed after her, fell prostrate right there in an unbroken cascade. That compassionate sage, consoling those people with gentle speech, asked the courtesan the cause of her distress. She spoke as if with shame, as if throwing herself at his feet, as if with depth of emotion: 'Venerable one! These people, unfit vessels for worldly happiness, seeking the wealth of spiritual assistance for the next world and the future, have come to the feet of the venerable one as their refuge.' Her mother, however, with joined palms, her loosened peacock-feather binding touching the ground she had freed, spoke: 'Venerable one, this your servant informs you of a fault of this my daughter. And the fault is mine — the non-performance of my own proper duties. For this is the duty of a courtesan's mother: bodily care of her daughter from birth itself; nourishment of the body through measured food that balances the humors, fire, and elements while promoting radiance, strength, complexion, and intelligence; not even showing the father from the fifth year onward; festive auspicious rites surpassing any celebration on birthdays and auspicious days; instruction in the arts of <s>Anaṅga</s> (love) together with their auxiliaries; proper training in dance, song, instrumental music, drama, painting, the culinary arts, perfumery, flower-arrangement, knowledge of scripts, skill in speech, and such; acquaintance with the rudiments of grammar, logic, and conventional learning; thorough mastery of the science of livelihood, skill in games, and the gambling arts both animate and inanimate; careful practical learning in the inner arts from trusted persons; public display of her, splendidly adorned and richly equipped, at festivals and processions and the like; securing a delay through captivating words previously gathered, when there is an occasion involving one fond of music and such things; proclamation of her fame in all quarters through specialists in their respective crafts; announcement of her auspicious marks by astrologers and such persons; introduction of her beauty, character, skill, grace, and sweetness by jesters, <s>pīṭhamardas</s>, <s>viṭas</s>, <s>vidūṣakas</s>, mendicant nuns, and others in gatherings of urbane gentlemen; setting her price — who has become the target of young men's desires — at the very highest fee; giving her to one who is independent, endowed with noble birth, beauty, youth, wealth, power, purity, generosity, courtesy, skill, character, and sweetness, and who is either naturally smitten with passion or maddened by seeing her state; offering her, even for a small price but with many pretexts, to one of superior qualities who is not independent but most wise; or, through a <s>Gāndharva</s> union with one who is not independent, extracting the bride-price from his elders; enforcing the claim through legal proceedings when a man who has voluntarily accepted her refuses to pay; making the enamored man observe the vow of exclusive devotion to her daughter; extracting by various devices the wealth of respectable wealthy lovers who have been won over by constant, occasional, and spontaneous displays of affection; if a miserly one refuses to give, stimulating the generosity of the greedy but passionate one by encouraging a rival; driving away the worthless one through verbal cuts, public reproaches, confining the daughter, inducing shame, bringing accusations of infidelity, and insults; examining those who give wealth, who ward off calamity, and who are blameless, weighing the prospects and risks, uniting again and again. And for the courtesan, there should be attachment toward a patron only as a professional engagement, not emotional involvement. Even when there is genuine affection, there should be no transgression of the commands of the mother or the head madam.' Given all this, this daughter, transgressing the sacred duty ordained by <s>Prajāpati</s> (the Creator), spending a mere month dallying at her own expense with some handsome but penniless young stranger, drove away many wealthy patrons by rejecting them in her anger. She ruined her own household. When I forbade her saying 'This foolish girl is no good,' she departed in anger for the forest life. And this intractable, irreversible girl — all these people here, having no other refuge, will perish right here by fasting unto death' — thus she wept. Then that courtesan was addressed by the ascetic: 'Dear girl, surely this forest-dwelling causes suffering. Its fruit is either <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) or heaven. The first of those, being attainable through the highest knowledge, is for the most part very difficult to achieve; but the second is easily accessible to one who fulfills the duties of one's own family calling. Therefore, ceasing from an impossible undertaking, follow your mother's counsel.' Though thus compassionately advised, if the feet of the venerable one are not [my] refuge, then let the golden-seeded Lord (<s>Śiva</s>) himself be my refuge, O wretched one — thus she raised a lament. That sage, deliberating, said to the courtesan's mother: 'Go home now. Wait a few days, while this delicate girl, accustomed to comfortable enjoyments, genuinely distressed by her resolve for forest-dwelling, being repeatedly instructed by us, will settle back into her natural [occupation].' 'So be it' — when her people had departed, that courtesan, not lightly devoted to the sage, wearing clean and simple garments, not overly concerned with bodily adornment, won him over in no great time through filling the water-pots of the forest trees, gathering flowers for worshipping the deities, labors of picking and arranging, preparations of various offerings, and also through activities for the worship of <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love) — incense, garlands, lamps, dance, song, instrumental music, and the like — and in private through stories relating to the three aims of life, and appropriate philosophical discourses. One day, perceiving him to be smitten in private, 'The world is truly foolish to reckon <s>artha</s> (wealth) and <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) alongside <s>dharma</s> (duty)' — thus she slightly smiled. 'Tell me then, in what respect is your preferred <s>dharma</s> superior to <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s>?' — prompted by <s>Marīci</s>, she began to speak with a slowness born of modesty: 'What need is there to explain to the venerable one, who surpasses all people, the relative strength and weakness of the three aims of life? Or perhaps this too is yet another form of grace toward your servants. Very well, let it be heard. Surely, without regard for <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s> do not even arise. <s>Dharma</s>, independent [of the other two], is the cause of the happiness of cessation, achievable by mental composure alone, and does not depend excessively on external means like <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s>. When reinforced by insight into reality, it is not obstructed by <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s> however they may be practiced. Even when obstructed, being easily restored with little effort, having removed even that fault, it conduces to no small welfare. For instance: <s>Pitāmaha</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>)'s desire for <s>Tilottamā</s>; the Lord of <s>Bhavānī</s> (<s>Śiva</s>)'s seduction of a thousand sages' wives; the Lotus-Naveled One (<s>Viṣṇu</s>)'s sporting in a harem of sixteen thousand; <s>Prajāpati</s>'s amorous inclination even toward his own daughter; the Lord of <s>Śacī</s> (<s>Indra</s>)'s adultery with <s>Ahalyā</s>; the Moon's violation of his guru's bed; the Sun's assault on <s>Vaḍavā</s>; the Wind's union with the wife of the lion (<s>Kesarin</s>); <s>Bṛhaspati</s>'s approach to <s>Utathya</s>'s wife; <s>Parāśara</s>'s seduction of the fisherman's daughter; <s>Parāśara</s>'s son (<s>Vyāsa</s>)'s intercourse with his brother's wives; <s>Atri</s>'s union with the doe. And the gods' deceptions of the <s>Asuras</s> in various affairs do not, through the power of knowledge, bring harm to <s>dharma</s>. And in a mind purified by <s>dharma</s>, as in the sky, no dust ever clings. Therefore I believe that <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s> do not touch even a hundredth part of <s>dharma</s>.' Hearing this, the sage, whose passionate disposition had been aroused, said: 'O charming one, you see truly — <s>dharma</s> is not obstructed by the enjoyment of sense-objects for those who have seen the truth. However, from birth we have been unacquainted with matters of <s>artha</s> and <s>kāma</s>. Tell me, what are these two like — what are their attendants and what their fruits?' She then said: '<s>Artha</s> (wealth) consists of acquisition, increase, and protection; its attendants are agriculture, animal husbandry, commerce, diplomacy and war, and the like; and its fruit is the accomplishment of charitable purposes. <s>Kāma</s> (pleasure), however, is that supreme happiness of a special touch between a man and a woman whose minds are excessively attached to sense-objects. Its attendants are whatever is delightful and brilliant in this world. Its fruit is supreme rapture — born of mutual embrace, sweet when remembered, unsurpassed when the pride it arouses is declared, direct, self-evident, and known only to oneself. For its sake alone, men of exalted station undergo terrible austerities, make great gifts, wage fierce battles, and undertake dreadful ocean-crossings and the like.' Whether from hearing this, or from the skill of that [courtesan], or from the dullness of his own mind, disregarding his own vows, he became attached to her. She, having led that utterly deluded soul far indeed by her enticements, brought him into the city, down the magnificent royal highway, to her own house. And there was a proclamation: 'Tomorrow is the Festival of <s>Kāma</s> (Love)!' The next day, having bathed, anointed, and adorned him beautifully with garlands, having initiated him into the ways of lovers, [yet] having extinguished his own desire for his former practices, though tormented even when she was away for a mere moment, she led him along the opulent royal highway to the festival assembly. In a certain garden, in the presence of a king surrounded by hundreds of young women, being told with a smile by him, 'Dear lady, sit with the king,' she made an obeisance with graceful charm and sat down with a smile. There, some chief woman rising with joined palms said: 'Lord, I have been defeated by her; I accept servitude to her from this day forward' — thus she praised the ruler. An uproar of wonder and joy arose among the people. The delighted king, honoring her with costly jeweled ornaments and a great retinue, dismissed her. Praised in groups by the chief courtesans and leading citizens, without even going to her own house, she addressed the sage: 'Venerable one, here are my joined palms [in salutation]; this servant has been long favored; now one's own purpose must be fulfilled.' But he, as if bitten by passion's fang, exclaimed with bewilderment: 'Beloved! What is this? Whence this indifference? Where has your unique love for me gone?' Then she said with a smile: 'Venerable one, she from whom today at the king's court I accepted defeat — in some quarrel of ours, she taunted me saying "You boast as if you have won over <s>Marīci</s>." By the bond of a wager of servitude, I engaged in this matter. And I am successful, by your grace.' He stood there, utterly disgraced, his mind empty as a void, and went away to the forest. That very ascetic who was thus treated by her — consider that to be me myself, O noble one. Having drawn out the passion planted by her own power, that very courtesan bestowed upon me great dispassion. Before long I will be able to make myself capable of serving your purpose. For now, stay in this very city of <s>Aṅga</s>, <s>Campā</s>.' Then, as if the sun set in fear of the touch of darkness that had not departed from that mind, [the day ended]. And passion, released from the sage, glimmered as if it were twilight. The lotus groves closed as if given dispassion by that tale. Having taken leave of the sage with his approval, worshipping the twilight with him, engaging him with appropriate stories, passing the night, when the fiery orb — like a forest-fire on the eastern mountain — rose, putting to shame the sprouts of the wish-granting trees, I bowed to him and set out for the city. On the way, I saw near the road, outside some Jain monastery, seated in a secluded grove of red <s>Aśoka</s> trees, a certain Jain monk who had not attained <s>samādhi</s> — of extremely emaciated form, foremost among the uncomely, of pitiable appearance. On his chest I noticed tear-drops falling from his face, whose accumulation of filth had loosened. Sitting near him, I asked: 'What have austerities to do with weeping? Unless it is a secret, I wish to hear the cause of your grief.' He said: 'Good sir, listen. I am the eldest son of a merchant named <s>Nidhipālita</s> in this very <s>Campā</s>, and my name is <s>Vasupālita</s>. Because of my ugliness, I was known as "the one with no looks." There was also here another man named <s>Sundaraka</s> ("the handsome one"), true to his name, rich in all artistic accomplishments but not very wealthy. Between him and me, a rivalry was fomented by mischief-making urban rogues, using our appearance and wealth as pretexts. Those very persons once, in a festival assembly of ours, having themselves created an exchange of insults rooted in mutual contempt, and then mediating, proclaimed: "Neither appearance nor wealth is the measure of manhood; rather, he whom the most distinguished courtesan desires — he is the true man. Therefore let <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, the very crest-jewel of young women, love whomever she wishes, and let him carry off the banner of good fortune." And we two, accepting the challenge, each sent messengers to her. I, it seems, was the cause of her love-madness. When we were both seated, she approached me, casting upon my body a garland-like sidelong glance of blue lotuses, and caused that crowd to hang their heads in shame. And I, thinking myself fortunate, made her the mistress of my wealth, my house, my retinue, my body, and my very life. She then drained me until I was reduced to nothing but my begging bowl, and having robbed me of everything, discarded me. Falling into the position of public ridicule and unable to bear the reproaches of the city elders, here in this Jain temple, instructed in the path of liberation by a certain monk, [thinking] "This garb is easy for those who have left the courtesan's house" — with surging dispassion, I also did not abandon that sluggishness. But then, caked in accumulated filth, pained by the severe pulling out of hair, tormented by extreme hunger, thirst, and other sufferings, harassed even in standing, sitting, lying, and eating by powerful restrictions — like an elephant newly captured — I reflected. "I am a <s>dvija</s> (twice-born). This descent into the path of heretics is not my own <s>dharma</s>. My ancestors followed the path prescribed by <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>. But for wretched me, this contemptible garb that is a great abode of suffering, with its constant hearing of slanders against <s>Hari</s>, <s>Hara</s>, <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>, and other deities, bearing the fruit of hell even in the next life — fruitless, mostly deceptive — such was this path of unrighteousness that was to be practiced as if it were righteous." Having thus recognized my own folly, I came to this secluded thicket and am weeping copiously.' Hearing this, I, filled with compassion, said: 'Good man, be patient. Dwell here for some time. I shall endeavor to make that very courtesan restore you with your own fortune. There are stratagems of such a kind.' Having thus consoled him, I rose. Entering the city itself, having ascertained from popular talk that it was a city teeming with greedy rich men, and intending to demonstrate the transience of wealth and restore things to their natural state, I formed a plan. Entering the gambling hall, I associated with dice-sharps. Among all twenty-five forms of gambling arts that serve as the basis of play, in dice, board games, hand games, and the like — their extremely difficult-to-detect cheating techniques, the swaggering provocative words rooted in those [tricks], the reckless aggressive gestures indifferent to life, the transactions that inspire confidence, the enforcement of accepted stakes that rely mainly on the power of law and prestige, the blandishments toward the powerful, the threats toward the weak, the skill in forming factions, the high and low enticements, the descriptions of varieties of stakes, the generosity in sharing winnings, the occasional near-dishonest commotions, and all these and other things — experiencing them, I never had my fill. I deliberately gave away some winnings to a certain gamester through feigned carelessness. The opposing gambler, scorching me as if with a gaze red with anger, said: 'You dare teach the art of gambling under the guise of jesting? Let this untaught wretch be. Let me first play against you, the clever one!' And by the authority of the gambling-master, he wagered against me. I defeated him and won sixteen thousand <s>dīnāras</s>. Giving half to the house and the players, I took the other half and rose. As I rose, there were words of praise pregnant with joy from those present. At the insistence of the gambling-masters who solicited me, I held a most lavish feast at that establishment. The one on whose account I had entered the gambling world — one named <s>Vimardaka</s> — became my most trusted second heart. Through him, having thoroughly assessed the entire city in terms of substance, deeds, and character, on the darkest night, black as the throat of <s>Dūrjaṭi</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), dressed in dark garments and half-shorts, wearing a sharp dagger, equipped with numerous implements — snake-mouth pincers, human-skull [lantern], magic powders, magic wicks, measuring strings, crabs, ropes, lamp-vessels, spinning tops, and such — going to the house of some newly wealthy man, I cut through the wall, observed the interior household activities through a fine crack in a cloth screen, and entered fearlessly as if into my own house. Taking a large, substantial purse, I went out. On the royal highway, darkened by dense masses of dark clouds, I suddenly perceived a flash of light like a lightning bolt. Then, as if the city's presiding goddess, angered by the theft from the city, had emerged at that undisturbed hour, a certain young woman appeared nearby, her ornaments glimmering. 'Who are you and where are you going?' — asked thus with kindness, she spoke with a voice faltering with fear: 'Sir, in the next street lives a most excellent gentleman named <s>Kuberadatta</s>. I am his daughter. My father betrothed me while still an infant to some merchant's son here named <s>Dhanamitra</s>. But he, through excessive generosity after his parents' death, having as it were bought poverty from the supplicant class with his own wealth, is now poor. Though they call him generous and have given him the additionally acclaimed name <s>Udāraka</s> ("the generous one"), and my father is willing to give me to him as I have come of age, my father, [saying] "he is poor," wishes to give me instead to some other man true to his name, a caravan-leader named <s>Arthapati</s> ("lord of wealth"). Knowing that this inauspicious [wedding] would take place tomorrow at dawn, I, having previously received a signal from my beloved, having deceived my family, slipped out by a path familiar from childhood, and am going to the house of my lover <s>Manmatha</s> (love's) — let me go! Take this bundle [of ornaments].' She untied it and gave it to me. Taking pity, I said: 'Come, virtuous lady, let me take you to your beloved's dwelling.' I walked three or four steps. Then came a patrol with torches whose light was dissolving the mass of darkness — a not inconsiderable civic guard, armed with staffs and swords. Seeing the girl trembling, I said: 'Dear girl, do not be afraid. Here is my arm, unequaled. But this is a gentle stratagem devised for your sake. I shall lie down as if convulsing from the effects of activated poison. You too must tell them: "We entered this city at night. My husband was bitten by a cobra in that corner of the assembly hall. If any among you is a knower of spells and is compassionate, let him revive him and save the life of this helpless woman."' That young girl too, having no alternative, with a voice faltering with fear, her eyes raining tears, trembling, somehow went and carried out my instructions. I lay there, manifesting the convulsions of activated poison. Among them, some self-important fellow, having unsuccessfully treated me with seals, thread-charms, <s>mantras</s>, meditation, and such, said: 'This one is already dead from the fatal bite. For see: his limbs are rigid and discolored, his gaze is fixed, his breath has ceased. Enough of grief; tomorrow we shall cremate him. Who can overcome fate?' And he departed with the others. I rose, took her to <s>Udāraka</s>'s [house], and said: 'I am some thief or other. With my mind drawn toward your plight, becoming your ally, I encountered you on the way going to your beloved, and out of compassion I brought you to his side. Here are her ornaments.' I also gave away those [stolen goods] whose darkness of concealment had been rent apart by the radiance. <s>Udāraka</s>, taking them, spoke to me with combined shyness, joy, and agitation: 'Sir, you yourself have given me my beloved this night. And yet my words have been stolen again — for I do not know how to express this marvel of your deed. Your own character does not seem marvelous to you. Nor can it be said that no one else has ever done such a thing — for the inherent power of things is fixed. No others' vices such as greed exist in you. That you take pride in it — well, from prior deeds of yours it does not please. "By this good deed of yours, this servant has been purchased" — thus you purchase with what is weightier than material things. This body is the counter-gift for the gift of a beloved — and should that fail, this life, ready for death, has also been given by you. Or rather, this much is fitting. From today this servant is to be maintained by you' — thus he fell at my feet. Raising him and embracing him to my chest, I said: 'Dear friend, what is your resolve now?' He replied: 'I cannot live here, having married her without my parents' consent. Therefore, this very night I wish to leave this place.' 'Who am I [to say otherwise]? Do as you command.' Then I said: 'That is so. "My own country" or "a foreign land" — this distinction means nothing to a clever man. But she is a young girl of no little delicacy. Forest paths are difficult and fraught with dangers. Some slackening of wisdom and courage might arise from such a catastrophe as leaving one's country. Therefore, stay right here comfortably with her. Come, let us take her to your own dwelling.' With his thoughtless consent, having immediately brought her to his house, with her as a willing accomplice, the two of us stole everything there down to the clay pots. Then, rushing out, having stashed the stolen goods somewhere, as we hurried along, in the press of the city patrol, we dragged from the roadside some sleeping, drunken elephant-rider, and I mounted on top of him. With his feet dangling loose from the elephant's neck-chain, being lifted up by me, having fallen and landing with his broad chest on the floor beneath the elephant, he — becoming a club of street-cleaning — scattered the guard force. With this same [elephant] we assaulted <s>Arthapati</s>'s house as well. Having removed the goods to some ruined garden, we descended by grasping tree-branches. Returning home, we bathed, and lay down in the glory of bed. Just then, like a ruby peak of the eastern mountain from the ocean, like the tawny pallava-leaves of the golden wish-granting tree, the orb of the sun rose. Rising, washing our faces, performing the morning auspicious rites, we wandered through the city, which was in an uproar over our exploits, and heard the commotion in the houses of the bride and groom. Then <s>Arthapati</s>, having been consoled by [his] wealth, arranged the wedding of <s>Kulapālikā</s> [with another] in a month's time. In private, I then instructed <s>Dhanamitra</s>: 'Approach, friend, the king of <s>Aṅga</s>, in a private audience, with this leather-jewel pouch held before you. And say: "The king surely knows me — I am the only son of <s>Vasumitra</s>, whose wealth amounts to many tens of millions, and my name is <s>Dhanabhi</s>. Having come to be called a spendthrift, I have been scorned by the supplicant class. For <s>Kulapālikā</s>, who was raised for my sake — when <s>Kuberadatta</s>, because of my poverty, wishes to give his daughter to <s>Arthapati</s> instead — in my distress, wishing to cast away my life, I entered the old forest by the city, and with a blade at my throat, was prevented by some ascetic with matted locks who said: 'What is the root of your reckless act?' I replied: 'Poverty, born of contempt.' He then compassionately continued: 'Son, you are foolish. Nothing is more sinful than self-destruction. The good uplift themselves by themselves without self-destruction. There are many means to earn wealth; not a single one exists for gaining back the life of one whose throat has been cut. What use is this? I am one who has perfected <s>mantras</s>. I have accomplished this leather-jewel pouch that yields a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. For a long time, through its grace, I lived in <s>Kāmarūpa</s> (Assam), granting desires to the people. Now in my old age, being about to enter the earth-heaven at this holy site, I have come. Accept this. The established belief about it is that it yields only for merchants or chief courtesans, not for others. But whatever has been wrongfully taken must be returned to the one from whom it was taken. What is rightfully earned, however, should be given to gods and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>. Now, if this [pouch] is placed in a clean spot and worshipped like a deity, every morning it will be seen filled with gold. And since this jewel-leather pouch is not to be presented to the king and not to be lived off, I have brought it here.' But the king is the authority." The king will certainly say: 'Dear man, I am pleased. Go. Enjoy this as you wish.' And say further: 'May it be so arranged that no one steals this.' That too he will certainly agree to. Then, going home, having made the prescribed offering of wealth, you will day by day worship it, fill it at night with stolen goods, and display it to the public in the morning. Then <s>Kuberadatta</s>, treating <s>Arthapati</s> as worthless straw, will be eager to give you his daughter of his own accord because of his greed for wealth. And if the angry <s>Arthapati</s>, in the pride of his wealth, attempts to litigate, we shall by various clever means reduce him to nothing but his loincloth. Our own thievery will be perfectly concealed by this very device.' Delighted, <s>Dhanamitra</s> carried out everything as instructed. That very day, at my direction, <s>Vimardaka</s>, devoted to <s>Arthapati</s>'s service, exacerbated the enmity between him and <s>Udāraka</s>. Then the greedy <s>Kuberadatta</s>, having rejected <s>Arthapati</s>, graciously wished to give his daughter to <s>Dhanamitra</s> instead. <s>Arthapati</s> too challenged this legally. During these very days, the younger sister of <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, named <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, was to perform a concert at the assembly of five heroes — and the cityfolk gathered with great eagerness. I too, together with my friend <s>Dhanamitra</s>, was present there. When she began to dance, my mind became a second stage. The cupid of five arrows, sheltered by the bow of her glancing eye-play of blue lotuses, as if having mustered his forces through the full complement of aesthetic sentiments, tormented me excessively. And she — like the city's presiding goddess angered by the city's robbery — bound me with the chains of her graceful sidelong-glance garlands, dark as blue-lotus petals. Rising from her dance, she — radiant with the beauty of accomplished perfection — whether from coquetry, or from desire, or for no reason at all, I do not know — repeatedly glanced at me with a sidelong gaze unnoticed even by her companions, with a gracefully arched eyebrow-vine, and having smiled slightly with deliberately revealed moonlight of teeth, departed, followed by the eyes and minds of the people. I, going home, my appetite destroyed by irresistible longing, pretending to feel a headache, lay down on a secluded bed with limbs relaxed. <s>Dhanamitra</s>, most thoroughly versed in the science of love, came to me and in secret said: 'Friend, that is indeed a fortunate courtesan-daughter on whom your mind has so fixed itself. I too have well observed her disposition. Before long, the five-arrowed one will lay her on the bed of arrows. For those firmly settled in their station, union is achievable through the left-hand method. However, she, a courtesan-daughter, with a noble and generous intention contrary to the courtesan's own professional <s>dharma</s>, has proclaimed: "I am one whose price is virtue, not wealth. And without a formal marriage, my youth is not to be enjoyed by another." When her sister <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>'s mother <s>Mādhavasenā</s> tried repeatedly to forbid this, to no avail, they petitioned the king with tears in their throats: "Lord, your servant <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, of beauty matched by character and artistic skill, would fulfill all desires — so we had the very highest hope, which is now cut at the root. If she, transgressing her own family <s>dharma</s>, indifferent to wealth, wishes to sell her youth to virtuous qualities alone and persists in conducting herself like a chaste wife, if this girl would return to her proper nature even by the command of your majesty's feet, that would be excellent."' Even when instructed by the king at their request, that girl remained immovable. Then her sister and mother, insisting with tears, told the king: 'If any rogue, against our wishes, seduces and ruins this young girl, he should be put to death like a thief.' Given this situation, one who despises wealth — her family will consent. But she will not agree to give her for money — thus I must devise a stratagem.' Then I said: 'What is there to ponder? Having won her through virtues, let us secretly satisfy her family with wealth.' Then, having won over a certain chief messenger of <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>'s — a Buddhist nun named <s>Dharmarakṣitā</s> — through gifts of robes, alms-food, and the like, through her I made a wager with that courtesan: 'If I steal the leather-jewel [pouch] from <s>Udāraka</s> and give it to you, then <s>Rāgamañjarī</s> shall be the counter-gift.' When she agreed to this, having accordingly arranged matters for that purpose, I grasped the hand-blossom of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, who had been maddened by [reports of] my virtues. And on the night of the leather-jewel theft accusation, at its very inception, under the pretext of some other business, the leading citizens having been summoned and listening, my agent <s>Vimardaka</s>, assuming the identity of <s>Arthapati</s>'s man, crossing over <s>Dhanamitra</s>'s [defense], loudly berated him. <s>Dhanamitra</s> said: 'Good sir, what is your business that you abuse me for another's sake? I do not recall even the slightest injury to you done by me.' He, threatening even more, said: 'There is the very pride of wealth, that you seek to re-appropriate another man's wife, bought with a bride-price, by enticing her parents with money. And you say "What injury to you was done by me?" — is it not well known that "<s>Vimardaka</s> is the outward life of <s>Arthapati</s> the caravan-leader"? I would give up my very life for his sake. I would not even shrink from the sin of <s>brahmahatyā</s> (slaying a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>). "This fever of the leather-jewel conceit of yours is the retribution for my single night's vigil."' Speaking thus, he was angrily restrained by the leading citizens and removed. This matter was reported to the king by <s>Dhanamitra</s>, who with feigned distress had first introduced the disappearance of the leather jewel. The king summoned <s>Arthapati</s> in private and asked: 'Tell me, do you have someone named <s>Vimardaka</s>?' And that fool replied: 'Yes, Lord — my dearest friend.' 'And what is his business?' — when this was told, the king said: 'Can you summon him?' 'Indeed I can' — going out, he searched diligently in his own house, in the courtesans' quarter, in the gambling hall, and in the marketplace, but did not find him. How could that wretch be found? For that <s>Vimardaka</s>, carrying identification tokens from me and your description, had at my direction departed that very day for <s>Ujjayinī</s> in search of you. <s>Arthapati</s>, not finding him, considering the offense committed by him to be linked to himself, either from delusion or fear, denied it. Then, when this was revealed again by <s>Dhanamitra</s>, the angry king arrested him and had him put in chains. During those very days, <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, wishing to milk the leather-jewel in the manner prescribed, secretly approached the deformed <s>Virūpaka</s>, who had been drained previously, returned to him all the wealth that had been taken from him, and having conciliated him with many respectful gestures, departed. He too, having somehow freed himself from the bonds of the Jain order at my instruction, most joyfully returned to his own <s>dharma</s>. <s>Kāmamañjarī</s> too, within just a few days, by her desire to milk the leather-jewel to the last drop, brought about her own ruin. Then, at my direction, <s>Dhanamitra</s> humbly informed the king: 'Lord, this courtesan <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, who was a target of public reproach as "Greed-blossom" (<s>Lobhamañjarī</s>) due to the excess of her avarice, is now renouncing even her pestles and mortars without a care. I believe the cause is her acquisition of my leather-jewel. For its nature is such — the established belief is that it yields only for merchants or chief courtesans, not for others. Therefore I have suspicion about her.' She was immediately summoned by the king along with her mother. And in private, I told her as if with a troubled expression: 'Surely, dear lady, through the overly conspicuous renunciation of all your wealth, the acquisition of the leather-jewel arouses suspicion. You have been summoned by the king of <s>Aṅga</s> for interrogation on this matter. And when you are pressed repeatedly, I shall certainly be named as its source. Then I shall suffer an elaborate execution. And with me dead, your sister will certainly not live either. You will be left destitute. And the leather-jewel will revert to <s>Dhanamitra</s>. This calamity leads to ruin on all sides. What then is to be done?' She and her mother, shedding tears, said: 'Indeed, through our foolishness the secret is all but broken. And with the king's insistence, even after denying it two, three, or four times, the source will certainly be traced to you. Once you are implicated, our entire household will be ruined. And upon <s>Arthapati</s>, that dishonor is [already] fixed. And his association with us, that of a kīnāśa (base man), is well known in the city of <s>Aṅga</s>. By claiming that he gave it to us, it would be better to protect oneself.' Having made me agree, they went to the king's court. And when interrogated by the king, [she said]: 'This is not the way of the courtesan family, to name one's patron. For men do not approach courtesans only with righteously earned wealth' — having thus repeatedly and emphatically denied it, when threatened with cutting of ears and nose, the two scorched courtesans pointed to that wretched <s>Arthapati</s> himself as the thief. The angry king ordered his execution. But <s>Dhanamitra</s> himself, with joined palms, intervened: 'Sir, this <s>Mauryadatta</s> is the chief of merchants. For such offenses, separation from life is not proper. If you are angry, let this sinner be stripped of all possessions and banished.' From this, <s>Dhanamitra</s>'s fame spread. And the king was pleased. <s>Arthapati</s>, stripped to a mere rag, was banished publicly before all the citizens in his pride of wealth. And <s>Kāmamañjarī</s>, the poor woman, stripped of all possessions by the mirage of the leather-jewel, was graciously supported by the king at the urging of <s>Dhanamitra</s>, with some portion of that [confiscated] wealth. And on an auspicious day, <s>Dhanamitra</s> married <s>Kulapālikā</s>. Thus, with my plans accomplished, I filled the house of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s> with gold and jewels. And in this city, the class of greedy rich men was so thoroughly plundered that the one with a begging-bowl in hand wandered for alms to the houses of the very class of the formerly destitute that had been enriched by my own largesse. For even the most exceedingly clever man cannot transcend the line written by fate. For one day, savoring every sip of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>'s love, I was intoxicated to the point of losing myself. For the conduct of those maddened by pride and intoxication is to engage only in their habitual actions, even by unaccustomed paths. Being intoxicated beyond measure, I [declared]: 'I could impoverish this entire city in a single night and fill your house!' — overriding the hundred oaths and suppliant folded-hands of my terrified beloved, like a mad elephant that has violently broken its chains, accompanied by some old nurse nicknamed 'Jackal-woman,' with scant preparation and alone, I set out with great speed. The city guards who attacked me I fearlessly engaged. Though beaten by them as a thief, not overly angered, playing as it were, with my sword that had fallen from my hand in my intoxicated state, having killed just two or three, I fell, eyes rolling and reddened. Then the Jackal-woman, uttering cries of distress, came near me. I was bound by the enemies. But the calamity, which sobered me from my intoxication, instantly produced in me a presence of mind, and I reflected: 'Alas, this great disaster, rooted in delusion, has befallen me! And <s>Dhanamitra</s>'s friendship with me is widely known, and <s>Rāgamañjarī</s> is known as my consort. In my intoxication, both are exposed; tomorrow they will certainly be arrested. This then is the course of action by which, being carried out, those two will be saved from my direction. And perhaps someday they will rescue me from this calamity.' Having devised some stratagem by myself, I instructed the Jackal-woman: 'Go away, old woman! That courtesan burnt to ashes, that <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, whom my enemy <s>Dhanamitra</s>, under the guise of friendship, has brought together with the leather-jewel-maddened — she is a dead woman! That sinner — from the theft of the leather-jewel and from the theft of your daughter's excellent ornaments — today I would freely give up my life without a thorn of regret.' She, being an expert in emergency situations, a supreme rogue, with tears and a faltering voice and joined palms, approached those men with a bow and begged before me: 'Good sirs, wait a little while until I ascertain what of our property has been stolen by this man.' When they agreed, she came again to my side: 'Good sir, forgive this servant-girl for one offense. Let <s>Dhanamitra</s> be indeed the seat of enmity, the violator of your wife. But remembering her long service to you, please be gracious to your servant <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>. For the livelihood of those who live by beauty is their ornaments. So tell me, where have you hidden her jewelry?' — she fell at my feet. Then, as if taking pity, I said: 'Very well, what use to one about to die is pursuing this enmity?' And saying this, I whispered in her ear: 'Proceed exactly thus.' She, having grasped the meaning, [said]: 'May you live long; may the gods be gracious to you; may the king of <s>Aṅga</s> too, pleased by your valor, release you; may these good men also have compassion on you' — and in a moment she vanished. I was brought to the prison. The next day, coming with increased arrogance, self-satisfied and thinking himself handsome, having recently assumed his post after his father's death, not yet fully mature in the intoxication of youth, a certain city official named <s>Kāntaka</s>, having somewhat threatened me, said: 'If you do not return the leather-jewel to <s>Dhanamitra</s>, or if you do not return the stolen goods to the citizens, you shall see the end of the eighteen tortures and finally death itself.' But I, smiling, replied: 'Good sir, even if I were to give away wealth accumulated since birth, I would never fulfill the leather-jewel expectations of <s>Dhanamitra</s>, that enemy of mine in the guise of a friend, the violator of <s>Arthapati</s>'s wife. Without giving even a fraction, I would endure ten thousand tortures. This is my final position.' In the same manner, as the daily interrogation progressed — alternating between blandishments and threats — through receiving decent food and drink, within just a few days, having recovered and returned to normal health, I was well. Then one day, as the day was waning, with its sun still wearing the garment of the sky, the Jackal-woman came with a radiant complexion and splendid attire, her attendants standing at a distance, embraced me and said: 'Sir, by good fortune you are alive! Your wise policy has borne fruit.' Following my instructions, I had told <s>Dhanamitra</s> — she said that he had spoken thus: 'Sir, your friend has fallen into this state' — and he said: 'Today I have been arrested for a drinking offense easily gotten into through association with courtesans. You must unhesitatingly petition the king today itself: "Lord, by the grace of your majesty alone, the leather-jewel that was stolen by <s>Arthapati</s> was recovered before. But the husband of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, a certain gambling-sharp, because of his extreme cleverness in arts, poetry, and worldly affairs, was associated with me, and through that connection, by daily sending garments, ornaments, and gifts, I attended upon his wife. That suspicious, base-minded gambler grew angry. And he, being angry, stole the leather-jewel and also her cosmetic-box. But he, caught again while prowling for theft, was seized by the civic guard. And having been tracked by this distressed one, the maidservant of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, following old affections, the location of the jewel-deposit was told to her. If he would also give me back my leather-jewel, and if my lord's grace would be bestowed..."' Thus informed, the king, [I was sure,] would not part me from my life; rather, by inducements he would try to make me return everything. That is to our advantage.' Having heard this, and confident because of your influence, without excessive fear, he carried it all out exactly so. Then I, from <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, made credible by tokens of your identity, receiving the desired possessions, was winning over <s>Māṅgalikā</s>, the nurse of the princess <s>Ambālikā</s>, by the path you had indicated. Using her as a go-between, the friendship between <s>Rāgamañjarī</s> and <s>Ambālikā</s> grew exceedingly. Day after day, bringing ever-novel gifts, telling captivating stories, I became the supreme object of her favor. One day, when she had gone up to the terrace, I, while pretending to replace an ear-lotus that was supposedly slipping from its place, deliberately dislodged it, and then picking it up from the ground, by that pretext having entered the courtyard near the princess's quarters, laughing on the pretext of startling the pigeons from the dovecote openings above where <s>Kāntaka</s> had entered the courtyard of the palace for some reason, I burst out laughing. He too, thinking himself blessed, looking up slightly with a smile — the laughter caused by my contrivance directed at the princess — as if a coquettish gesture, an expression rooted in her own desire, he interpreted it so. By me too, a certain clever gesture was made as if by sign-language so that he would interpret it thus. Pierced by the god of love who had drawn his bow, struck by an arrow of uncertain aim, the very naive one somehow departed. In the evening, I had a maidservant deliver to <s>Kāntaka</s>'s house, via <s>Rāgamañjarī</s> as [supposed sender], a wicker basket containing betel, a pair of silk garments, ornamental items, and a ring stamped with the royal princess's seal. Plunged in the fathomless ocean of passion, he found me like a boat and was overjoyed. As I described to him the increasingly dire states of the princess, that fool was intoxicated from afar. Pressed by him, I brought the next day — supposedly sent by your beloved — my own chewed betel-remnant, body-ointment, wilted garland, and soiled garment, as if from the princess. And his own [gifts] were taken as if meant for the princess and secretly carried away. Thus, with his fire of love stoked, he was taken aside by me one day and counseled: 'Sir, the very signs are undeceiving. For my next-door neighbor, a certain astrologer, [has said]: "Both <s>Kāntaka</s> and this princess desire you. She, the only daughter, and the king — even upon discovering you together — though angered, will not destroy you for fear of his daughter's death. On the contrary, he will bestow the position of crown prince. Thus this venture is one that leads to further gain. Why then, my lord, do you not pursue it? If you cannot conceive a means of entering the princess's quarters, surely the wall of the prison is adjacent to that of the royal garden. By having some skilled hand-worker dig a tunnel of that length, once you have entered the garden, your protection from above is entirely in our hands. For her retinue, deeply devoted to her, will not betray the secret."' He said: 'Well said, dear friend, you have shown the way. There is a certain thief, in the art of digging one of the very sons of <s>Sagara</s>, as it were. If he can be obtained, he will accomplish this work in a moment.' 'Who is he and how can he be obtained?' — when I asked, 'The one who stole <s>Dhanamitra</s>'s leather-jewel' — he pointed to me myself. 'If that is so, come — if he accomplishes this task, I shall by various means secure his release' — thus, having extracted an oath from him, for the purpose of the venture, having me put back in chains, [he told the king]: 'That spy is fully in hand, but he is not of bold disposition. The one with the deepest enmity — he will reveal the leather-jewel' — thus informing the king, [and me saying]: 'You will execute him by elaborate means, and thereby the property will be recovered, and the secret will not leak' — overjoyed at this, he accepted, and saying 'The little I have said is nothing; your policy here is the greater part — bring him,' and I, pleased, said: 'Bring him.' Then, when he was brought, an oath was made for my release. And I was also made to swear secrecy. Having been given bathing, food, and ointments, from the perpetual darkness of the prison corner, I dug a tunnel with a serpent-mouth [tool]. And I thought: 'This man made the oath for my release with the very intention of killing me. Therefore, even having killed him, I am not touched by the sin of falsehood.' As I was emerging and he was extending his hands to put me in chains again, I struck him on the chest with my foot, and as he fell, I cut off his head with his own scimitar. I told the Jackal-woman: 'Tell me, dear woman, what is the layout of the princess's quarters? This is a great effort — let it not be in vain. I shall steal something there and return.' Having entered the women's inner quarters according to the layout she described, while jeweled lamps were blazing, amid other attendants deeply asleep from the fatigue of many diversions, upon a couch with legs fashioned like lion-figures inlaid with magnificent costly gems, furnished with bedding and pillows stuffed with swan's down, its edges strewn with flowers — I beheld the princess: the top of one foot tucked under the heel of the right foot, the ankles slightly turned with sweet joints, the shanks mutually embraced, both soft knees drawn up with the pair of thighs slightly wavering, the girdle-zone deeply sunk into the hips, delicate at the tip of one vine-like arm released and dangling from the drooping buttocks, the other vine-like arm with its bud-like hand turned palm upward — bent at the far end of a support, clad in closely fitting Chinese silk undergarment, the slender waist not overly curved, the firm lotus-buds of her breasts trembling with the onset of deep breaths, a ruby pendant strung on a thread of refined gold visible at the region of the gorgeously curved neck, an earring half-visible nestled in the hair by the lower ear, the loosened hair-knot yellowed and pierced by the clusters of rays from the jeweled earring turned above the ear-lobe, the gap between the upper and lower lips barely discernible in the radiance of her own luminosity, the cheek-surface showing the function of an ear-ornament through the hand-sprout resting there, a decorative mark created by the pattern of the ornamental canopy-leaf adhering to the mirror-surface of the upper cheek, the blue-lotus eyes gently closed, the banner of the eyebrows untroubled, the loosened sandal-paste forehead-mark broken by sprouting drops of perspiration and goose-bumps, curling locks facing the moon of her countenance — trustingly deep in sleep, mostly submerged on one side in the exceedingly white coverlet, motionless from the weariness of long sport, like a flash of lightning reposing in the lap of an autumn cloud — I beheld the princess. Having seen her, with passion for <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love) flaring up, startled, with no desire left for stealing, my heart being stolen by her alone, bewildered as to what to do, I stood for a moment. And I reflected: 'If I cannot obtain this beautiful-eyed one, the friend of spring (<s>Kāma</s>) will not permit me to live. But if touched without prior arrangement, this very young girl will surely cry out in distress and destroy my hopes.'

atha niśīthe bhūya eva vāyunighnaḥ "nihatya kāntakaṃ nṛpatiduhitrā rameya' iti raṃhasā pareṇa rājapathamabhyapatat /
nirūpya cāhaṃ putramevaṅgatamasyāṃ velāyāmanudhāvāmi /
tatprasīdata /
baddhvainaṃ mahyamarpayata' iti yāvadasaukrandati tāvadahaṃ "sthavire, kena devo mātariśvā baddhapūrvaḥ /
kimete kākāḥśauṅgeyasya me nigrahītāraḥ /
śāntaṃ pāpam' ityabhyadhāvam /
asāvapyamībhiḥ "tvamevonmattā yānunmatta ityunmattaṃ muktadavatī /
kastamidānīṃ badhnāti' iti ninditā kadarthitā rudatyevamāmanvadhāvat /
gatvā ca rāgamañjarīgṛhaṃ ciravirahakhedavihvalāmimāṃ bahuvidhaṃ samāśvāsya taṃ niśāśeṣamanayam /
pratyūṣe punarudārakeṇa ca samagacche /
atha bhagavantaṃ marīciṃ veśakṛcchudutthāya punaḥ pratitaptatapaḥprabhāvapratyāpannādivyacakṣuṣamupasaṃgamya tenāsmyevaṃbhūtatvaddarśanamavagamitaḥ /
siṃhaghoṣaśca kāntakāpacāraṃ nirbhidya tatapade prasannena rājñā pratiṣṭhāpitaḥ tenaiva cārakasuraṅgāpathena kanyāpurapraveśaṃ bhūyo 'pi me samapādayat /
samagaṃsi cāhaṃ śṛgālikāmukhaniḥsṛtavārtānuraktayā rājaduhitrā /
taṣveve divaseṣu caṇḍavarmā siṃhavarmāvadhūtaduhitṛprārthanaḥ kupito 'bhiyujya puramavāruṇat /
amarṣaṇaścāṅgarājo yāvadariḥ pāragrāmikaṃ vidhimācikīrṣati tāvatsvayameva prākāraṃ nirbhidya pratyāsannānapi sahāyānapratīkṣamāṇo nirgatyābhyadhikabalena vidviṣā mahati saṃparāye bhinnavarmā siṃhavarmā balādagṛhyata /
ambālikā ca balavadabhigṛhya caṇḍavarmaṇā haṭhātpariṇetumātmabhavanamanīyat /
kautukaṃ ca sa kila kṣapāvasāne vivāha ityabadhnāt /
ahaṃ ca dhanamitragṛhe tadvivāhāyaiva pinaddhamaṅgalapratisarastamevamavocam-"sakhe, samāpatitamevāṅgarājābhisaraṃ rājamaṇḍalam /
sugūḍhameva saṃbhūya pauravṛddhaistadupāvartaya /
upāvṛttaśca kṛttaśirasameva śutruṃ drakṣyasi' iti /
"tathā' iti tenābhyupagate gatāyuṣo 'muṣya bhavanamutsavākulamupasamādhīyamānapariṇayopakaraṇamistataḥ praveśanirgamapravṛttalokasaṃbādhamalakṣyaśastrikaḥ saha praviśya maṅgalapāṭhakairambalikāpāṇipallavamagnau sākṣiṇyātharvaṇena vidhinārpyamāṇamāditsamānasyāyāminaṃ bāhuduṇḍamākṛṣya cchurikayorasi prāharṣam /
sphurataśca katipayānanyānapi yamaviṣayamagamayam /
hatavidhvastadaṃ ca tadgṛhaman vicaranvepamānamadhuragātrīṃ viśālalocanāmabhiniśāmya tadāliṅganasukhamanububhūṣustāmādāya garbhagṛhamavikṣam /
children.translated_text: Then, roaming through that house where [the enemy forces] had been slain and routed, I beheld a trembling, sweet-limbed, large-eyed maiden, and desiring to experience the bliss of her embrace, I took her and entered the inner chamber.

children.text: asminneva kṣaṇe tavāsmi navāmbuvāhastanitagambhīreṇa svareṇānugṛhītaḥ' iti /
children.translated_text: At that very moment, I was graced by your [Majesty's] voice, deep as the rumbling of a fresh rain-cloud.'

children.text: śrutvā ca smitvā ca devo 'pi rajavāhanaḥ "kathamasi kārkasyena karṇīsutamapyatikrāntaḥ' ityabhidhāya punaravekṣyopahāravarmāṇam ācakṣva, tavedānīmavasaraḥ' ityabhāṣata /
children.translated_text: Having heard this, the lord <s>Rājavāhana</s> too smiled and said: 'How is it that by your audacity you have surpassed even the son of <s>Karṇī</s> [i.e., the legendary thief]!' Then, looking again [at the assembly], he said: '<s>Upahāravarmā</s>, speak now — this is your turn.'

children.text: so 'pi sasmitaṃ praṇasyārabhatābhidhātum // Dkc_2,2 //
children.translated_text: He too, smiling and bowing, began to narrate.

Having used from a golden casket a betel-roll stored with <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) and a pellet of camphor, and a <s>pārijātaka</s> (coral-tree) flower, I drew with the <s>alaktaka</s>-reddened fluid, without spitting, a pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds on the auspicious wall. Having also exchanged rings, I somehow made my way out. Returning through the underground passage to the prison, I advised the imprisoned noble citizen named <s>Siṃhaghoṣa</s>, who had become my friend during those very days — 'I, the wretched one, have killed <s>Kāntaka</s>; therefore, you should break open the secret [passage] and obtain your freedom' — and with <s>Śṛgālikā</s> (the vixen/female companion), I emerged. On the royal highway, I was seized by the guards. I thought: 'I am indeed swift enough to escape without being touched by these men. But this poor girl would be captured. Therefore, this is the right course here.' Rushing back toward those very [guards], standing with my back turned, placing my elbows on my own back, I said: 'Good sirs, if I am a thief, then bind me. This is your jurisdiction, but not over this elderly woman.' She, her intention having been thus elevated, approaching them with a bow, [said]: 'Good sirs, this is my son who was seized by a wind-disease and was long treated. The day before yesterday, he became almost calm and returned to his normal state. I, having developed confidence, brought him out from confinement, bathed and anointed him, dressed him in a pair of unsewn garments, fed him the best food, and on the <s>Auśīra</s> day he was allowed to roam freely. But at midnight, again struck by the wind-disease, [thinking] "having killed <s>Kāntaka</s>, I shall sport with the king's daughter," he rushed with great speed onto the royal highway. Having observed my son in this state, I am chasing after him at this hour. Therefore, be gracious — bind him and hand him over to me.' While she was still crying out thus, I [shouted]: 'Old woman, who has ever before bound the god <s>Vāyu</s> (Wind)? Are these crows to restrain me, a born <s>Śauṅgeya</s>? Heaven forbid this evil!' — and I ran. She too, rebuked and humiliated by them — [saying] 'You yourself are mad, [you] who let a madman go free [saying] he is mad. Who will bind him now?' — weeping, she followed me. Having gone to the house of <s>Rāgamañjarī</s>, I consoled this one who was distressed from long separation in many ways, and passed the rest of that night. At dawn, I met again with the youth [<s>Udāraka</s>]. Then, having risen early, I approached the blessed <s>Marīci</s>, the disguise-maker, who had regained his divine vision through the power of his re-performed austerities, and was informed by him about such-and-such a form of your [Majesty's] appearance. <s>Siṃhaghoṣa</s>, having broken open [the prison through] the offense of <s>Kāntaka</s>, was established in that [man's] position by the delighted king, and he arranged my entry into the women's quarters again through that very spy-tunnel path. And I was united with the king's daughter, who was enamored through the reports issued from <s>Śṛgālikā</s>'s mouth. In those very days, <s>Caṇḍavarman</s>, angered by <s>Siṃhavarman</s>'s rejection of his suit for [the king's] daughter, attacked and besieged the city. And the fierce king of <s>Aṅga</s>, while the enemy was about to perform a ritual for foreign [gods], himself broke through the rampart, and without waiting even for allies who were nearby, went forth — and in a great battle against a superior enemy force, <s>Siṃhavarman</s>, his armor shattered, was forcibly captured. <s>Ambālikā</s> too was forcibly seized by <s>Caṇḍavarman</s> and taken to his own palace to be married by force. And he set the auspicious time for the wedding at the end of the night. I, at the house of my friend <s>Dhanamitra</s>, where the auspicious threads had been fastened for that very wedding, spoke to him thus: 'Friend, the circle of kings allied with the king of <s>Aṅga</s> has already arrived. In utmost secrecy, assemble the city elders and have them turn [their allegiance] back. Once they have turned, you will see the enemy with his head cut off.' When he agreed [saying] 'So be it,' I entered the doomed one's mansion — bustling with festive preparations, with wedding paraphernalia being arranged, with people coming and going creating a press of crowds — with my weapons concealed, entering along with [the crowd]. When the officiating priests were placing the sprouting hand of <s>Ambālikā</s> in the fire as witness, according to the <s>Atharvaṇa</s> (Vedic) rite, as he was about to seize it — I pulled back his long arm by force and struck him in the chest with a dagger. And several others who were convulsing I dispatched to the realm of <s>Yama</s> (death).

iti śrīdaṇḍinaḥ kṛtau daśakumāracarite 'pahāravarmacaritaṃ nāma dvitīya ucchvāsaḥ

children.translated_text: Thus, in the composition of the illustrious <s>Daṇḍin</s>, in the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s>, [this is] the second chapter (<s>ucchvāsa</s>) named 'The Adventures of <s>Apahāravarmā</s>.'

tṛtīyocchvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Third Chapter (<s>Tṛtīyocchvāsa</s>).

children.text:
eṣo 'smi paryaṭannekadā gato videheṣu /
mitilāmapraviśyaiva bahiḥ kvacinmaṭhikāyāṃ viśramitumetya kayāpi vṛddhatāpasyā dattapādyaḥ kṣaṇamalindabhūmāvavāsthiṣi /
tasyāstu maddarśanādeva kimapyābaddhadhāramaśru prāvartata /
"kimetadamba, kathaya kāraṇam' iti pṛṣṭā sakaruṇamācaṣṭa--"jaivātṛka, nanu śrūyate pātirasyā mithilāyāḥ prāharavarmā nāmāsīt /
tasya khalu magadharājo rājahaṃsaḥ paraṃ mitramāsīt /
tayośca vallabhe balaśambalayoriva vasumatīpriyaṃvade sakhyamapratimamadhattām /
atha prathamagarbābhinanditāṃ tāṃ ca priyasakhīṃ didṛkṣuḥ priyaṃvadā vasumatīṃ saha bhartrā puṣpapuramagamat /
tasminneva ca samaye mālavena magadharājasya mahajjanyamajani /
tatra leśato 'pi durlakṣyāṃ gatimagamanmagadharājaḥ, maithilendrastu mālavendraprayatnaprāṇitaḥ svaviṣayaṃ pratinivṛtto jyeṣṭhasya saṃhāravarmaṇaḥ sutairvikaṭavarmaprabhṛtibhirvyāptaṃ rājyamākarṇya svasrīyātsuhyapaterdaṇḍāvayavamāditsuraṭavīpadamavagāhyalubdhakaluptasarvasvo 'bhūt /
tatsutena ca kanīyasā hastavartinā sahaikākinā vanacaraśaravarṣabhayapalāyitā vanamagāhiṣi /
tatra ca me śārdūlanakhāvalījhanipatitāyāḥ pāṇibhraṣṭaḥ sa bālakaḥ kasyāpi kapilāśavasya kroḍamabhyalīyata /
tacchavākarṣiṇaśca vyāghrasyāsūniṣuriṣvasanayantramuktaḥ kṣaṇādalikṣat /
bhilladārakaiḥsa bālo 'pāhāri /
sātvahaṃ mohasuptā kenāpi vṛṣṇipālenopanīya svaṃ kuṭīramāveśyakṛpayopakrāntavraṇā svasthībhūya svabharturantikamupatiṣṭhāsurasahāyatayā yāvadvyākulībhavāmi tāvanmamaiva duhītā saha yūnā kenāpi tamevoddeśamāgamat /
sā bhṛśaṃ rūroda /
ruditānte ca sā sārthaghāte svahastagatasya rājaputrasya kirātabhartṛhastagamanam, ātmanaśca kenāpi vanacareṇa vraṇaviropaṇam, svasthāyāśca punastenopayantuṃ cintitāyā nikṛṣṭajātisaṃsargavaiklavyātpratyākhyānapāruṣyam, tadakṣaṇeṇa cāmunā vivikte vipine svaśiraḥ- kartanodyamam, anena yūnā yadṛcchayā dṛṣṭena tasya durātmano hananam, ātmanaścopayamanamityakathayat /
sa tu pṛṣṭo maithilendrasyaiva ko 'pi sevakaḥ kāraṇavilambī tanmārgānusāri jātaḥ /
saha tena bharturantikamupasṛtya putravṛttāntena śrotramasya devyāḥ priyaṃvadāyāścādahāva /
sa ca rājā diṣṭadoṣājjyeṣṭhaputraiściraṃ vigṛhya punarasahiṣṇutayātimātraṃ ciraṃ prayudhya baddhaḥ /
devī ca bandhanaṃ gamitā /
dagdhā punarahamasminnapivārdhake hatajīvitamapārayantī hātuṃ pravrajyāṃ kilāgrahīpam /
duhītā tu mama hatajīvitākṛṣṭā vikaṭavarmamahādevī kalpasundarī kilāśiśriyat /
tau cedrājaputraunirupadravāvevāvardhiṣyetām, iyatā kālena tavemāṃ vayovasthāmamprakṣyetām /
tayośca satorna dāyādā narendrasya prasahyakāriṇo bhaveyuḥ' iti pramanyurabhiruroda /
śrutvā ca tāpasīgiramahamapi pravṛddhavāppo nigṛḍhamabhyadhām-"yadyevamamba, samāśvasihi /
nanvanti kaścinmunistvayā tadavasthayā putrābhyupapādanārthaṃ yācitastena sa labdho vardhataśca /
vārteyamatimahatī /
kimanayā /
so 'hamasmi /
śakyaśca mayāsau vikaṭavarmā yatākathañcidupaśliṣya vyāpādayitum /
anujāḥ punaratibahavaḥ, tairapi ghaṭante paurajānapadāḥ /
māṃ tu na kaścidihatyarḥ idṛktayā jano jānāti /
pitarāvapi tāvanmāṃ na saṃvidāte, kimutetare tamenamarthamupāyena sādhayiṣyāmi' ityagādipam /
sā tu harṣanirbharanipīḍitā ciraṃ prarudya bahuṃ vilapya śāntā punaḥ svamātrā rājāntaḥpuravṛttāntākhyāne nyayujyata /
uktaṃ ca tayā-"kumāra,kāmarūpeśvarasya kalindavarmanāmnaḥ kanyā kalpasundarī kalāsu rūpe cāpsaraso 'payatikrāntā patimabhibhūya vartate /
tadekavallabhaḥ, sa tu bahvavarodho 'pi vikaṭavarmā' iti /
tāmavocam-"upasarpaināṃ matprayuktairgandhamālyaiḥ /
upajanayacāsamānadoṣanindādinā svabhartari dveṣam /
anurūpabhartṛgāminīnāṃ ca vāsavadattādīnāṃ varṇanena grāhayānuśayam /
avarodhanāntareṣu ca rājño vilasitāni sugūḍhānyapi prayatnenānvipya prakāśayantī mānasasyā vardhaya' iti /
punaridamambāmavocam-"itthameva tvayāpyananyavyāpārayā nṛpāṅganāsāvupasthātavyā /
pratyahaṃ ca yadyatra vṛttaṃ tadasmi tvayaiva bodhyaḥ, maduktā punariyamudarkasvāduno 'smatkarmaṇaḥ prasādhanāya cchāyevānayāyinī kalpasundarīmanuvartatām' iti /
tena ca tamarthaṃ tathaivānvatiṣṭhatām /
keṣuciddineṣu gateṣvācaṣṭa māṃ madambā "vatsa, mādhavīva picumandāśleṣiṇī yathāsau śocyamātmānaṃ manyeta tathopapādya sthāpitā /
kiṃ bhūyaḥ kṛtyam' iti /
punarahamabhilikhyātmanaḥ pratikṛtam "ityamamuṣyai neyā /
nītāṃ caināṃ nirvarṇya sā niyatamevaṃ vakṣyati /
"nanvasti kaścidīdṛśākāraḥ pumān' iti /
pratibrūhyenām-"yadi syāttataḥ kim' iti /
tasya yaduttaraṃ sā dāsyati "tadahamasmi pratibodhanīyaḥ' iti /
sā "tathā iti rājakulamupasaṃkramya pratinivṛttā māmekānte nyavedayat-"vatsa, darśito 'sau citrapaṭastasyai mattakāśinyai /
citrīyamāṇā cāsau bhuvanamidaṃ sanāthīkṛtaṃ yaddeve 'pi kusumadhanvani nedṛśī vapuḥśrīḥ saṃnidhatte /
citrametaccitrataram /
na ca tamavaimi yar idṛśamidamihatyo nirmimīte /
kenedamālikhitam, ityādṛtavatī vyāhṛtavatī ca /
mayā ca smerayodīritam-"devi, sadṛśamājñāpayasi /
bhagavānmakaraketurapyevaṃsundaraṃ iti na śakyameva saṃbhavāyitum /
atha ca vistīrṇeyamarṇavanemiḥ /
kvacidīdṛśamapi rūpaṃ daivaśaktyā saṃbhavet /
atha tu yadyevaṃrūpo rūpānurūpaśilpaśīlavidayājñānakauśalo yuvā mahākulīnaśca kaścitsaṃnihitaḥ syāt, sa kiṃ lapsyate' iti /
tayoktam-"amba, kiṃ bravīmi /
śarīraṃ hṛdayaṃ jīvitamiti sarvamidamalpamanarhaṃ ca /
tato na kiñcillapsyate na cedayaṃ vipralambhastasyāmupya darśanānubhavena yathedaṃ cakṣuścaritārthaṃ bhavettathānugrahaḥ kāryaḥ' iti /
bhūyo 'pi mayā dṛḍhatarīkartumupanyastam-"asti ko 'pi rājasūnurnigūḍhaṃ caran /
amupya vasantotsave sahasakhībhirnagaropavanavihāriṇīratiriva vigrahiṇī yadṛcchayā darśanapathaṃ gatāsi /
gataścāsau kāmaśaraikalakṣyatāṃ māmanvavartiṣṭa /
mayā ca vāmanyonyānurūpairanyadurlabhairākārādibhirguṇātiśayaiśca preryamāṇayā tadracitaireva kusumaśekharasraganulepanādibhiściramupāsitāsi /
sādṛśyaṃ ca svamanena svayamevābhilikhya tvatsamādhigāḍhatvadarśanāya preṣitam /
eṣa cedartho niścitastasyāmupyātimānuṣaprāṇasattavaprajñāprakarṣasya na kiñcidduṣkaraṃ nāma /
tamadyaiva darśayeyam /
saṃketo deyaḥ' iti /
tayā tadu kiñcidiva dhyātvā punarabhihitam--"amba, tava naitadidānīṃ gopyatam /
ataḥ kathayāmi /
mama tātasya rājña prahāravarmaṇā saha mahatī prītirāsīt /
mātuśca me mānavatyāḥ priyavayasyā devī priyaṃvadāsīt /
tābhyāṃ punarajātāpatyābhyāmevakṛtaḥ samayo 'bhūt--"āvayoḥ putramatyāḥ putarāya duhitṛmatyā duhitā deyā' iti /
tātastu māṃ jātāṃ pranaṣṭāpatyā priyaṃvadeti prārthayamānāya vikaṭavarmaṇe daivāddattavān /
ayaṃ ca niṣṭhuraḥ pitṛdrohī nāpyupapannasaṃsthānaḥ kāmopacāreṣvalabdhavaicakṣaṇyaḥ kalāsu kāvyanāṭakādiṣu mandābhiniveśaḥ sauryonmādī durvikatthano 'nṛtavādī cāsthānavarpī /
nātirocate ma eṣa bhartā viśeṣataścaiṣu vāsareṣu yadayamudyāne madantaraṅgabhūtāṃ puṣkarikāmapyupāntavartinīmanādṛtya mayi baddhasāpatnyamatasarāmanātmajñāmātmanāṭakīyāṃ ramayantikāṃ nāmāpatyanirviśeṣaṃ matsaṃvardhitāyāścampakalatāyāṃ svayamavacitābhiḥ sumanobhiralamakārṣit /
madupabhuktamukte citrakūṭagarbhavedikāgate ratnatasya tayā saha vyahārṣit /
ayogyaśca pumānavajñātaṃ ca pravṛttaḥ /
tatkimityapekṣyate paralokabhayaṃ caihikena duḥkhenāntaritam /
aviṣahyaṃ hi yoṣitāmanaṅgaśaraniṣaṅgībhūtacetasāmaniṣṭajanasaṃvāsayantraṇāduḥkham /
ato 'munā puruṣeṇa mamādyodyānamādhavīgṛhe samāgamaya /
tadvārthāśravaṇamātreṇaiva hi mamātimātraṃ mano 'nuraktam /
asti cāyamartharāśiḥ /
anenāmupya pade pratiṣṭhāpya tamevātyantamupacarya jīviṣyāmi' iti /
mayāpi tadabhyupetya pratyāgatam /
ataḥ paraṃ bhartṛdārakaḥ pramāṇam' iti /
tatastasyā eva sakāśādantaḥpuraniveśamantarvaṃśikapuruṣasthān pramadavanapradeśānapi vibhāgenāvagamya, astagirikūṭapātakṣubhitaśoṇita iva śoṇībhavati bhānubimbe, paścimāmbudhiṣayaḥpātanirvāpitapataṅgāṅgāradhūmasaṃbhāra iva bharitanabhasitamasi vijṛmbhate, paradāraparāmarśonmukhasya mamācāryakamiva kartumutthite guruparigrahaślāghini grahāgresare kṣapākare, kalpasundarīvadanapuṇḍarīkeṇeva maddarśanātirāgaprathamopanatena smayamānena candramaṇḍalena saṃdhukṣyamāṇatejasi bhuvanavijigīṣodyate deve kusumadhanvani, yatocitaṃ śayanīyamabhaje /
vyacīcaraṃ ca-"siddhaprāya evāyamarthaḥ /
kintu parakalatralaṅghānāddharmapīḍā bhavet, sāpyarthakāmayordvayorupalambheśāstrakārairanumataiveti /
gurujanabandhamokṣopāyasaṃdhinā mayā caipa vyatikramaḥ kṛtaḥ, tadapi pāpaṃ nirhṛtya kiyatyāpi dharmakalayā māṃ samagrayediti /
api tvetadākarṇya devo rājavāhanaḥ suhṛdo vā kiṃ nu vakṣyanti' iti cintāparādhīna eva nidrayā parāmṛśye /
adṛsyata ca svapno hastivakro bhagavān /

arīramaṃ cānaṅgarāgapeśalaviśālalocanām /

aśrumukhī tu sā "yadi prāyāsi nātha, prayātameva me jīvitaṃ gaṇaya /
naya māmapi /

atha cālayiṣyasi ghaṇṭām /

sa niyatamabhyupaiṣyati /

avasitaśca paśurasau /

akūjacaca sā taṃ janaṃ kṛtāntadṛtīvāhvayantī /
prāvartiṣi cāhamagurucandanapramukhāni hotum /
āyāsīcca rājā yathoktaṃ deśam /
śaṅkāpannamiva kiñcitsavismayaṃ vicārya tiṣṭhantamabravam--"brūhi satyaṃ bhūyo 'pi me bhagavantaṃ citrabhānumeva sākṣīkṛtya /

smitvā punarmayoktam--"kiṃ vā śapathena /

so 'bravīt--"asti baddho matpituḥ kanīyānbhrātā prahāravarmā /

pauravṛddhaśca pāñcālikaḥ paritrātaśca sārthavāhaḥ svanatināmno yavanādvajramekaṃ vasuṃdharāmūlyaṃ ladhīyasārdheṇa labhyamiti mamaikānte 'mantrayetām /
gṛhapatiśca mamāntaraṅgabhūto janapadamahattaraḥ śatahaliralīkavādaśīlamavalepavantaṃ duṣṭagrāmaṇyamanantasīraṃ janapadakopena ghātayeyamiti daṇḍadharānuddhārakarmaṇi matprayogānniyoktumabhyupāgamat /
itthamidamaciraprastutaṃ rahasyam' /
ityākarṇya-tam "iyattavāyuḥ /

abhūccāsau bhasmasāt /
atha strīsvabhāvādīṣadvihvalāṃ hṛdayavallabhāṃ samāśvāsya hastakisalaye 'valambya gatvā tadgṛhamanujñayāsyāḥ sarvāṇyantaḥpurāṇyāhūya sadya eva sevāṃ dattavān /
savismitavilāsinīsārthamadhye kañcidvihṛtya kālaṃ visṛṣṭāvarodhamaṇḍalastāmeva saṃhatorūmūrūpapīḍaṃ bhujopapīḍaṃ copaguhya talpe 'bhiramayannalpāmiva tāṃ niśāmatyanaiṣam /
alabhe ca tanmukhāttadrājakulasya śīlam /
uṣasi snātvā kṛtamaṅgalo mantribhiḥ saha samagacche /
tāṃścābravam--"āryāḥ, rūpeṇaiva saha parivṛttau mama svabhāvaḥ /
ya eva viṣānnena hantu cintitaḥ patā me sa muktvā svametadrājyaṃ bhūya eva grāhayitavyaḥ /
pitṛvadamuṣminvayaṃ śuśrūṣayaiva vartāmahe /
na hyasti pitṛvadhātparaṃ pātakam' iti /
bhrātaraṃ ca viśālavarmāṇamāhūyoktavān--"vatsa, na subhikṣāḥ sāṃprataṃ puṇḍrāḥ te duḥkhamohopahatāstyaktātmāno rāṣṭraṃ no na samṛddhamabhidraveyuḥ /
ato muṣṭivadhaḥ sasyavadho vā yadotpadyate tadābhiyāsyasi, nādya yātrā yuktā' iti /
nagaravṛddhāvapyavalāpiṣam--"alpīyasā mūlyena mahārhaṃ vastu māstu me labhyaṃ dharmarakṣāyai, tadanuguṇenaiva mūlyenādaḥ krīyatām' iti /
śatahaliṃ ca rāṣṭramukhyamāhūyākhyātavān--"yo 'sāvanantasīraḥ prahāravarmaṇaḥ pakṣa iti nināśayiṣitaḥ, so 'pi pitari me prakṛtisthi kimiti nāśyeta, tattvayāpi tasminsaṃrambho na kāryaḥ' iti /
ta ime sarvamābhijñānikamupalabhya "sa evāyam' iti niścinvānā vismayamānāśca māṃ mahādevīṃ ca praśaṃsanto mantrabalāni coddhopayanto bandhanātpitarau niṣkrāmayya svaṃ rājyaṃ pratyapādayan /
ahaṃ ca tayā me dhātryā sarvamidaṃ mamāceṣṭitaṃ rahasi pitroravagamayya praharṣakāṣṭhādhirūḍhayostayoḥ pādamūlamabhaje /
abhajye ca yauvarājyalakṣmyā tadanujñātayā /
