abhavaṃ ca bhūmitsvatpādalakṣmīsākṣātkriyāmahotsavānandarāśeḥ' iti /

śrutvaitaddevo rājavāhanaḥ sanmitamavādīt--"paśyata pāratalpikamupadhiyuktamapi gurujanūndhavyasanamuktihetutayā duṣṭāmitrapramāpaṇābhyupāyatayā rājyopalabdhimūlatayā ca puṣkalāvarthadharmāvapyarīradhat /
children.translated_text: Having heard this, Lord <s>Rājavāhana</s> spoke approvingly: 'Behold! Though the stratagem of sleeping on another's wife's bed was employed through deception, [<s>Upahāravarman</s>] nourished both abundant wealth and <s>dharma</s> — as a means of freeing his elders from affliction, as a stratagem for destroying wicked enemies, and as the root-cause of obtaining a kingdom /

children.text: kiṃ hi buddhimatprayuktaṃ nābhyupaiti śobhām' iti /
children.translated_text: For what, when employed by the wise, does not attain splendor?' /

children.text: arthapālamukhe nidhāya snigdhadīrghāṃ dṛṣṭim "ācaṣṭāṃ bhavānātmīyacaritam' ityādideśa /
children.translated_text: Placing his affectionate, lingering gaze upon the face of <s>Arthapāla</s>, he commanded: 'Let your honor narrate your own adventures.' /

children.text: so 'pi baddhāñjalirabhidadhe // Dkc_2,3 //
children.translated_text: He too, with hands joined in salutation, began to speak. // Dkc_2,3 //

Here I am! Once while wandering I went to the land of the <s>Videhas</s>. Without entering <s>Mithilā</s> itself, I went outside to rest at some hermitage and, having been offered water for the feet by an aged female ascetic, sat for a moment on the veranda. At the very sight of me, tears began to flow from her eyes in an unbroken stream. When I asked, 'What is this, mother? Tell me the reason,' she spoke with compassion: 'My child, it is heard that the lord of this <s>Mithilā</s> was one named <s>Prāharavarman</s>. The king of <s>Magadha</s>, <s>Rājahaṃsa</s>, was indeed his closest friend. And their wives, <s>Vasumatī</s> and <s>Priyaṃvadā</s>, had an incomparable friendship, like that of <s>Bala</s> and <s>Śambala</s>. Then, wishing to see her dear friend who was rejoicing in her first pregnancy, <s>Priyaṃvadā</s> went with her husband to <s>Puṣpapura</s>. At that very time, a great battle arose between the <s>Mālava</s> lord and the king of <s>Magadha</s>. There, the king of <s>Magadha</s> went to a fate untraceable even in the slightest. The lord of <s>Maithila</s>, however, spared by the efforts of the lord of <s>Mālava</s>, returned to his own territory. Learning that the kingdom had been seized by the sons of his elder [brother] <s>Saṃhāravarman</s>, led by <s>Vikaṭavarman</s> and others, he entered the wilderness seeking military support from his brother-in-law, the lord of <s>Suhma</s>, and was stripped of everything by forest robbers. Alone with his younger son, who was in his arms, fleeing from a rain of arrows by forest-dwellers, I entered the deep forest. There, when I was struck by the claws of a tiger and fell, the boy slipped from my hands and hid in the lap of some tawny-colored corpse. An arrow released from a bow-machine instantly killed the tiger that was dragging that corpse. The boy was carried off by <s>Bhilla</s> children. As for me, fallen unconscious, I was carried by some cowherd to his hut, where my wounds were treated with compassion. Having recovered, as I was growing anxious due to my helplessness in wishing to reach my husband, my own daughter arrived at that very place with some young man. She wept bitterly. After her weeping ended, she narrated how, during the plundering of the caravan, the royal prince who had been in her hands had passed into the hands of a <s>Kirāta</s> chieftain; how her own wounds had been healed by some forest-dweller; how, when she had recovered and was thinking of going to him again, she had been harshly rejected due to the distress of association with a person of low birth; how at that very moment, in a secluded forest, he had attempted to cut off his own head; how this young man, who had chanced to see him, killed that villain and then married her. That [young man], when questioned, turned out to be some servant of the king of <s>Maithila</s> himself, who had been delayed by circumstances and had followed the same path. Together with him, having reached the presence of [my] husband, we burned his ears and those of Queen <s>Priyaṃvadā</s> with the account of our son. That king, after long conflict with his elder sons due to the fault of fate, and again fighting excessively in his intolerability, was captured. The queen too was imprisoned. And I, reduced to ashes, unable in this old age to endure the ruination of my life, took to the life of a wandering ascetic. My daughter, drawn away with her ruined life, took refuge with <s>Kalpasundarī</s>, the chief queen of <s>Vikaṭavarman</s>. If those two princes had grown up without calamity, by now they would have reached your age. And with them alive, the successors of the king would not have been violent usurpers' — thus she wept with great indignation. Hearing the words of the ascetic woman, I too, with tears swelling, said in secret: 'If that is so, mother, take comfort! Was there not some sage whom you, in that situation, entreated for the purpose of providing a son? By him that [son] was obtained and is growing up. This is news of the greatest import. What [use] is this [grief]? I am he. And I am able to somehow approach and destroy that <s>Vikaṭavarman</s> by getting close to him. The younger brothers are very numerous; the townspeople and country-folk also side with them. No one here of such [low] status knows me. Even my parents, for the time being, do not recognize me — how much less others! I shall accomplish this matter by stratagem.' She, overcome with joy, wept for a long time, lamented much, then calmed down, and was engaged by my mother in narrating the affairs of the royal inner palace. She said: 'Prince, the daughter of the king of <s>Kāmarūpa</s>, named <s>Kalindavarman</s>, [is] <s>Kalpasundarī</s>, who has surpassed even the celestial nymphs in arts and beauty, and dominates her husband. He has her as sole beloved, yet that <s>Vikaṭavarman</s>, though having many wives...' I said to her: 'Approach her with perfumes and garlands sent by me. Generate hatred toward her own husband through censure of their common faults. And by describing women like <s>Vāsavadattā</s> who followed husbands worthy of them, instill remorse. And by carefully discovering even the most secret dalliances of the king among his other wives, and revealing them, increase her jealousy.' And I further told my mother: 'In this way, you too, engaged in no other occupation, must attend upon that royal lady. And whatever happens here each day, I must be informed by you. And let this [companion], instructed by me, follow <s>Kalpasundarī</s> like a shadow, for the accomplishment of our enterprise whose fruit will be sweet.' And they carried out that task exactly as [directed]. After some days had passed, my mother told me: 'Son, like a <s>mādhavī</s> creeper clinging to a <s>nimba</s> tree, she has been brought to consider herself pitiable and has been established [in that state]. What more is to be done?' Then I drew my own portrait and said: 'Take this to her. Having been taken and having examined it, she will surely say: "Is there indeed such a man of such appearance?" Tell her: "If there were, what then?" Whatever answer she gives — I must be informed.' She [replied] 'So be it,' and going to the royal palace and returning, reported to me in private: 'Son, I showed that painting to that proud beauty. And she, gazing at it, [said:] "The world is blessed that even in the god <s>Kusumadhanvan</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) such bodily splendor does not reside! This painting is most wondrous. I do not know who here in this world creates such [beauty]. By whom was this painted?" — thus she spoke with delight. And I said with a smile: "Queen, you speak fittingly. Even the blessed <s>Makaraketu</s> (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) — it cannot even be imagined that he is this beautiful. And yet, this ocean-shore is vast. Somewhere, by the power of fate, such beauty may indeed exist. But if a young man of such form, with skills, character, learning, and accomplishments befitting such beauty, of great lineage, were present — what would he obtain?" She said: "Mother, what shall I say? My body, my heart, my life — all this is trifling and unworthy. Therefore he would obtain nothing — unless this is a deception. Rather, let him come to her; by the experience of seeing [her], let the favor be granted so that these eyes may be fulfilled." I pressed further to make it firmer: "There is a certain prince moving about in secret. At the spring festival, when you were strolling in the city garden with your friends, you happened to enter his line of sight, as if <s>Rati</s> herself had taken form. And he, having become the sole target of <s>Kāma's</s> arrow, followed me. And I, impelled by qualities and beauties that matched each other and were rare in any other — with garlands of flowers, unguents, and other offerings fashioned by him — have long served you. And having himself painted his own likeness, he sent it to demonstrate the firmness of his attachment to you. If this matter is settled, for him — whose excellence of life-force, courage, and wisdom is superhuman — nothing is difficult. I could show him to you this very day. A rendezvous should be given." She, having reflected on that for a moment, then said: "Mother, this should not now be concealed from you. Therefore I tell you. My father, King <s>Prāharavarman</s>, had a great friendship with [her father]. And my mother <s>Mānavatī's</s> dear friend was Queen <s>Priyaṃvadā</s>. By those two, who were without offspring, this agreement was made: 'The one of us who has a son and the other a daughter — the daughter shall be given [to the son].' But my father gave me, once born, to <s>Vikaṭavarman</s> who was demanding me, since <s>Priyaṃvadā</s> had lost her children — [he gave me] by the force of fate. And this [<s>Vikaṭavarman</s>] is cruel, treacherous to his father, of ill-proportioned body, unskilled in the arts of love, of dull inclination toward poetry, drama, and the like, a braggart mad with false valor, a liar, and one who quarrels without cause. This husband does not please me at all — especially in these days when, in the garden, disregarding <s>Puṣkarikā</s>, who is the innermost [companion] of my heart and close by, he has formed a rival attachment to me with a base dancing girl named <s>Ramayantikā</s>, who does not know herself, and adorned her with flowers he himself plucked from the <s>campaka</s> creeper that I had nurtured like my own child. In the jeweled pavilion of the painted chamber where I had enjoyed and discarded [him], he dallied with her. He is an unworthy man, and what he has done is contemptible. So why should one fear the next world when it is obscured by suffering in this one? For unbearable is the suffering of women whose hearts have become quivers for <s>Anaṅga's</s> arrows, [condemned to] the torture of cohabitation with an unwanted person. Therefore, arrange for me a meeting with that man today in the <s>mādhavī</s> bower of this garden. For merely upon hearing this report, my mind has become excessively attached. And here is this heap of wealth. With this, having established him in a position, serving him alone forever — I shall live." Having agreed to that, I returned. Henceforth, the young lord is the authority.' Then, from her very person, having learned the layout of the inner palace — the positions of the inner guards, and even the areas of the pleasure-garden — in detail, when the disk of the sun was reddening as if agitated by blood from falling on the peak of the western mountain, when darkness was spreading as if the mass of smoke from the embers of the sun-bird had been extinguished by falling into the western ocean, when the moon was rising as if to act as my teacher in approaching another's wife — the moon that boasts of embracing <s>Guru</s>'s (Jupiter's) wife, that forerunner of the planets — when the god of the flower-bow (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) was setting forth to conquer the world, his radiance kindled by the moon-orb that seemed to be the lotus-face of <s>Kalpasundarī</s>, smiling with the first onset of desire at my sight — I took to my proper bed. And I deliberated: 'This matter is nearly accomplished. But from violating another's wife, there would be injury to <s>dharma</s> — yet even that is sanctioned by the authors of the <s>śāstras</s> when one obtains both wealth (<s>artha</s>) and pleasure (<s>kāma</s>). And by me, through the stratagem of liberating my parents from bondage, this transgression has been committed — yet even that sin, redeemed by whatever measure of <s>dharma</s>, would make me whole.' And 'But upon hearing this, what will Lord <s>Rājavāhana</s> or my friends say?' — absorbed in such reflections, I was touched by sleep. And I saw a dream: Lord <s>Gaṇeśa</s>, the elephant-faced one, appeared. And he said: 'Good <s>Upahāravarman</s>, let there be no evil doubt in you, for you are a portion of me. This celestial river, worthy of being cradled in <s>Śaṅkara's</s> matted locks, is that beautiful woman. And she once, unable to endure my churning [of her], cursed me: "Go, become mortal!" And she was cursed by me: "Just as you enjoy many here, so too, having obtained human birth, be shared by many." And she herself entreated: "Having been devoted to one first, I would serve you alone and delight as long as I live." Therefore this matter is indeed auspicious, and you should have no apprehension.' Having awakened with joy, I spent that day too in the memory of the anticipated rendezvous with my beloved. The next day, <s>Anaṅga</s>, unchanged in his ways, rained his arrow-shower upon me alone. The luminous lake dried up. A mass of darkness-mud spread. Clad in dark garments, with a firm girdle, sword in hand, carrying prepared implements — remembering the tokens of recognition given by my mother — I approached the moat of the royal palace. Then, through a tunnel at the door of my mother's house, taking the bamboo staff that had been first placed there by <s>Puṣkarikā</s>, and with the moat drained by her, and the rampart-wall scaled by her placement [of the staff] — climbing by a stairway path on the surface of the barbican built of ripe bricks, I descended to the ground. Having descended, crossing the <s>bakula</s> avenue, approaching gently by the path of the <s>campaka</s> row, I heard the piteous cry of a <s>cakravāka</s> couple to the north. Then, going northward by the <s>pāṭalī</s> path, through the interior of a broad palace wall reachable by touch, covering a distance [as short as] an arrow's flight, then turning eastward along a sandy path adorned on both sides by groves of clustered <s>piṇḍī</s>-<s>bhaṇḍīra</s> trees, advancing slightly northward, I then entered a <s>cūta</s> (mango) avenue to the west. From there, in the deeper interior, I discerned by the slightly opened, glimmering lamp-wick a <s>mādhavī</s>-creeper bower with jeweled platforms rising within it. Entering the inner chamber on one side, surrounded by walls of unbroken rows of blooming <s>kuraṇṭaka</s> shrubs, I pushed open a door — mottled with fresh flower-bud spots on the newly-fallen red <s>aśoka</s>-vine, ruddy with layers of fresh coral-[red] shoots — and went in. There was a well-spread bed of flowers, and vessels containing the accessories for love-making. Having sat down and rested for a moment, I inhaled the surpassingly intense fragrance. I heard soft, soft footsteps. Having heard, I emerged from the rendezvous-chamber and stood with my body concealed beside the trunk of a red <s>aśoka</s> tree. The beautiful-browed one, desiring a charming lover, approached slowly, and not seeing me there, was greatly distressed. She uttered words with the charmingly faltering cadence of a passionate royal swan: 'Clearly I have been deceived! There is no means to live. O heart, why do you resolve upon this improper thing as if it were proper? Since it is impossible, why do you swoon so? O blessed Five-arrowed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), what offense have I committed against you that you burn me thus and yet do not reduce me to ashes?' Then I appeared, with the lamp-vessel uncovered, [and said:] 'O passionate lady, indeed much offense has been committed by you against the flower-born (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), since <s>Rati</s>, who is his very life, has been scorned by this stolen form of yours: his bow-staff by your eyebrow-creepers, his bowstring of bees by the luster of your dark locks, his weapons by the showers of your sidelong glances, his great banner-cloth dyed with royal vermilion by the rays of your lips, his foremost friend the <s>Malaya</s> breeze by your exhalation-wind surpassing [it] in fragrance, his cuckoo by your exceedingly sweet prattle, his floral flag by your arm-staffs, his victory-procession pair of full pots by the pair of your breast-pots, his pleasure-lake by the circle of your navel, his war-chariot by the circle of your hips, his twin jeweled gateway-pillars by your pair of thighs, his playful ear-ornament of sprouts by the radiance of the soles of your feet. Therefore it is rightly that the Fish-bannered one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) torments you. But he afflicts me even more, though I am guiltless — that alone is his fault. So be gracious, O beautiful one — revive me, bitten by the serpent of <s>Anaṅga</s>, with the life-giving herbs of your sidelong glances!' — and I embraced her. And I delighted in the broad-eyed one, lovely with the passion of <s>Anaṅga</s>. And observing her when passion was spent — her eyes rolling with crimson, the roots of her cheeks broken out in fine drops of perspiration, prattling incessantly and sweetly, with the disarray of mutual scratching and biting — seeing her with utterly loosened limbs, as if in agony, I relaxed both my mental and physical restraint and brought myself too into the same state as hers. Released from union at that very moment, undergoing the concluding rites of love-making, we stayed for a moment with the intimate trust of long acquaintances. Then I sighed — a long, hot sigh — and with a somewhat sorrowful gaze, extending both arms with trembling care, I embraced her not too tightly and kissed her not too clearly. But she, her face streaked with tears, [said:] 'If you depart, my lord, consider my life as already departed. Take me too! If not, this servant is of no use' — and she brought her joined palms to her forehead. I told her: 'O innocent one, what sensible person does not welcome a woman who desires him? If your intention of devotion to me is firm, carry out my instruction without deliberation. Show the king in private the painting containing my likeness. And say: "Is this the ultimate pinnacle of masculine beauty, or not?" He will surely say: "Indeed it is!" Then say further: "If so, there is a certain female ascetic, made bold by wandering in foreign lands, who is like a mother to me." She, presenting this painted portrait, has told me: "There is such a <s>mantra</s> by which you, having fasted on the sacred day, in a secluded place, after the priests have offered oblations and the sacred fire has been kindled, alone at night, offering a hundred sandalwood sticks, a hundred <s>aguru</s> sticks, a handful of camphor, and many fine silk cloths — you shall become of this form. And then you shall ring a bell. Your husband, summoned by the ringing of the bell, having confided all his secrets to you and closing his eyes, if he embraces you — this form shall pass to him. And you shall become as you were before, if it pleases both you and your lord. And in this rite, no deception must be practiced."' 'And [say:] "This body too, which you desire, together with ministers, friends, brothers, townspeople and country-folk, must be deliberated upon, and only when they too approve should the rite be undertaken."' He will certainly agree. 'Then again, in this very corner of the pleasure-garden, having performed an <s>Ātharvaṇika</s> rite with a sacrificed animal, when the golden-seeded [fire] has been kindled and the smoke-curtain has been entered by me, I shall stand in this very creeper-bower. And you, in the deep dusk, whispering in <s>Vikaṭavarman's</s> ear with a playful, amused smile, shall say: "You rogue! You are ungrateful! With the beauty obtained by my grace, [a beauty] that is a festival for the eyes of the world, you will delight my co-wives! I would not perform the raising of a <s>vetāla</s> for my own destruction!" Having heard your words, whatever he says — come to me alone and report it. Thereafter I myself shall know [what to do]. And let <s>Puṣkarikā</s> erase my footprints in the garden.' She [said] 'So be it' and, treating my words like the teaching of a <s>śāstra</s>, though her passion for love-making was unsated, somehow she went inside the palace. And I too, exiting as I had entered, went to my own lodging. Now that proud beauty carried out that plan exactly. And that fool <s>Vikaṭavarman</s> agreed to it. And this amazing rumor spread among the townspeople and country-folk: 'The king, <s>Vikaṭavarman</s>, will supposedly obtain a body worthy of the gods through the queen's power of <s>mantras</s>! Surely this is a deception and not particularly auspicious! What need to speak of the danger? Right in his own inner-palace garden, by his own chief queen, this affair is supposedly to be accomplished! And yet it has been deliberated and approved even by ministers whose intelligence rivals <s>Bṛhaspati's</s>! If this is to be, there is nothing more wonderful than this! For inconceivable is the power of gems, <s>mantras</s>, and contrivances.' As such popular rumors were circulating, on the sacred day, in the deep, darkest dusk, from the inner-palace garden there arose a column of smoke, dark as the throat of <s>Śiva</s>. And the fragrance of oblations of milk, ghee, curd, sesame, white serpent-fat, flesh, and blood spread in every direction, carried by the wind. When the smoke-column suddenly subsided, I entered. The elephant-gaited one came to the night-garden. Embracing me with a smile, she said: 'Rogue! Your scheme has succeeded! That beast has been finished. To tempt him, as directed by you, I said: "Scoundrel! I will not accomplish beauty for you! With such beauty you would become desirable even to <s>apsarases</s>, let alone mortal women! Fickle by nature like a bee, a cruel one like you would attach himself anywhere without discrimination!" He, falling at my feet, said: "O beautiful-thighed one, forgive my misdeeds! I would not even think of another woman hereafter! Proceed with the undertaking!" So I have come to you adorned in this bridal attire. Previously too, with <s>Anaṅga</s> as witness to the fire of passion, this wife has already been given to you through beauty and virtue. And now again, having made this sacrificial fire the witness, she is given by her own heart.' And pressing my instep with [her] toe, raising her heel, entwining her delicate fingers with mine, encircling my neck with both vine-like arms, playfully bending [my] face downward while she herself raised her lotus-face, with wide, trembling gaze, she kissed me again and again. Then I said to her: 'Wait here in this <s>kuraṇṭaka</s> thicket while I go out and accomplish what is to be accomplished' — and leaving her, I approached the area of the sacrificial fire and rang the bell hanging from an <s>aśoka</s> branch. It clanged as if summoning that man to his death. I began to offer <s>aguru</s>, sandalwood, and other [substances]. The king came to the designated place. To him — standing there with some suspicion, deliberating with a touch of wonder — I said: 'Speak the truth once more, making the blessed <s>Citrabhānu</s> (Fire) himself the witness! If you do not delight my co-wives with this form, then I shall transfer this beauty to myself.' He, with conviction having clearly arisen [that] 'this is indeed the Queen herself, not a fraud,' proceeded to swear an oath. Then I said with a smile: 'What use is an oath? What mortal woman would surpass me? If you consort with <s>apsarases</s>, consort [with them] as you please! Tell me — what are your secrets? For at the end of their telling, there will be the loss of your own form.' He said: 'My father's younger brother <s>Prāharavarman</s> is imprisoned. Having killed him with poisoned food, we intend to proclaim it as a case of indigestion — this was resolved together with the ministers. To the younger brother <s>Viśālavarman</s>, the military command is to be given for an expedition against the <s>Puṇḍra</s> country. And a city elder <s>Pāñcālika</s> and a protected caravan-leader were privately conferring with me that from a <s>Yavana</s> named after his own clan, a single diamond of the value of [an entire] land could be obtained for a trifling price. And a householder intimate to me, the rural chief <s>Śatahalin</s>, has undertaken to have me appoint, in a punitive operation, the killing of the corrupt village-headman <s>Anantasīra</s>, who is of deceitful nature and arrogant, through the wrath of the country-folk. Such is this secret, recently devised.' Having heard this, [I said:] 'Your lifespan extends thus far! Attain the fate befitting your deeds!' — and cleaving him in two with a dagger, I offered the just-severed [body] into that very blazing, ghee-rich, golden-seeded [fire]. And he was reduced to ashes. Then, consoling my heart's beloved who was slightly shaken by feminine nature, taking her by the hand, going to his palace, having by her permission summoned all the women of the inner quarters, I immediately assumed authority. Having amused myself for some time amid the company of astonished court ladies, having dismissed the circle of palace women, I took that very one — pressing thigh against thigh, arm against arm — and delighting her on the bed, I spent what seemed a brief night. And from her lips I learned the character of that royal family. At dawn, having bathed and performed auspicious rites, I met with the ministers. And I said to them: 'Noble sirs, along with my form, my character too has changed. He who was intended to be killed by poisoned food — my uncle — should be released and made to rule his own kingdom once again. We shall attend upon him with devotion, as upon a father. For there is no greater sin than patricide.' And summoning [my] younger brother <s>Viśālavarman</s>, I said: 'Son, the <s>Puṇḍras</s> are not prosperous now — they are afflicted by suffering and confusion, their spirits broken — they would not attack our unprosperous realm. Therefore you shall march only when an insurrection or crop-destruction arises — a campaign today is not appropriate.' And to the city elders I said: 'Let a treasure of great value not be obtained by me for a trifling price, for the sake of protecting <s>dharma</s> — let it be purchased only at a commensurate price.' And summoning <s>Śatahalin</s>, the rural chief, I declared: 'That <s>Anantasīra</s>, who was intended to be destroyed as a partisan of <s>Prāharavarman</s> — he too is a loyalist of my father; why should he be destroyed? Therefore you too should harbor no hostility toward him.' These [ministers], perceiving all this as the behavior of one who knows the truth, concluding 'this is indeed he [himself, transformed],' and marveling, praising me and the chief queen and extolling the powers of <s>mantras</s>, released my parents from prison and restored their own kingdom. And I, having my nurse reveal all my doings in secret to my parents — who ascended to the pinnacle of joy — bowed at their feet. And I was invested with the glory of the <s>yuvarāja</s> (crown prince) at their command. Having prepared myself, enduring the misfortune of pleasures rendered joyless by separation from the Lord's feet, and then learning from a letter of <s>Siṃhavarman</s>, my father's friend, of the attack of <s>Caṇḍavarman</s> upon <s>Campā</s> — [thinking] 'the destruction of the enemy and the protection of a friend are both duties that must be performed' — with a substantial army of swift mobilization, I marched forth. And I have become [one who has attained] the mass of joy that is the festival of the direct realization of the glory of [your] feet, O lord of the earth.'

children.text: iti śrīdaṇḍinaḥ katau daśakumāracarite upahāravarmacaritaṃ nāma tṛtīya ucchvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, in the composition of the illustrious <s>Daṇḍin</s>, in the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s>, [ends] the third chapter named 'The Adventures of <s>Upahāravarman</s>.'

children.text:
deva, so 'hamapyobhireva suhṛdbhirekakarmormimālinemibhūmivalayaṃ paribhramannupāsaraṃ kadācitkāśīpurīṃ vārāṇasīm /
upaspṛśya maṇibhaṅganirmalāmbhasi maṇikarṇikāyāmavimukteśvaraṃ bhagavantamandhakamathanamabhipraṇamya pradakṣiṇaṃ paribhramanpuruṣamekamāyāmavantamāyasapari ghapīvarābhyāṃ bhujābhyāmābadhvamānaparikaramavirataruditocchūnatāmradṛṣṭimadrākṣam /
atarkayaṃ ca-"karkaśo 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ kārpaṇyamiva varṣapi kṣīṇatāraṃ cakṣuḥ, ārambhaśca sāhasānuvādī, nūnamasau prāṇaniḥspṛhaḥ kimapi kṛcchraṃ priyajanavyasanamūlaṃ pratipatsyate /
tatpṛccheyamenam /
asti cenmamāpi ko 'pi sāhāyyadānāvakāśastamenamabhyupetyetyapṛccham-"bhadra, saṃnāho 'yaṃ sāhasamavagamayati /
na cedgopyamicchāmi śrotuṃ śokahetum' iti /
sa māṃ sabahumānaṃ nirvarṇya "ko doṣaḥ, śrūyatām' iti /
kvacitkaravīratale mayā saha niṣaṇṇaḥ kathāmakāraṣit-"mahābhāga, so 'hamasmi pūrveṣu kāmacaraḥ pūrṇabhadro nāma gṛhapatiputraḥ /
prayatnasaṃvardhito 'pi pitrā daivacchandānuvartī cauryavṛttirāsam /
athāsyāṃ kāśīpuryāmaryavaryasya kasyacidgṛhe corayitvā rūpābhigrāhito baddhaḥ /
vadhye ca mayi mattahastī mṛtyuvijayo nāma hiṃsāvihārī rājagopuroparitalādhirūḍhasya paśyataḥ kāmapālanāmna uttamāmātyasya śāsanājjanakaṇṭharavadviguṇitaghaṇṭāravo maṇḍalitahastakāṇḍaṃ samabhyadhāvat /
abhipatya ca mayā nibhayana nirbhartsitaḥ pariṇamandārukhaṇḍasuṣirānupraviṣṭobhayabhujadaṇḍaghaṭitapratimāno bhītavannyavartiṣṭa /
bhūyaśca netrā jātasaṃrambheṇa nikāmadāruṇairvāgaṅkuśapādapātairabhimukhīkṛtaḥ /
mayāpi dviguṇābaddhamanyunā nirbhartsyābhihato nivṛtyāpādravat /
atha mayopetya sarabhasamākruṣṭo ruṣṭaśca yantā "hanta, mṛto 'si kuñjarāpasada' iti niśitena vāraṇena vāraṇaṃ muhurmuhurabhighnanniryāṇabhāge kathamapi madabhimukhamakarot /
athāvocyam--"apasaratu dvikakīṭa eṣaḥ /
anyaḥ kaścinmātaṅgaphatirānīyatām /
yenāhaṃ muhūrtaṃ vihṛtya gacchāmi gantavyāṃ gatim' iti /
dṛṣṭaiva sa māṃ ruṣṭamudgarjantamutkrāntayantṛniṣṭhurājñaḥ palāyiṣṭa /
mantriṇā punarahamāhūyābhyadhāyiṣi--"bhadra, mṛtyurevaiṣa mṛtyuvijayo nāma hiṃsāvihārī /
so 'yamapi tāvattvayaivaṃbhūtaḥ kṛtaḥ /
tadviram karmaṇo 'smānmalīmasātkimalamasi pratipadyāsmānāryavṛttyā vartitum' iti /
"yathājñāpito 'smi' iti vijñāpito 'yaṃ mayā mitravanmayyavartiṣṭa /
pṛṣṭaśca mayaikadā rahasi jātaviśrambheṇābhāṣata svacaritam--"āsītkusumapure rājño ripuñjayasya mantrī dharmapālo nāma viśrutadhīḥ śrutaṛṣiḥ /
amuṣya putraḥ sumitro nāma pitraiva samaḥ prajñāguṇeṣu /
tasyāsmi dvaimāturaḥ kanīyanbhrātāham /
veśeṣu vilasantaṃ māmasau vinayaruciravārayat /
avāryadurnayaścāhamapasṛtya diṅmukheṣu bhramanyadṛcchayāsyāṃ vāraṇasyāṃ pramadavane madanadamanārādhanāya nirgatya sahasakhībhiḥ kandukenānukrīḍamānāṃ kāśībhartuścaṇḍasiṃhasya kanyāṃ kāntimatīṃ nāma cakame /
kathamapi samagacche ca /
atha channaṃ ca viharatā kumārīpure sā mayāsīdāpannasattvā /
kañcitsutaṃ ca prasūtavatī /
mṛtajāta iti so 'paviddho rahasyanirbhedabhayātparijanena krīḍāśaile /
śabaryā ca smaśānābhayāśaṃ nītaḥ /
tayaiva nivartamānayā niśīthe rājyavidhyamārakṣikapuruṣairabhigṛhaṃya tarjitayā daṇḍapārupyabhītayā nirbhinnaprāyaṃ rahasyam /
rājajñayā niśīthe 'hamākrījanagiridarīgṛhe viśrabdhaprasuptastayopadaraśito yathopapannarajjubaddhaḥ śmaśānamupanīya mātaṅgodyatena kṛpāṇena prājihīrṣye niyatibalāllūnabandhastamasimācchidyāntyajaṃ tamanyāṃśca kāṃścitprahṛtyāpāsaram /
aśaraṇśca bhramannaṭavyāmekadāśrumukhyā kayāpi divyākārayā saparicārayā kanyayopāsthāyipi /
sā māmañjalikisalayottaṃsitena mukhavilolakuntalena mūrdhnā praṇamya mayā saha vanavaṭadrumasya kasyāpi mahataḥ pracchāyaśītale tale niṣaṇṇā, "kāsi vāsu, kuto 'syāgatā, kasya hetorasya me prasīdasi' iti sābhilāṣamābhāṣitā mayā vāṅmayaṃ madhuvarṣamavarṣat-"ārya, nāthasya yakṣāṇāṃ maṇibhadrasyāsmi duhitā tārāvalī nāma /
sāhaṃ kadācidagastyapatnīṃ lopāmudrāṃ namaskṛtyāpāvartamānā malayagireḥ paretāvāse vārāṇasyāḥ kamapi dārakaṃ rudantamadrākṣam /
ādāya cainaṃ tīvrasnehānmamapitroḥ saṃnidhimanaiṣam /
anaipīcca me pitā devasyālakeśvarasyāsthānīm /
athāhamāhūyājñaptā harasakhena, "bāle bāle 'sminkīdṛśaste bhāvaḥ' iti /
"aurasa ivāsminvatse vatsalatā' iti mayā vijñāpitaḥ "satyamāha varākī' iti tanmūlāmatimahatīṃ kathāmakarot /
tatraitāvanmayāvagatam "tvaṃ kila śaunakaḥ śūdrakaḥ kāmapālaścābhinnaḥ /
bandhumatī vinayavatī kāntimatī cābhinnā /
vedimatyāryadāsī somadevī vaikaiva /
haṃsāvalī śūrasenā sulocanā cānanyā /
nandinī raṅgapatākendrasenā cāpṛthagbhūtā /
yā kila śaunakāvasthāyāmagnisākṣikamātmasātkṛtā gopakanyā saiva kilāryadāsī punaścādya tārāvalītyabhūvam /
bālaśca kilaśūdrakāvasthe tvayyāryadāsyavasthāyāṃ mayyudabhūt /
avardhyata ca vinayavatyā snehavāsanayā /
sa tu tasyāṃ kāntimatyavasthāyāmadyodabhūt /
evamanekamṛtyumukhaparibhraṣṭaṃ daivānmayopalabdhaṃ tamekapiṅgādeśādvane tapasyato rājahaṃsasya devyai vasumatyai tatsutasya bhāvicakravartino rājavāhanasya paricaryārthaṃ samarpya gurubhirabhyanujñātā kṛtāntayogātkṛtāntamukhabhraṣṭasya te pādapadmaśuśrūṣārthamāgatāsmi' iti /
śrutvā tāmanekajanmaramaṇīmasakṛdāśliṣya harṣāśrumukho muhurmuhuḥ sāntvayitvā tatprabhāvadarśite mahati mandire 'harniśaṃ bhūmidurlabhānbhogānanvabhūvam /
dvitrāṇi danānyatikramya mattakāśinīṃ tāmavādiṣam-"priye, pratyapakṛtya matprāṇadgohiṇaścaṇḍasiṃhasya vairaniryātanasukhamanububhūṣāmi' iti tayā sasmitamabhihitam-"ehi kānta, kāntimatīdarśanāya nayāmi tvām' iti /
sthiter'dharātre rājño vāsagṛhanīye /
tatastacchirobhāgavartinīmādāyāsiyaṣṭiṃ prabodhyainaṃ prasphurantamabravam--"ahamasmi bhavajjāmātā /
bhavadanumatyā vinā tava kanyābhimarśī /
tamaparādhamanuvṛttyā pramārṣṭumāgataḥ' iti /
so 'tibhītomāmabhipraṇamyāha-"ahameva mūḍho 'parāddhaḥ yastava duhitṛsaṃsargānugrāhiṇo grahagrasta ivotkrāntasīmā bhavadadhīnam' ityavādīt /
athāparedyuḥ prakṛtiṇḍalaṃ saṃnipātya vidhivadātmajāyāḥ pāṇimagrāhayat /
aśrāvayacca tanayavārtāṃ tārāvalī kāntimatyai, somadevīsulocanendrasenābhyaśca pūrvajātivṛttāntam /
itthamahaṃ mantripadāpadeśaṃ yauvarājyamanubhavanviharāmi vilāsinībhiḥ' iti /
sa evaṃ mādṛśe 'pi jantau paricaryānubandhī bandhurekaḥ sarvabhūtānāmalasakena svargate śvaśure, jyāyasi jantau paricaryānubandhī bandhurekaḥ sarvabhūtānāmalasakena svargate śvaśure, jyāyasi ca śyāle caṇḍaghoṣanāmni strīṣvatiprasaṅgātprāgeva kṣayakṣīṇāyuṣi, pañcavarṣadeśīyaṃ sihaghoṣanāmānaṃ paiśunyavādināṃ durmantriṇaḥ katicidāsannantaraṅgabhūtāḥ /
taiḥ kilāsāvitthamagrāhyata-"prasaṅyaiva svasā tavāmunā bhujaṅgena saṃgṛhītā /
punaḥ prasupte rājani prāhartumadyutāsirāsīt /
tenāsmai talkṣaṇapravṛddhena bhītyānunīya dattā kanyā /
taṃ ca devajyeṣṭhaṃ caṇḍaghoṣaṃ viṣeṇa hatvā bālo 'yamasamartha iti tvamadyāpi prakṛtiviśrambhaṇāyopekṣitaḥ /
kṣiṇoti ca purā sa kṛtaghno bhavantam /
tamevāntakapuramabhigamayituṃ yatasva' iti /
sa tathā dūṣito 'pi yakṣiṇībhayānnāmuṣminpāpamācaritumaśakat /
eṣu kila divaseṣvayathāpūrvamākṛtau kāntimatyāḥ samupalakṣya rājamahiṣī sulakṣaṇā nāma sapraṇayamapṛcchat-"devi, nāhamāyathātathyena vipralambhanīyā /
kathaya tathyaṃ kenedamayathāpūrvamānanāravinde tavaiṣu vāsareṣu' iti /
sā tvavadīt-"bhadre, smarasi kimadyāpyāyathātathyena kiñcinmayoktapūrvam /
sakhī me tārāvalī sapatnī ca kimapi kaluṣitāśayā rahasi bhartrā madgotrāpadiṣṭā praṇayamapyupekṣya praṇamyamānāpyasmabhirupoḍhamatsarā prāvasat /
avasīdati ca naḥ patiḥ /
ato me daurmanatyam' iti /
tatprāyeṇaikānte sulakṣaṇayā kāntāya kathitam /
"athāsau nirbhayo 'dya priyatamāvirahapāṇḍubhiravayairghairyastambhitāśruparyākulena cakṣuṣoṣmaśvāsaśoṣitābhirivānatipeśalābhirvāgbhirviyogaṃ darśayantam, kathamapi rājakule kāryāṇi kārayantam, pūrvasaṃketitaiḥ puruṣairabhigrāhyābandhayat /
tasya kila sthāne sthāne doṣānuddhoṣya tathoddharaṇīye cakṣuṣī yathā tanmūlamevāsya maraṇaṃ bhavet' iti /
ato 'traikānte yatheṣṭamaśru muktvā tasya sādhoḥ puraḥ prāṇānmoktukāmo badhnāmi parikaram' iti /
mayāpi tatpitṛvyasanamākarṇya paryaśruṇā so 'bhihitaḥ-"saumya, kiṃ tava gopāyitvā /
yastasya suto yakṣakanyayā devasya rājavāhanasya pādaśuśrūṣārthaṃ devyā vasumatyā hastanyāsaḥ kṛtaḥ so 'hamasmi /
śakṣyāmi sahasramapi subhaṭānāmudāyudhānāṃ hatvā pitaraṃ mocayitum /
api tu saṃkule yadi kaścitpātayettadaṅge śastrikāṃ sarva eva me yatno bhasmāni hutamiva bhavet' iti /
anavasitavacana eva mayi mahānāśīviṣaḥ prākārarandhreṇodairayacchiraḥ /
tamahaṃ mantrauṣadhabalenābhigṛhya pūrṇabhadramabravam-"bhadra, siddhaṃ naḥ samīhitam /
anena tātamalakṣyamāṇaḥ saṃkule yadṛcchayā patitena nāma daṃśayitvā tathā viṣaṃ stambhavevaṃ yathā mṛta ityudāsyeta /
tvayā tu muktasādhvasena mātā me bodhayitavyā-" yā yakṣyā vane devyā vasumatyā hastārpito yuṣmatsūnuḥ so 'nuprāptaḥ pituravasthāṃ madupalabhya buddhibalāditthāmācariṣyati /
tvayā tu muktatrāsayā rājñe preṣaṇīyam-"eṣa khalu kṣātradharmo yadbandhurabandhurvā duṣṭaḥ sa nirapekṣaṃ nirgrāhya iti /
strīdharmaścaiṣa yadaduṣṭasya duṣṭasya vā bharturgatirgantavyeti /
tadahamamunaiva saha citāgnimārokṣyāmi /
yuvatijanānukūlaḥ paścimo vidhiranujñātavyaḥ' iti /
sa eva nivedito niyatamanujñāsyati /
tataḥ svamevāgāramānīya kāṇḍapaṭīparikṣipte viviktodderśe darbhasastaraṇamadhiśāyya svayaṃ kṛtānumaraṇamaṇḍanayā tvayā ca tatra saṃnidheyam /
ahaṃ ca bāhyakakṣāgatastvayā praveśayiṣye /
tataḥ pitaramujjīvya tadabhirucitenābhyupāyena ceṣṭiṣyāmahe' iti /
sa "tathā' iti hṛṣṭatarastūrṇamagamat /
ahaṃ tu ghoṣaṇasthāne ciñcāvṛkṣaṃ ghanataravipulaśākhamāruhya gūḍhatanuratiṣṭham /
ārūḍhaśca loko yathāyathamuccaisthānāni /
uccāvacapralāpāḥ prastutāḥ /
tāvanme pitaraṃ taskaramiva paścādbaddhabhujamuddhuradhvani mahājanānuyātamānīya madabhyāśa eva sthāpayitvā mātaṅgastriraghoṣayat-"eṣa mantrī kāmapālo rājyalobhadbhartāraṃ caṇḍasiṃham, yuvarājaṃ caṇḍaghoṣaṃ ca viṣānnenopāṃśu hatvā punardevo 'pi siṃhaghoṣaḥ pūrṇayauvana ityamuṣminpāpamācariṣyanviśvāsādrahasyabhūmau punaramātyaṃ śivanāgamāhūya sthūṇamaṅgāravarṣaṃ ca rājavadhāyopajapya taiḥ svāmibhaktyā vivṛtaguhyo rājyakāmukasyāsya brāhmaṇasyāndhatamasapraveśo nyāyya iti prāṅvivākavākyādakṣyuddharaṇāya nīyate /
punaranyo 'pi yadi syādanyāyavṛttistamaṣyevameva yathārheṇa daṇḍena yojayiṣyati devaḥ' iti /
śrutvaitadbhaddhakalakale mahājane pituraṅge pradīptaśirasamāśīviṣaṃ vyakṣipam /
ahaṃ ca bhīto nāmāvaplutya tatraiva janādanulīnaḥ kruddhvayāladaṣṭasya tātasya vihitajīvarakṣo viṣakṣaṇādastambhayam /
apataccaiṣa bhūmau mṛtakalpaḥ /
prālapaṃ ca "satyamidaṃ rājāvamāninaṃ daivo daṇḍa eva spṛśatīti /
yadayamakṣibhyāṃ vināvanipena cikīrṣitaḥ, prāṇaireva viyojito vidhinā' iti /
maduktaṃ ca kecidanvamanyanta, apare punarnininduḥ /
darvīkarastu tamapi caṇḍālaṃ daṣṭvā rūḍhatrāsadrutalokadattamārgaḥ prādravat /
atha madambā pūrṇabhadrabodhitārthā tādṛśe 'pi vyasane nātivihvalā kulaparijanānuyātā padbhyāmeva dhīramāgatya matpituruttamāṅgamutsaṅgena dhārayantyāsitvā rājñe samādiśat-"eṣa me patistavāpakartā na veti daivameva jānāti /
na me 'nayāsti cintayā phalam /
asya tu pāṇigrāhakasya gatimananuprapadyamānā bhavatkulaṃ kalaṅkayeyam' ato 'numantumarhasi bhartrā saha citādhirohaṇāya mām' iti /
śrutvā caitatprītiyuktaḥ samādikṣatkṣitīśvaraḥ-"kriyatāṃ kulocitaḥ saṃskāraḥ /
utsavo ttaraṃ ca paścimaṃ vidhisaṃskāramanubhavatu me bhaginīpatiḥ' iti caṇḍāle tu matpratiṣiddhasakalamantravādiprayāse saṃsthite "kāmapālo 'pi kāladaṣṭa eva' iti svabhavanopanayanamamuṣya svamāhātmyaprakāśanāya mahīpatiranvamaṃsta /
ānītaśca pitā me viviktāyāṃ bhūmau darbhaśayyāmadhiśāyya sthito 'bhūt /
atha madambā maraṇamaṇḍanamanuṣṭhāya sakaruṇaṃ sakhīrāmantrya, muhurabhiprāṇamya bhava nadevatā yatnanivāritaparijanākranditā piturme śayanasthānamekākinī prāvikṣat /
tatra ca pūrvameva pūrṇabhadropasthāpitena ca mayā vainateyatāṃ gatena nirviṣīkṛtaṃ bhartāramaikṣata /
hṛṣṭatamā patyuḥ pādayoḥ paryaśrumukhī praṇipatya māṃ ca muhurmuhuḥ prasnutastanī pariṣvajya saharṣabāṣpagadgadamagadat-"putra, yo 'si jātamātraḥ pāpayā mayā parityaktaḥ, sa kimarthamevaṃ māmatinirghṛṇāmanugṛhṇāsi /
athavaipaniraparādha eva te jagayitā /
yuktamasya pratyānayanamantakānanāt /
krūrā khalu tārāvalī yā tvāsupalabhyāpi tattvataḥ kuberādasamarpya mahyamarpitavatī devyai vasumatyai saiva vā sadṛśakāriṇī /
nahi tādṛśādbhāgyarāśervinā mādṛśo jano 'lpapuṇyastavarhati kalapralāpāmṛtāni karṇābhyāṃ pātum /
ehi, pariṣvajasva' iti bhūyobhūyaḥ śirasi jighranyaṅkamāropayantī, tārāvalīṃ garhayantyāliṅgayantyaśrubhirabhiṣiñcatī cotkampitāṅgayaṣṭiranyādṛśīva kṣaṇamajaniṣṭa /
janayitāpime narakādiva svargam, tādṛśādavyasanāttathābūtamabhyudayamārūḍhaḥ pūrṇabhadreṇa vistareṇa yathāva-ttāntamāvedito bhagavato maghavato 'pi bhāgyavantamātmānamajīgaṇat /
managiva ca matsaṃbandhamākhyāya harpavismitātmanoḥ pitrorakathayam-"ājñāpayataṃ kādya naḥ pritapattiḥ' iti /
pitā me prābravīt-"vatsa, gṛhamevedamasmadīyamativiśālaprākārabalayamakṣayyānudhasthānam /
alaṅghyatamā ca guptiḥ /
upakṛtāścamayātibahavaḥ santi sāmantāḥ /
prakṛtayaśca bhūyasyo na me vyasanamanurudhyante /
subhaṭānāṃ cānekasahasramastyeva samuhṛtputradāram /
ato 'traiva katapayānyahāni sthitvā bāhyabhyantaraṅgānkopānutpādayiṣyāmaḥ /
kupitāṃśañca saṃgṛhya protsāhyāsya prakṛtyamitrānutthāpya sahajāṃśca dviṣaḥ, durdāntamenamucchetsyāmaḥ' iti /
"ko doṣaḥ, tathāstu' iti tātasya matamanvamaṃsi /
tathāsmāsu pratividhāya tiṣṭhatsu rājāpi vijñāpitodanto jātānutāpaḥ pāraprāmikānprayogānprāyaḥ prāyuṅka /
te cāsmābhiḥ pratyahamahanyanta /
asminnevāvakāśa pūrṇabhadramukhācca rājñaḥ śayyāsthānamavagasya tadaiva svodavasitabhittikoṇādārabhyoragāsyena suraṅgāmakārṣam /
gatā ca sā bhūmisvargakalpamanalpakanyakājanaṃ kamapyuddeśam /
avyathiṣṭa ca dṛṣṭaiva sa māṃ nārījanaḥ /
tatra kācidindukaleva svalāvaṇyena rasātalāndhakārāṃnahnuvānā vigrahiṇīva devī viśvaṃbharāḥharagṛhiṇīvāsuravijayāyāvatīrṇā, pātālamāgatā gṛhiṇīva bhagavataḥ kusumadhanvanaḥ gatalakṣmīrivānekadurnṛpadarśanaparihārāya mahīvivaraṃ praviṣṭā, niṣṭaptakanakaputrikevāvadātakāntiḥ kanyakā, candanalateva malayamārutena, maddarśanenodrakampatra /
tathā bhūte ca tasminnaṅganāsamāje, kusumiteva kāśayaṣṭiḥ, pāṇḍuśirasijñā nyavigakāciccaraṇayorme nipatya trāsadīnamabrūta-"dīyatāmabhayadānamasmā ananyaśaraṇāya strījanāya /
kimasi devakumāro danujayuddhatṛṣṇayā rasātalaṃvivikṣuḥ /
ājñāpayako 'si /
kasya hetorāgato 'si' iti /
sātu mayā pratyavādi--"sudatyaḥ, māsma bhavatyo bhaiṣuḥ /
ahamasmi dvijātivṛṣātkāmapālāddevyāṃ kāntimatyāmutpannor'tha pālo nāma /
satyarthe nijagṛhānnṛpagṛhaṃ suraṅgayopasarasannihāntare vo dṛṣṭavān /
kathayata ka stha yūyam /
kathamiha nivasatha' iti /
sodañjalirudīritavatī-"bhartṛdāraka, bhāgyavatyo vayam, yāstvāmebhireva cakṣurbhiranaghamadrākṣma /
śrūyatām /
yastavamātāmahaścaṇaaḍasihaḥ, tenāsyāṃ devyāṃ līlāvatayāṃ caṇḍaghoṣaḥ kāntimatītyapatyadvayamudapādi /
caṇḍaghopastu yuvarājo 'tyāsaṅgādaṅganāsu rājayakṣmaṇā surakṣayamagādantarvartnyāṃ devyāmācāravatyām /
amuyā ceyaṃ maṇikarṇikā nāma kanyā prasṛtā /
atha prasavavedanayā muktajīvitācāravatī patyurantikamagamat /
atha devaścaṇḍasiho māmāhūyopahvare samājñāpayat-"ṛddhimati, kanyakeyaṃ kalyāṇalakṣaṇā /
tāmimāṃ mālavendranandanāya darṣasārāya vidhivadvardhayitvā ditsāmi /
bibhemi ca kāntimatībṛttāntādārabhya kanyakānāṃ prakāśāvasthāpanāt /
ata iyamarātivayasanāya kārite mahati bhūmigṛhe kṛtrimaśailagarbhotkīrṇanānāmaṇaaḍapaprekṣāgṛhe pracuraparibarhayā bhavatyā saṃvardhyatām /
astyatira bhogyavastu varpaśatenāpyakṣayyam' iti /
sa tathoktvā nijavāsagṛhasya dvyaṅgulabhittāvardhapādaṃ kiṣkuviṣkambhamuddhṛtya tenaiva dvāreṇa tthānābhidamasmānavīviśat /
iha ca no vasantīnāṃ dvādaśasamāḥ samatyayuḥ /
iyaṃ ca vatsā taruṇībūtā /
na cādyāpi smarati rājā /
kāmamiyaṃ pitāmahena darpasārāya saṃkagalpitā /
tvadambayā kāntimatyā ceyaṃ garbhasthaiva dyṛtajitā svamātrātavaiva jāyātvena samakalpyata /
"tadatra prāptarūpaṃ cintyatāṃ kumāreṇaiva' iti /
tāṃ punaravocam-"adyaiva rājagṛhe kimapi kāryaṃ sādhayitvā pratinivṛtto yuṣmāsu yathārhaṃ pratipatsye' iti /
tenaiva dīpadarśitabilapathena gatvā sthiter'dharātre tadardhapādaṃ pratyuddhṛtya vāsagṛhaṃ praviṣṭo visrabdhasuptaṃ sihaghoṣaṃ jīvagrāhamagrahīṣam /
ākṛṣya ca tamahimivāhiśatruḥ sphurantamamunaiva bhittirandhrapathena straiṇasaṃnidhimanaiṣam /
ānīya ca svabhavanamāyasanigaḍasaṃditacaraṇayugalamavanāmitamalinavanamaśrubahularaktacakṣuṣamekānte janayitroradarśayam /
akathayaṃ ca bilakathām /
atha pitarau prahṛṣṭatarau taṃ nikṛṣṭāśayaṃ niśamya bandhane niyamya tasyā dārikāyā yathārheṇa karmaṇā māṃ pāṇimagrāhayetām /
anāthakaṃ ca tadrājyamasmadāyattameva jātam /
prakṛtikopabhayāttu manmātrā mumukṣito 'pi na mukta eva siṃhaghoṣaḥ /
tathāsthitāśca vayamaṅgarājaḥ siṃhavarmā devapādānāṃ bhaktimānkṛtakarmā cetyamitrābhiyuktamenamabhyasarāma /
children.translated_text: And being thus situated, we — the king of <s>Aṅga</s>, <s>Siṃhavarman</s>, and I who am a devoted servant accomplished in deeds for your lordship's feet — advanced against him who was assailed by enemies /

children.translated_text: And great use has been made of intelligence. Let your freed father-in-law come see me.' Having spoken thus, looking once more at <s>Pramati</s> with a smile of affection, he commanded: 'Let your own adventures now be recounted.' // Dkc_2,4 //

O Lord, I too, with these same companions, wandering over the girdle of the earth whose waves of activity are unified, once approached the city of <s>Kāśī</s>, <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. Having bathed in the waters of <s>Maṇikarṇikā</s>, clear as the gleam of broken gems, and having reverently bowed to the blessed Lord <s>Avimukteśvara</s>, slayer of <s>Andhaka</s>, while circumambulating I saw a certain man of great stature, with arms stout as iron bars, girding himself for action, his eyes reddened and swollen from unceasing weeping. And I reasoned thus: 'This is a hardened man who sheds tears as if even his harshness were exhausted, and his undertaking bespeaks reckless daring; surely he is indifferent to life and is about to attempt some desperate deed rooted in the misfortune of a loved one. I should ask him. If there is some opportunity for me too to render aid.' Approaching him, I asked: 'Good sir, this arming of yourself suggests a reckless venture. If it is not secret, I wish to hear the cause of your grief.' He regarded me with respect and said: 'What harm? Listen then.' Sitting down with me somewhere at the foot of an oleander tree, he began his tale: 'Noble one, I am <s>Pūrṇabhadra</s> by name, the son of a householder, formerly a free-roaming wanderer. Though carefully raised by my father, by fate's disposition I took to the ways of thievery. Then in this very city of <s>Kāśī</s>, having committed a robbery in the house of a certain eminent gentleman, I was captivated by beauty, caught, and bound. When I was condemned to death, a maddened elephant named <s>Mṛtyuvijaya</s>, a creature delighting in destruction, at the command of the chief minister named <s>Kāmapāla</s> — who watched from atop the royal gate-tower — charged at me with redoubled clanging of bells around its neck like a living death-knell, its trunk coiled and ready. But when it rushed at me, I, undaunted, rebuked it fiercely; it retreated in fear, having wedged both its tusks into the hollow of a broken post nearby. Again the mahout, enraged, drove it toward me with mercilessly harsh voice-goads and kicks. But I, with redoubled fury, rebuked and struck it, and it turned and fled. Then the mahout, dragged forward violently by me, was enraged and cried: "Wretch! You are dead, you disgrace among elephants!" — and striking the elephant repeatedly with a sharp goad at the exit-way, somehow forced it to face me again. Then I declared: "Remove this two-legged insect! Let some other elephant of true mettle be brought, so that I may sport for a moment before departing to whatever destination awaits me." Seeing me roaring in fury, the elephant, overriding the mahout's harsh commands, fled. The minister then summoned me and addressed me: "Good sir, this <s>Mṛtyuvijaya</s> named beast, this destruction-loving elephant — even he has been reduced to this state by you. Therefore desist from this wicked conduct. What use is it? Will you not commit to living by noble ways?" I replied: "As you command," and he, thus informed, treated me as a friend. Once, when I had gained his confidence, being asked in private, he told me his own story: "In <s>Kusumapura</s> there was a minister of King <s>Ripuñjaya</s> named <s>Dharmapāla</s>, of renowned intellect, a sage of learning. His son, named <s>Sumitra</s>, was equal to his father in the qualities of wisdom. I am his younger half-brother. When I was reveling in the pleasure quarters, he tried to restrain me with gentle decorum. But I, incorrigible in my waywardness, slipped away and, wandering aimlessly through the quarters of the world, by chance arrived in this <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. There, having gone out to worship <s>Madanadamana</s> (the Subduer of Love) in the pleasure garden, I saw the daughter of the lord of <s>Kāśī</s>, <s>Caṇḍasiṃha</s>, named <s>Kāntimatī</s>, playing ball with her companions, and fell in love with her. Somehow we came together. And while I was secretly enjoying myself in the maidens' quarters, she became pregnant by me. She bore a son. He was declared stillborn and abandoned by the attendants on the pleasure-hill, out of fear of the secret being exposed. A <s>Śabarī</s> (tribal woman) carried him to the cremation ground of fearlessness. But she, while returning at midnight, was seized and threatened by the king's patrol guards, and, frightened of punishment, left the child at the doorstep of some <s>Drāviḍa</s> (southern) <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>'s house. Once, for this very reason, Queen <s>Kāntimatī</s> herself, together with her daughter, sent word to me through a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> dependent near my pleasure-hill. He came to me and said: "Noble lord, this is the son of you both," and <s>Kāntimatī</s> had him placed in the care of her own daughter at the play-viewing area — and when this was told to me, my joy was immeasurable, streaming forth in torrents. But I, ill-fated, though I desired that son with all my being even amid the pleasures of love, had to abandon him and entrust him to this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> who was privy to the full secret of events past and future. Once again, having won over a confidante of <s>Kāntimatī</s>'s attendant queen through a female messenger, I was secretly told: "Enter at night through the hollow of the sacred fig tree at <s>Gupteśvara</s>, emerge through the tunnel, and feign sleep" — and thus I was united with <s>Kāntimatī</s>. But on one occasion, through a secret passage indicated by a <s>Drāviḍa</s> intermediary — a hole in the wall of the royal palace near the crossroads — I was spotted by the chief of guards who had been following my trail near the <s>Darpasāra</s> crossroads. The <s>Darpasāra</s> attendants seized me and reported to <s>Darpasāra</s> that the shadow-bodied one had fought with me. But he, recognizing me as the <s>Drāviḍa</s> <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> by lamplight, said with half-affectionate bewilderment: "The delusion of this strange creature — let it be observed. I shall set things firmly." He spoke one thing and left the other unsaid. Then, out of fear of punishment, the <s>Drāviḍa</s> <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> falsely denounced me to the royal household as an enemy in disguise. And <s>Darpasāra</s>, out of compassion, sparing me from death though I was deemed unworthy of such consideration, instructing me that this concealed passage through the inner wall was to be known only as mine under the name <s>Ghanaghōṣa</s>, banished me by the king's order of exile. Like <s>Dāśarathi</s> (Rāma) sent to the forest by a scoundrel's trick, I was cast out wearing golden bark-garments as my refuge. Like a wild mare entering a domain of lion-enemies. Even <s>Kāntimatī</s>'s people, though grateful, treated me as if of slavish birth even while carrying out their duties. Exiled to a distant land, I was made to dwell in the midst of a confined thieves' prison. Unknown to all, under the name <s>Vatsarāja</s>, right here in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>. In short, thus have hundredfold sufferings been heaped upon me by fate in every manner. And for reaching <s>Kāntimatī</s>, my kinsmen devised hundreds of tales of intricate paths through daring of arms. Thus did the minister, bearing the very name <s>Kāmapāla</s>, become my friend from those former times. And once, having been convinced by him, at his direction in the still of midnight, through the authority of the rod of justice, through his agency, having astonished <s>Darpasāra</s> with various arguments, demonstrations of knowledge, and visions of the future, having retrieved my daughter from the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>'s custody and bringing her to the outer gate, and having shown the boy to <s>Kāntimatī</s> — he who had thus learned the full inner account of <s>Darpasāra</s>'s affairs and wished to return to his own country — desired to enter the vacant inner palace of the lord of <s>Kāśī</s> at night through the passage within the wall, while the king was away on his departure from the city. This is the self-imposed ordeal of one who was condemned to death by the maddened lord of <s>Kāśī</s>.' Thus having understood <s>Pūrṇabhadra</s>'s account, I said: 'Do not distress yourself. Even an unrecognized fall of the body would benefit the earth, how much more so for one of your inner worth.' Having heard the full account, I, moved with compassion, said: 'Let another plan be devised.' He said with a smile: 'I think of nothing else. With this ally of mine who has lodged comfortably in my dwelling, great good fortune is assured for you, dear friend. And through your fire-like energy, <s>Udayin</s>, the desired outcome shall be achieved. Therefore, by your devoted and skillful service, having pleased our circle of friends, let protection now be awaited from Lord <s>Kāmapāla</s>.' And I, having observed Lord <s>Kāmapāla</s> for myself and having reported to him all these tidings, and having deliberated with my mother, brought <s>Kāmapāla</s> to a private meeting. Having narrated <s>Pūrṇabhadra</s>'s entire story and learning through him the full inner mind of <s>Darpasāra</s>, thereafter the rogue day by day grew increasingly impatient with me, unable to bear his elephant-bondage torment. 'Having come and been given the opportunity, a lamp was placed in the dwelling at night, where by someone for a single one whose exploits are foremost among the characters of the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s> (Tale of the Ten Princes) — there is a tunnel entrance to enter the inner palace from the elevated grounds' — thus was I informed through the passage in the wall. At night, in the still of midnight, I, being the master of the household watch, having found the house-guard asleep and the rest of the women's quarters occupied, having employed thousands of devices to search for the neighboring people, and having overcome the formidable <s>Śāṇḍilā</s> women of that household watch and the hostile ones — endowed with mixed qualities of all limbs, superior, capable of subduing resistance — I showed the boy and the girl together with the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> parents to my own parents, who received them with great hospitality and abundant virtues. And this daughter has now grown into a young woman. Even now the king does not remember. The grandfather had intended her for <s>Darpasāra</s>. But your mother <s>Kāntimatī</s> had vowed even while this girl was in the womb that she would be given in marriage to none other than you, her own mother's son. "Therefore, let the prince himself consider what is fitting in this matter." To her I replied: "This very day, having accomplished a certain task at the royal palace, I shall return and deal with you all as is proper." Going by the tunnel path shown by the lamp, in the still of midnight, having removed the half-bolt of that dwelling, I entered the chamber and seized <s>Siṃhaghoṣa</s>, who was sleeping in deep confidence, alive — like <s>Garuḍa</s> (the serpent's enemy) seizing a snake. Dragging him, still struggling, through that very wall-passage, I brought him into the presence of the women. Having brought him to my own house, with his feet bound in iron fetters, his head bowed low, his face soiled and wretched, his eyes red and streaming with tears, I showed him to my parents in private. And I told the tale of the tunnel. Then my parents, overjoyed upon hearing of that vile-minded one's deeds, having confined him in bonds, had me married to that maiden with proper rites. And that kingless realm came under our control. But my mother, though she wished to release <s>Siṃhaghoṣa</s>, would not set him free, out of fear of the populace's anger.

children.text: iti śrīdaṇḍinaḥ kṛtau daśakumāracariter'thapālacaritaṃ nāma caturtha ucchvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, in the composition of the illustrious <s>Daṇḍin</s>, in the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s>, [ends] the fourth chapter named 'The Adventures of <s>Arthapāla</s>.'

children.translated_text: 'Now then, let the honorable [<s>Mitragupta</s>] enter [and speak]' — thus the son of the king looked toward <s>Mitragupta</s>.

He too, bowing, reported: "Lord, while wandering in all directions in search of the lord, beneath a tree growing on the slope of the <s>Vindhya</s> — one that even a mynah bird could not perch on — when the face of the western quarter was adorned with the tender young foliage of the setting sun, having touched the water of a pool and performed the twilight worship, unable to traverse the uneven terrain made uniform by darkness, preparing a bed of tender shoots on the ground and about to lie down, making an anjali gesture at my head, [I prayed:] 'May whatever deity dwells in this tree be my refuge — for I sleep alone in this great forest, terrible with the wheeling of autumn fires, with deep caverns swollen by the flood of nocturnal darkness dark as <s>Śarva</s>'s throat' — placing my left arm [under my head], I fell asleep.
Then, in a moment, my limbs were somehow made comfortable by a touch rare on earth, my senses were delighted, my inner self was gladdened, my body-hair especially stood erect, and my right arm throbbed.
'How is this?' — slowly opening my eyes, I beheld overhead a canopy of white cloth, like panels of translucent moonlight.
Glancing to the left, I noticed against the palace wall a group of women sleeping deeply in trust on painted couches.
Casting my gaze to the right, I beheld some young woman — her breast-cloth slipped away, lying on a bed white as a sheet of ambrosia-foam, caught in the net of rays from the primordial Boar's tusk, her upper garment of milk-ocean silk fallen from her shoulders, [the earth itself seeming] to have fainted from fear and awe, rekindling with the fragrance-bearing breezes of her sighs — which caused the dancing of tender young shoots from the rays of her rosy lips — the god of love as if burnt by the fire of <s>Śiva</s>'s eye and remaining as mere embers, bearing a face with sleep-closed blue-lotus eyes like a lotus with its inner bees asleep, [looking] like some precious creeper of the wish-fulfilling trees of <s>Nandana</s> garden, uprooted and cast away by the streams of <s>Airāvata</s>'s rut-fluid.
And I wondered: 'Where has that great forest gone? Whence has this palace come, its banner-topped spire-peaks scratching the vault of the sky? Where is that bed of leaves spread on the forest ground, and whence this bed radiant with moonbeam-stores, of goose-down silk? And who are these beautiful women, sleeping at ease like a troupe of celestial nymphs fallen in a faint from the swing-rope of cool moonbeams? And who is this goddess, with lotus in hand, lying upon a bed-surface under an upper cover spotless as the autumn moon's disc?
She is surely not a celestial woman, for, gently massaged by the moonbeams, she contracts like a lotus-pond. Her cheek appears marked with perspiration lines like a pale-ripe mango fruit speckled with drops of juice from a broken stem; on her breast-slope, hot with the unrestrained heat of fresh youth, the birthmark loses its color. And her garments show a dustiness appropriate to use — therefore she is indeed human.
And fortunately she is of untouched youth, for though delicate, her limbs appear firm; though extremely smooth, her complexion seems tinged with pallor; from not knowing the torments of love, the redness on her face is not very vivid; her cheek-surface is firm like a campaka bud-petal, with coral-lustred lower lip-jewel and incompletely reddened base; and she sleeps with confident sweetness, free from the apprehension of love's arrow-fall; nor is this breast-surface one with breasts spread by merciless pressure; and I — whose mind has not transgressed the boundaries of propriety — have an attraction for this woman.
But if, in accordance with proximity, I embrace her, clearly she will abandon sleep with a cry of distress. And I shall not be able to lie down without embracing her. Therefore, let what will be, be. "I shall test my fortune here" — thus, as if touched-yet-untouched, with some sign of suppressed passion, I remained lying still.
She then — her left side made comfortable by something trembling and goose-bumped, with body languid from the onset of gentle yawning, half-opening her eyes with drowsy pupils not fully freed from the astringency of unfinished sleep at the outer corners — was made to pass through various states wonderfully produced by Love: fear, surprise, joy, passion, doubt, coquetry, confusion, with intervals of shame. Somehow restraining her voice that was rising to wake her attendants, her heart overpowered by love's rush, and her limbs bound by the sweat and goose-bumps of bashful exertion, scrutinizing my limbs with a longing gaze sweetly narrowed to three-quarters and very slowly directed — though she had drawn her upper body far away, she lay down with a start on that very same bed.
Some sleep overcame me even though my mind was filled with passion. Then, my limbs distressed by the pain of unfavorable contact, I awoke. And upon awakening — behold! — the great forest, that same tree-base, that same bed of leaves was mine. And the night had passed.
And I thought: 'Was this a dream, or a deception, or some demonic or divine illusion? Let what will be, be. I shall not — without truly understanding this — leave this bed on the ground. I shall lie here devoted to the local deity for as long as I live.' With this resolve I remained.
Then there appeared some woman — her body dark as a garland of blue lotuses scorched by the sun's rays, her garment and upper cloth worn, with lower lip pale from lack of lac-dye and its luster weakened by the heat of sighs — as if vomiting the tawny-smoke-colored fire of separation, bearing two eyes made even more red from the residue of blood caused by the continuous discharge of streams of tears, with her mass of hair become a single braid through the loosening of the bonds of family propriety, wrapped in strips of dark cloth like a flag of wifely devotion moving about, thin and gaunt yet by divine power not entirely diminished in the space of her beauty — this married woman, raising me as I prostrated with both vine-like arms trembling with joy, embracing me like a son, smelling my head, shedding [tears of] affection from both breasts under the pretext of breast-milk, with cool tears, her throat choked, spoke with love-stammering voice:
'My child, if the queen of the king of <s>Magadha</s>, <s>Vasumatī</s>, has told you — having placed the young <s>Arthapāla</s> in my hand and narrating a story connected with her lord, sons, and friends, set in motion by the king of kings, and then disappeared saying she was the daughter of <s>Maṇibhadra</s> — I am your mother.
Having left the presence of your father <s>Kāmapāla</s>, son of <s>Dharmapāla</s>, younger brother of <s>Sumantra</s>, my mind troubled by his causeless anger, distressed by the pain of separation, I was cursed in a dream by some being in demonic form who approached me: "I shall dwell at the [temple of] <s>Caṇḍikā</s> within you for just one year, to your suffering in exile" — even as he spoke thus, I was possessed and I awoke.
And that year passed, long as a thousand years. But when the night had passed, having experienced the festival-gathering of the god of gods, the three-eyed Lord [<s>Śiva</s>], at <s>Śrāvastī</s>, and seeing my kinsmen assembled from their various places, freed from the curse, I set out to go to my husband's side — and just then you arrived here and, saying "I have taken refuge with the deity here," fell asleep.
Thus, being afflicted by the suffering of the curse, I did not truly recognize you at that time; but since you had come seeking refuge, it would have been improper to abandon you in this great forest full of constant dangers — so I transported you too, as if in a dream.
And as I approached that divine house again, I thought: "How shall I go to the gathering with this young man?" Then, finding by chance the daughter of the king of <s>Śrāvastī</s> — whose name suited his nature — <s>Dharmavardhana</s>, finding <s>Navamālikā</s> lying on a broad, smooth bed-surface atop the pleasure-pavilion of the women's quarters in the pleasant heat-season, and thinking "Fortunately she is asleep, and her attendants are in deep sleep — let this <s>Brahmin</s> youth sleep here for a short while until I return having accomplished my purpose" — I laid you there and went to that place.
And having seen the festival splendor, having enjoyed the happiness of seeing my own people, having saluted the lord of the three worlds, and having bowed to the goddess <s>Ambikā</s> with a heart devoted in worship — having felt alarm at the abandonment of my own disguise — by that daughter of the mountain, the goddess, I was told with a smile: "O blessed one, do not fear! You shall now go to your husband's side. Your curse is gone." Thus favored, immediately restored to my full power, I returned and recognized you properly upon seeing you: "How — this is indeed my son, the beloved friend of my dear <s>Arthapāla</s>, named <s>Pramati</s> — and wretchedly I showed indifference to him in my ignorance!
Moreover, he is attached to this woman. And the princess desires him. He is young. And both of them, having lain together as if marked by love, do not reveal themselves to each other out of modesty and bashfulness. And I must go. And this princess, though her love was aroused, has not confided in any friend or attendant for the sake of keeping the secret. Let me take the prince back. And in the future, having found an opportunity, he will accomplish this aim by whatever means are suitable." With this thought, having put you to sleep by my power, I brought you back to this very bed of leaves.
Thus it happened. And now I shall go to your father's feet.' — saying this, embracing me again and again as I stood with palms joined, smelling my head, kissing both my cheeks, overcome with affection, she departed.
And I, subject to the five-arrowed one [the god of love], proceeded toward <s>Śrāvastī</s>. On the road, in a great market-town, there was a great commotion among the townspeople about red-crested [fighting cocks]. I was present there and smiled at something. An old gambler — some <s>Brahmin</s> — sitting near me, quietly and smilingly asked me about it. And I said: 'How is it that the eastern-yard rooster of the coconut breed has not been recognized by these men to be superior in strength? A stork-breed red-crest has thus been set loose against one of greater power.'
He too, being knowledgeable, said: 'What use being instructed by these ignorants? Be silent' — and taking betel with camphor from a small box, giving it to me, telling amusing stories, he stood for a moment. And the two birds fought most fiercely, each side urging its champion with lion-like roars. And that western-yard rooster was defeated. The old gambler, delighted at his own rooster's victory, forming a friendship with me — incongruous in age — that very day had me bathed and fed at his house, and the next day, as I was departing for <s>Śrāvastī</s>, accompanied me and said 'Remember me when the occasion is right' — dismissing me like a friend, he returned.
And I, having gone to <s>Śrāvastī</s>, weary from the journey, lay down in a creeper-bower in a <s>Brahmin</s> park. Awakened by the cry of geese at dawn, I arose and saw some young woman approaching me with feet musical with tinkling anklets. She, having come, looked alternately — with surprise, speculation, and joy — at some male portrait drawn on a painting-cloth held in her own hand, and at me, and stood for a moment. And I too, seeing in that painting-cloth a resemblance to myself, considering her gaze and gestures to be not accidental, said: 'Is not this a beautiful garden-area common to all? Why endure the trouble of standing here long? Please sit down.' She, with a smile, said 'I am favored' and sat down.
And some conversation arose between us, interspersed with local news. And she, speaking in the course of the conversation, said: 'You are a visitor from another land. And your limbs appear weary from travel. If there is no fault in it, please grace my house to rest today.' And I said: 'O simple one, that is no fault but a virtue indeed!' — and following her path, I went to her house, was honored with bathing, food, and such befitting a king, and seated comfortably in private, I was asked: 'Noble sir, wandering to distant regions, have you encountered anything wonderful?'
And in my mind I thought: 'This is a great opportunity. She is surely the friend of the princess, whose love has been observed by her entire retinue. And in this painting-cloth too, there is the pavilion-terrace above with a white canopy arranged over it, and the broad bed upon it, white as autumn cloud-layers, and lying upon it — with eyes licked by sleep — this is indeed a portrait of myself! Therefore the princess too has surely been brought to such a state by the god of love. Being unbearably tormented by the fever of passion and driven to madness, when asked by her friend persistently about the cause of her altered state, she gave a fitting reply cleverly through this very portrait. And from the resemblance in form, she has questioned me out of doubt — let me resolve her doubt by narrating my experience.' Having thus determined, I said: 'Good lady, give me the painting-cloth.'
She handed it to me. Then, taking it, I drew upon it that very beloved — who was pretending to sleep, trembling with the surge of awakening passion — and wrote: 'A certain such young woman, sleeping beside such a man in a forest — was observed by me who had been asleep. Was this indeed a dream?'
She, delighted, asked me in detail, and I told her the entire account. And she described her friend's states that had occurred on my account. And hearing this — since her friend's mind was inclined to favor me — [she said:] 'Spend some days here. Let me contrive some means for you to live fearlessly in the women's quarters, and I shall return.' Somehow obtaining her consent, I went back to that same village and met the old gambler.
He too, with eagerness, gave me rest and provided bathing and food as before. I asked him in private: 'Sir, for what reason have you returned so soon?' I replied to him: 'The elder asks at the right place. Listen: there is a city named <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Its lord is a king named <s>Dharmavardhana</s>, another <s>Dharma</s> incarnate. His daughter — a reproach to beauty itself, the very life-breath of the flower-bowed god of love, mocking tender jasmine with her delicacy — a maiden named <s>Navamālikā</s>. She, seen by me in a trance-vision, scattered upon my vital parts a garland of glances like a volley of love's arrows. And no physician other than you, equal to <s>Dhanvantari</s>, is capable of extracting that shaft — therefore I have returned. So please devise some plan.
Here am I — in woman's disguise — I shall become your so-called daughter. And you, accompanied by me, shall approach <s>Dharmavardhana</s> seated on the throne of justice and say: 'This is my only daughter. Her mother died when she was just born. Being both father and mother, I alone raised her. To earn the bride-price of learning, her husband-to-be — some <s>Brahmin</s> youth born in our marriage-alliance family — went to the invincible city of <s>Avantī</s>. She was promised to him, and is suitable for no other. And she has reached womanhood, while he is delayed. Therefore, to bring him and have him take her hand, I — with my charge entrusted to the king — shall renounce the world. For daughters, once past childhood — especially motherless ones — are hard to protect. I have come to the lord, who stands in the place of father and mother to his subjects, a refuge for the afflicted. If the lord, distinguished in the conduct of primordial kings, counts this old <s>Brahmin</s> — a humble scholar, homeless, and a guest — among those worthy of favor, then let this daughter dwell under the shade of your arm's tree, with her virtue intact, until I bring the one who shall take her hand.'
Addressed thus, he will surely be honored, and will have me lodged near his own daughter. And you — when the month of <s>Phālguna</s> arrives, on the <s>Uttara-Phalgunī</s> lunar day, there will be a festival of pilgrimage for the people of the royal harem. At a distance of one cow's range east of the pilgrimage site, in the middle of a reed-cluster, at the shrine of <s>Kārtikeya</s>, you shall stand holding a pair of white garments in your hand.
Then I, having spent that time in intimacy with the princess without suspicion, will once again at that festival — while sporting in the waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> amidst the confusion of the pleasure-excursion in the assembly of maidens — dive in and rise up near you. Then, putting on the garments you offer, having removed the woman's disguise, becoming the so-called son-in-law, I shall follow you. And the princess, searching for me here and there and not finding me, will stand weeping in the harem saying "Without her, I shall not eat." And at the great commotion arising from that — with attendants wailing, friends weeping, townspeople grieving, and the king with his ministers bewildered and at a loss — you shall come to the audience-hall and, placing me before them, say:
"Lord, this is my son-in-law, worthy of serving your majesty's arm. He has studied the four <s>Vedas</s>, mastered the six auxiliary sciences, is skilled in logic (<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>), expert in the practice of the sixty-four arts, especially knowledgeable in the science of elephants, chariots, and horses, unmatched in archery, weapon-play, and mace-fighting, versed in the <s>Purāṇas</s> and <s>Itihāsas</s>, a composer of poems, plays, and tales, a knower of political science (<s>arthaśāstra</s>) with its <s>Upaniṣads</s>, free from jealousy toward others' virtues, trusting in friends, capable, generous, retentive of what he has learned, and free from pride. I cannot find even an atom of fault in him, nor anything absent among his virtues. For one such as me — a mere <s>Brahmin</s> — such a son-in-law is not easily found. Having given my daughter to him, I would pass to the final stage of life appropriate to old age, if the lord approves."
He, hearing this, his face overcome with pallor and filled with the utmost embarrassment, will begin to console this gentleman, along with his ministers, by speaking of the impermanence of such arrangements.
But you, deaf to their words, having wept at full throat, your voice hoarse from tears, will gather firewood, kindle a fire, and prepare to ascend a pyre at the gate of the royal palace.
Then at once, the king with his ministers, falling at your feet, will appease you with ample wealth, give his daughter to me, and — his satisfaction won by my worthiness — will entrust the entire burden of the kingdom to me.
This is the plan to be executed, if it pleases you.'
And that sharp one — the foremost of gamblers, who had practiced cunning and deception many times — <s>Pāñcālaśarman</s>, carried out what was said, and even more skillfully. And there was a perfect fulfillment of my desires without any delay.
