He too narrated: 'Lord, I too, having set out to wander with friends for the common cause, observed a great festival gathering in the outer garden of a city called <s>Dāmalipta</s> in the <s>Suhma</s> country. There, in a bower of <s>atimuktaka</s> creepers, I saw a certain young man, lovesick, entertaining himself by playing the <s>vīṇā</s>. I asked him: "Good sir, what is this festival? For what purpose has it been begun? And for what reason do you stand apart, seemingly lovesick, with only your lute for company, disregarding the festival?" He replied: "Friend, the lord of <s>Suhma</s>, named <s>Tuṅgadhanvan</s>, being childless, had prayed at that temple to the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s>, who dwells there though the passion of <s>Vindhya</s> has been forgotten, for two children." And indeed, to him as he lay sleeping, she commanded in a dream: "You shall have one son, and one daughter shall be born. He shall serve as the husband of that [daughter]. But she, from her seventh year until her marriage, should worship me each month during the <s>Kṛttikā</s> asterism with ball-dancing, for the attainment of a virtuous husband. And she should be given to whomever she desires. And let that festival be named the Ball Festival (<s>Kandukotsava</s>)." Then, after a short time, the king's beloved queen named <s>Medinī</s> bore one son. And one daughter was also born. Today the princess named <s>Kandukāvatī</s> is going to worship the goddess <s>Somāpīḍā</s> with ball-play. Now, her friend and foster-sister named <s>Candrasenā</s> was my beloved. And in these days she has been forcefully pursued by the prince <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s>. Therefore I sit here lovesick, my mind tormented by the pain of <s>Manmatha</s>'s (Love's) arrow-shafts, somewhat consoling myself with the soft sound of the <s>vīṇā</s> in this secluded spot." And at that very moment, the tinkling of anklets was heard. A certain woman arrived, and the moment he saw her, he rose with eyes blooming with joy, and she having embraced his neck, they sat down together right there. He confided: "This is she who is as dear as my life, whose separation burns me like fire. And the prince who is stealing my life has rendered me as cold as death itself. Yet I cannot commit a sin against the king's son. Therefore, having her look upon me one last time, I shall give up my life for which there is no remedy." But she, her face streaming with tears, replied: "Do not, my lord, resolve upon such a rash act on my account. You who, born from the best caravan-leader <s>Arthadāsa</s>, were named <s>Kośadāsa</s> by your elders, and then, because of your excessive attachment to me, were proclaimed <s>Veśadāsa</s> (slave of a courtesan) by your enemies — if you were to die and I were to live, the world would conclude: 'The courtesan-house is merciless.' Therefore take me today to whatever country you wish." He then asked me: "Good sir, among the kingdoms you have seen, which is prosperous, rich in harvests, and most populated by virtuous people?" I replied to him with a slight smile: "Good sir, this [earth] is vast, bounded by the ocean and sky. There is no end to delightful countries in various places. However, I could not even here devise any means for you two to live comfortably. Therefore I would have to be your guide." Meanwhile, the jingling of jeweled anklets arose. She, becoming flustered, said: "The king's daughter <s>Kandukāvatī</s> has arrived to worship the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s> with ball-play. And she may be seen without restriction at this ball-festival. May your eyes be blessed. Come, both of you, to watch. I shall remain near her" — and she departed. We two followed her. On a great jeweled stage-platform I first beheld that red-lipped one. And she instantly took her place in my heart. She had not been seen before by me or anyone else in the interval. I thought in astonishment: "Is this <s>Lakṣmī</s> (the goddess of Fortune)? No, no! For <s>Lakṣmī</s> holds a lotus in her hand, but this one's hand itself is a lotus. And that [goddess] was previously enjoyed by the ancient man and former kings, whereas this one's youth is blameless and unwithered." Even as I thought thus, she, of faultless limbs throughout, with the tips of her interlaced hand-shoots touching the ground, with swaying dark curly locks, having reverently bowed to the goddess with graceful charm, took up the ball — like <s>Anaṅga</s> (the Bodiless Love-god) himself, with eyes reddened by passion. She dropped it playfully to the ground. As it rose gently, with her slightly curved thumb and softly extended fingers, striking it with her hand-shoot and tossing it up with the back of her hand, she caught it in mid-air as it fell — marked by flirtatious glances, like a cluster of flowers strung with garlands of bees. She released it. Striking it softly and gently in a rhythm alternating between slow and fast, she displayed in that instant a pulverized footwork. And having calmed it, she sent it soaring again with merciless blows. And conversely, she brought it to rest. Hitting it alternately with left and right hands as it came in a straight path, she made it rise like a bird. Catching it as it fell from a great height, she wove a musical pattern. Sending it in every direction, she made it return. Thus playing with a sweetness of manifold techniques, receiving ever-varying words of praise from the audience seated in the arena, their hearts enraptured, moment by moment her charm increasing — with <s>Kośadāsa</s> leaning on her shoulder, his cheeks prickling with goosebumps, his eyes wide — she stood facing me. Her sidelong glance first descended from <s>Kāma</s> (Love), her playfully arched brow following that path, the rays of her lips, agitated by the wind of her breath, like playful shoots, striking as if eager to catch the fragrance of her face-lotus, during circular revolutions the ball moving so swiftly it seemed as if she were entering a cage of flowers out of modesty at seeing me, when it came in five bounces all five seeming to attack simultaneously like the five arrows of the Five-Arrowed One, startling with terror, in zigzag paths displaying the thick play of passion like a flash of lightning — her foot-movements keeping musical time with the jingling of ornamental jewels, her <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips bathed in the radiance of a pretended smile, the burden of her crest re-gathered after slipping from her shoulder, the girdle-string of jeweled bells jingling as they clashed together, brilliantly flashing with the hem of her garment dangling and swaying from her broad upraised hips, her graceful ball struck by extended, contracted, and undulating vine-arms, her arm-nooses thrown back, her playful curls clinging to her twisting torso above, quickly readjusting the golden leaf-ornament that had slipped from her ear without interrupting her natural play, the ball repeatedly tossed between her hands and feet and spinning inside and outside her arms, her slender middle-stalk invisible from the continuous bending and rising, her pearl necklace flying free from the uncontrolled falling and rising — the perspiration beading on her cheeks spoiling the leaf-designs whose drying was attended by the breeze of the ear-shoot, one hand-shoot occupied with restraining the garment slipping from the slope of her breasts — now sitting, now rising, now closing, now opening her eyes, now standing, now moving — the princess played in an exceedingly wondrous fashion. Striking [the ball] both on the ground and in the air, she displayed varieties of play-figures, remarkable, with one ball or with many. And having sported with her dear friends <s>Candrasenā</s> and others, at the end of the play having bowed to the goddess, accompanied by her retinue with what seemed like loving intent toward me — bestowing upon me a sidelong glance like a blue-lotus arrow of the Flower-armed [Love-god] — with a pretended [look back], repeatedly turning the moon-circle of her face, as if sending her heart near me to see whether it would return or not, she went with her friends to the maidens' quarters. And I, overwhelmed by <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love), having gone to my lodging, was lavishly attended by <s>Kośadāsa</s> with bathing, dining, and such comforts. In the evening, <s>Candrasenā</s> approached, bowed to me in private, and pressing her husband's shoulder affectionately against hers, sat down beside me. And the delighted <s>Kośadāsa</s> announced: "May you always be thus for as long as you live, O long-eyed one — a vessel of your grace!" I replied with a smile: "Friend, why wish for this? There is a certain collyrium. If this one applies it to her eyes, the prince, seeing her as a monkey, will be disgusted and abandon her." And she said with a smile: "This servant is exceedingly graced by you, that in this very birth of mine, my human form will be removed and I shall be made into a monkey! Let that be. Our desire is accomplished by other means too. Today at the ball-festival, the princess, desiring you — whose love-god form she laughed at [pretending to mock] — will be exceedingly overcome by the enemy of <s>Śambara</s> [i.e., <s>Kāma</s>] as if in anger. This matter, being understood by me who knows the situation, will be communicated to my own mother, and by her to her [the princess's] mother, and by the queen to the king. And the king, once informed, will have his daughter's hand given to you. Then the prince shall have to be your subordinate. For this is the ordinance commanded by the deity. And when the kingdom is in your power, <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s> will not be able to seize me against your will. So let him endure three or four days." Having addressed me thus and embracing her beloved, she departed. And for <s>Kośadāsa</s> and me, pondering many alternatives according to her words, the night somehow passed. At the end of the night, having performed the proper observances, I went to that same garden-spot, rendered beautiful by the sight of my beloved. There the prince too approached, and courteously engaging me with agreeable conversation, without any arrogance, he sat for a while. Having taken me to a place of service, he attended to me with bathing, dining, sleeping, and such exchanges as befitting an equal. But as I lay on the bed, experiencing in a dream the joy of seeing and embracing my beloved, I was bound with a heavy iron fetter by many strong men, restrained by their massive arm-staves, overpowering me. And being suddenly awakened, he abruptly spoke: "O wretch! The words of the slain <s>Candrasenā</s> were overheard, having escaped through the lattice-window, and by this hunchback woman, sent to observe her movements — you are apparently desired by the wretched <s>Kandukāvatī</s>, and I am apparently to serve you, and apparently at your command I am to give <s>Candrasenā</s> to <s>Kośadāsa</s>!" — having said this, he looked at one of his attendants and ordered: "Throw this one into the ocean." And that one, delighted as if he had obtained a kingdom, said "Lord, as you command" and did as instructed. But I, without any support, flailing my arms here and there, clutching some piece of driftwood given by fate to my chest, floated along until the day retreated and the entire night [had passed]. At dawn, some vessel appeared. The <s>Yavanas</s> (Greeks/foreigners) aboard it, having pulled me out, told the captain of the ship named <s>Rāmeṣu</s>: "Who is this person found in the water, bound in iron fetters? This one too could water a thousand grapevines in a single moment [i.e., he looks strong enough for hard labor]." At that very instant, some [other ship] pursued my [rescuer's ship], surrounded by many vessels. The <s>Yavanas</s> were attacked. Then the enemy ships, swift as hounds upon a boar, surrounded our boat. Battle commenced. The <s>Yavanas</s> were being defeated. I consoled those sinking, helpless ones and declared: "Remove my iron fetters! I myself shall crush your enemies." They did so, and with a terrible-twanging bow raining showers of broad arrows, I cut all those opposing warriors into tiny pieces. Leaping onto the enemy boat that was locked with ours — its warriors slain and shattered — I rushed at the captain there and seized him alive. And he turned out to be none other than <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s> himself. Having recognized him, I spoke to the ashamed one: "Father, have you seen the play of Destiny?" The sailors, having bound him extremely tightly with my very own chain, raised joyful cries and honored me. But that ship, driven irresistibly by unfavorable winds, traveled far and clung fast to some island. There, desiring sweet water, grains, and roots, fruits, and tubers, we descended into a firmly cast ring of boulders. There was a great mountain there. And I, [thinking] "Ah, how delightful is this mountain-slope! How lovely is this foothill region, rich in fragrant stones! How cool is this mountain-stream, superior in drops of nectar from the blue-lotus and lotus! How charming is this expanse of tree-groves burdened with clusters of flowers of many colors!" — gazing with ever-unsatisfied eyes at many things, having unknowingly climbed to the summit of the mountain, I reached a certain lake, grey with lotus-pollen, reddened by the radiance of ruby stairway-stones. And having bathed and savored some lotus-root stalks sweet as nectar, while a <s>kahlāra</s> lotus clung to my shoulder, I was accosted by some terrifying <s>Brahmārākṣasa</s> (Brahmin-demon) lurking on the shore, who charged at me threatening: "Who are you? Where are you from?" And I, fearlessly, answered him: "Friend, I am a twice-born. From the shore to the ocean, from the ocean to the <s>Yavana</s> ship, from the <s>Yavana</s> ship to this best of mountains with its marvelous stones I have come, and by chance I rest in this lake. May it be well with you." He said: "If you do not answer my questions, I shall eat you."

children.translated_text: Human effort is abundant when the occasion arises.' Having spoken thus, with a smile anointing his row of teeth, Lord <s>Rājavāhana</s> cast his gaze, blooming with delight, upon <s>Mantragupta</s>. He, it is said, with one hand slightly covering his face, his lip-jewel trembling with agitation from the tooth-marks eagerly bestowed by his lovely beloved, narrated his own adventures with the lip-consonants omitted. // Dkc_2,6 //

Therein, '<s>Dhūminī</s>, <s>Gominī</s>, <s>Nimbavatī</s>, and <s>Nitambavatī</s> are the authorities,' thus instructed by me, he said—'Tell me, what are they like?' Here is the illustration— 'There is a country called <s>Trigarta</s>. There lived three householders, brothers rich in abundant wealth, named <s>Dhanaka</s>, <s>Dhānyaka</s>, and <s>Dhanyaka</s>. While they were alive, the thousand-eyed one (<s>Indra</s>) did not rain for twelve years; the crops lost their essence, the herbs became barren, the forest trees bore no fruit, the clouds were impotent, the rivers diminished in their streams, the pools were reduced to mere mud, the spring-circles had no outflow, roots, tubers, and fruits became scarce, stories of prosperity ceased, auspicious festival rites declined, bands of thieves multiplied, the people devoured one another, human skulls white as cranes rolled here and there, gaunt flocks of crows wandered about, and cities, villages, hamlets, market-towns, and rivers became deserted. These householders, having consumed all their stores of grain, having eaten in order their goats and sheep, their herds of buffaloes, their cattle, their male and female servants, their children, and their eldest and middle wives, resolved—"Tomorrow <s>Dhūminī</s>, the youngest wife, shall be eaten by <s>Dhanaka</s>." Then the youngest brother <s>Dhanyaka</s>, unable to bear the thought of his beloved being eaten, fled with her that very night. Carrying her, exhausted from the journey, he entered the forest. As he led her, whose hunger and thirst were allayed by his own flesh and blood, he saw on the way some man writhing on the ground with his hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off. Being tender-hearted, he carried that man too on his shoulders and dwelt for a long time in a dense region rich in roots and game, in a leaf-hut carefully constructed. He nourished that man, whose wounds he treated with <s>iguḍī</s> oil and other remedies, with meat and vegetables no differently from himself. And when that man, now well-nourished and with restored vitality, was encountered one day while <s>Dhanyaka</s> had gone out hunting for game, that <s>Dhūminī</s> approached him with amorous desire. Though rebuked by him, she forcibly enjoyed him. When her husband returned and asked for water, she said "Draw it from the well and drink; my head aches from a headache," and threw the bucket with its rope before him. And as he was drawing up water from the well, she went behind him in an instant and pushed him in. She then carried that crippled man on her shoulders, wandering from region to region, and gained the reputation of a devoted wife, and received many kinds of honors. Then, through the grace of the king of <s>Avantī</s>, she lived in exceedingly great prosperity. Now when her husband, who had been seen and rescued from the well by caravan travelers seeking water, was found wandering in <s>Avantī</s> seeking food, that <s>Dhūminī</s> caused the unknowing king to decree an elaborate execution for that virtuous man, saying "This is the wretch who maimed my husband." But <s>Dhanyaka</s>, given a last hearing while being led to the execution ground, since some life remained to him, humbly told the officer—"The crippled man whom I am said to have maimed is an ascetic; if he were to testify about my sin, then my punishment would be justified." When that crippled man was brought before him upon the inquiry "What fault is there?" the maimed man, with tears, fell at his feet and, being noble-minded, truthfully declared his benefactor's virtue and that faithless woman's misconduct of such a kind. The enraged king had her face disfigured, and that evildoer was made a cook for the dogs. And <s>Dhanyaka</s> was shown royal favor. Therefore I say—"The heart of a woman is cruel." When further questioned, he narrated the story of <s>Gominī</s>— "There is in <s>Draviḍa</s> a city named <s>Kāñcī</s>. In it there was a merchant's son named <s>Śaktikumāra</s>, whose wealth amounted to many <s>koṭis</s> (tens of millions). He, being about eighteen years of age, fell into reflection—"Neither for those without wives nor for those with unsuitable wives is there any happiness. So how might I find a virtuous spouse?" Then, not perceiving the fortuitous good fortune in wives obtained through the reports of matchmakers, he assumed the guise of a fortune-teller named <s>Kārtāntika</s>, and with a measure of rice wrapped in the end of his garment, he wandered the land. Thinking "This man knows the science of bodily marks," fathers of daughters showed their daughters to him. Whenever he saw any well-marked maiden of suitable caste, he would say—"Good lady, can you prepare a wholesome meal for us with this measure of rice?" Being laughed at and dismissed, he wandered from house to house. But one day, among the <s>Śibis</s>, in a town, he saw a certain maiden with sparse ornaments being shown by her nurse—one whose father had departed along with his uncles, whose household had fallen into ruin. Fixing his gaze upon her, he reflected—"Indeed, every limb of this maiden is neither too stout nor too thin, neither too short nor too long, not misshapen, and well-groomed. Her hands are marked with many auspicious lines in the shapes of red-soled fingers, fish, lotus, and water-pot; her feet have even ankles, are fleshy, and veinless; her shanks are proportionately rounded; her knees are as if swallowed by her plump thighs, hard to discern; her hip region is divided at once into a square shape, adorned by the division of the <s>kundara</s> (waist), and arranged in the form of a chariot wheel; her navel circle is thin, slightly depressed, and deep; her belly is adorned with three folds; her breasts, which spread across the chest area, have raised nipples and are beautiful in their broad expanse; the soles of her palms are marked with lines signifying abundance of wealth, grain, and sons, with smooth, prominent, tender nails, straight, proportionately rounded, copper-colored fingers, and her forearms, delicate at the depressed shoulder region, with concealed joints, are graceful; her neck is slender, conch-shaped, round, and curved; her lower lip is round in the middle with distinct color; her chin is shapely and not compressed; her cheek-circles are full and firm; her brow-creepers are joined, curved, dark, and glossy; her nose resembles an unblown <s>tilaka</s> (sesame) flower, not overly large; her eyes are slow-moving, gentle yet steady in their gaze, brilliant in three parts of deep black, white, and red, and beautifully elongated; her forehead is lovely as a crescent moon; her rows of curls are charming as dark sapphire stone; her lotus-face has ear-ornaments hanging gracefully like doubled, coiled, tender lotus stalks; her mass of hair is not excessively curly, abundant, beautiful in color even at the tips without tawny hue, each strand naturally uniform, glossy, dark blue, and fragrant. This form does not belie good character. And my heart is attached to this one alone. Therefore, I shall test her and then marry her. For those who act without deliberation surely encounter endless chains of regret." With an affectionate gaze he said—"Good lady, is there skill to prepare us a fine meal from this measure of rice?" Thereupon the old maidservant was glanced at meaningfully by her. Taking just that measure of grain from his hand, she seated him in a certain veranda area, well-sprinkled and swept, having offered him water to wash his feet. That maiden herself husked those fragrant rice grains, dried them in the sun by the proper measure, turning them again and again, and on firm, level ground, gently pressing them with the back of a bamboo tube, she separated the unbroken grains from the husks. She told the nurse—"Mother, goldsmiths want these husks, which are suitable for polishing ornaments. Give them these, and with the <s>kākiṇīs</s> (small coins) obtained, bring firewood that is neither too moist nor too dry but of moderate firmness, a cooking pot of measured capacity, and two bowls." When this was done, she placed those rice grains in a mortar of <s>kakubha</s> wood with a neither too deep nor too shallow and wide belly, and with a heavy pestle of <s>khādira</s> wood wrapped in iron at the tip, equal-bodied, with visible slenderness at the middle, elongated, she exerted her arms with four graceful strokes of throwing and lifting, repeatedly picking up the grains with her fingers, winnowing them to remove the bran and chaff, washing them several times with water, and having offered worship at the hearth, cast them into water boiled to five times its volume. When the grains became loose-limbed, when they began to swell and were passing beyond the budding stage at the greatest rate, she reduced the fire, and with the pot covered at the mouth, she strained out the rice-water. Stirring with a ladle, turning by measure, when the grains were evenly cooked, she set that pot upside down. She sprinkled the inner-cored firewood with water, extinguished the fire, turned them to black charcoal, and sent them to those who wanted them. "With the <s>kākiṇīs</s> obtained from these, bring vegetables, ghee, yogurt, oil, <s>āmalaka</s> (gooseberry), <s>ciñcā</s> (tamarind) fruit, and whatever else is available." When the nurse had done so, having prepared two or three relishes, she cooled that rice-water by placing the moist vessel upon fresh sand, using gentle breeze from a palmyra fan, prepared it with salt and spices, and gave it a fumigation of charcoal smoke; she also ground that <s>āmalaka</s> smooth until it was fragrant as a lotus, and through the nurse's mouth urged him to bathe. Having bathed with the oil and <s>āmalaka</s> provided by the freshly bathed nurse, he bathed in due order. Having bathed, he ascended a wooden plank on the sprinkled and swept floor, and sat touching the two bowls placed upon a moist, cut banana leaf from the courtyard, of which one-third remained, pale and green. She first served him that rice-water. Having drunk it, his travel-fatigue was removed; he stood joyful, with his whole body refreshed. Then, giving him two spoonfuls of that rice, she served a measure of ghee, soup, and a relish. She fed him the remaining rice with yogurt, with powder of <s>trijātaka</s> (three spices), and with fragrant, cool <s>kālaśeya</s> (dark grape juice) and <s>kāñjika</s> (fermented gruel). Even with rice remaining, he was no longer hungry. And he asked for drinking water. Then she poured water collected in a new pitcher, fumigated with <s>aguru</s> (aloe) incense, scented with fresh <s>pāṭalā</s> flowers, endowed with the fragrance of blooming <s>utpala</s> (blue lotus) woven into it, pouring it in a stream from a tube. And he, with the bowl held to his mouth, his eyelashes reddening with cool dewdrop-like particles, his ears delighted by the sound of the flowing stream, his cheeks rough with goosebumps arising from the pleasure of touch, his nostrils expanded by the fragrance squeezed from coral-like blossoms, his sense of taste overwhelmed by the excellence of sweetness—drank that clear water to his throat's fill. Stopped by a signal of her head-shaking, the maiden then gave him rinse-water from another vessel for sipping. The old nurse, clearing away his leftovers, spread her own upper garment as a cloth on the floor smeared with fresh green cow-dung, and he rested for a moment. Being fully satisfied, he married the maiden with proper rites and took her home. Having taken her, heedless of this, he took some courtesan into his household. That wife treated her like a dear friend. And she served her husband like a god, free from sloth. She carried out household duties without fail. Being a treasure of courtesy, she brought the household servants under her own authority. And her husband, conquered by her virtues, entrusted the entire household to her alone, and with his life and body dependent on her alone, he pursued the three aims of life (<s>trivarga</s>). Therefore I say—"The virtues of a wife serve the dear welfare of the householder." Then, questioned by him, he narrated the story of <s>Nimbavatī</s>— "There is in <s>Saurāṣṭra</s> a city named <s>Valabhī</s>. In it, a daughter named <s>Ratnavatī</s> belonged to a ship-captain named <s>Guhagupta</s>, equal in wealth to <s>Kubera</s>, lord of the <s>Guhyakas</s>. Her hand was sought by a caravan-leader's son named <s>Balabhadra</s>, who came by way of the river <s>Madhumatī</s>. But that new bride, whose conjugal pleasure was rudely interrupted by his haste, quickly developed no small aversion toward him. She did not wish to see him again. He too, transgressing hundreds of entreaties from friends, abandoned even visits to her house out of shame. From that very time onward, her own family and servants mocked that unfortunate woman, saying "This is not <s>Ratnavatī</s> (jewel-woman), but <s>Nimbavatī</s> (bitter-neem-woman)." After some time had passed, she, filled with remorse and pondering "What is my recourse?" saw a certain elderly female mendicant whom she regarded as a mother, who had come with flower-offerings left over from worship. Before her, in private, she wept pitifully. That woman too, having consoled the tear-faced girl in many ways, asked the cause of her weeping; and she, though embarrassed, spoke out due to the gravity of the matter—"Mother, what shall I say? Ill fortune is truly a living death for women, especially for wives of good families. I am the very illustration of that. Even my kinfolk, headed by my mother, look upon me only with contempt. Therefore make me one who is looked upon favorably by him. Otherwise, I shall this very day abandon these purposeless vital breaths. And until I am relieved, my secret must not be disclosed," and she fell at her feet. Raising her up, with eyes brimming with tears, she said—"Child, do not resolve upon rash action. I am here, obedient to your command. To the extent I am of use, to that extent I am under no one else's authority. If you are truly so distressed, practice austerity under my guidance, for worldly welfare. Is this not the consequence of past misdeeds, that possessing such form, such character, and such birth, you have incurred your husband's hatred? If there is some remedy for counteracting the husband's aversion, show it to me, for your intelligence is superior." Then she, somehow, with downcast face, meditated for a moment, and preceded by a long, hot sigh, spoke—"Venerable one, the husband is the sole deity of women, especially of those born in good families. Therefore something must be done that would serve as a means for his devoted service. There is a merchant in our neighborhood who surpasses all the citizens in noble lineage, wealth, and intimacy with the king. His daughter, named <s>Kanakavatī</s>, is my very dear friend, equal to me in beauty and form. With her, on the terrace of his mansion, I shall sport, adorned twice over. But you must somehow bring my husband to this house, having conveyed a piteous request to that girl's mother. When you all are nearby, I shall, pretending to be absorbed in play, drop a ball. Then, taking it and placing it in his hand, you shall say—'Son, this is your wife's friend, <s>Kanakavatī</s> by name, the daughter of <s>Nidhipatidatta</s>, chief of all merchants. She censures you greatly on <s>Ratnavatī</s>'s account, saying you are heartless and merciless. Therefore this ball, being the property of the opposing party, must be returned.' When thus addressed, he will surely become eager and, thinking that very dear friend to be the one, will ardently present himself to me, bowing with joined palms, when I plead, being further entreated by you. Through that opening, having drawn close and kindled his passion, the means must be arranged so that he will make a tryst and take me away to another land." And she, overflowing with joy, arranged everything exactly so. Then <s>Balabhadra</s>, deceived by the old ascetic woman into thinking this was <s>Kanakavatī</s>, took her along with her finest jewel-laden ornaments and departed at night in pitch darkness. That ascetic woman then spread the story—"Foolish as I was, I neglected <s>Ratnavatī</s> without cause. <s>Balabhadra</s> told me yesterday, 'I am ashamed of how I treated my in-laws and ignored my friends. I wish to live here reconciled.' Surely he has taken her, and the truth will soon come to light." Hearing this, her relatives relaxed their efforts to search for her. <s>Ratnavatī</s>, meanwhile, on the road, secured a certain slave-woman for sale, and supplied with provisions and other necessities carried by that woman, traveled to the city of <s>Khaṭakapura</s>. There, <s>Balabhadra</s>, skilled in trade, earned great wealth from a small capital. He became foremost among the citizens. A large retinue also gathered, drawn by his wealth. Then he harshly scolded that original slave-woman—"You do not work, you steal what is in sight, you speak unpleasantly"—and beat her severely. The maidservant, enraged, revealed a portion of the secret story that had been told during a time of seeking favor. Hearing this, the greedy magistrate harshly rebuked him in the presence of the city elders—"This evil-minded <s>Balabhadra</s>, having stolen <s>Kanakavatī</s>, the daughter of <s>Nidhipatidatta</s>, by deception, is living in our city. Should not his entire property be confiscated by you?" <s>Ratnavatī</s> then addressed the frightened <s>Balabhadra</s>—"Do not be afraid. Say: This is not <s>Kanakavatī</s>, daughter of <s>Nidhipatidatta</s>. This is <s>Ratnavatī</s>, daughter of the ship-captain <s>Guhagupta</s> of <s>Valabhī</s>, given to me by her parents and lawfully married. If you do not believe it, send an envoy to her kinsmen's side." <s>Balabhadra</s>, having spoken thus, remained under the surety of his guild until <s>Guhagupta</s>, having learned the facts through a letter from the city elders, came to <s>Khaṭakapura</s> and, greatly pleased, took back his daughter along with his son-in-law. Having thus seen <s>Ratnavatī</s>, whom he still imagined to be <s>Kanakavatī</s>, <s>Balabhadra</s> became exceedingly devoted to her. Therefore I say—"Desire is indeed imagination." After that, he asked about the story of <s>Nitambavatī</s>. I said— "There is in <s>Śūrasena</s> a city named <s>Mathurā</s>. There a certain young man of good family, exceedingly fond of arts and courtesans, having single-handedly fought many quarrels for the sake of friends, lived there, called by the rough folk <s>Kalahakaṇṭhaka</s> (Quarrel-thorn). He once saw a painted scroll in the hand of some itinerant artist. Therein, a certain young woman depicted in a painting captured <s>Kalahakaṇṭhaka</s>'s passion-stricken mind at the mere sight. He said to the artist—'Friend, this seems contradictory, for: the form is rare for a woman of good family, yet the humility suggests noble birth; the complexion of the face is pale, yet the body has the beauty of one not excessively enjoyed; and the gaze is tinged with maturity. Nor is she one whose husband is away, since there is no sign such as a disheveled braid indicating separation. And this mark is on the right side. Therefore she must be the wife of some elderly merchant of insufficient virility, frustrated by the lack of proper conjugal enjoyment, and painted by you from life with great skill.' The artist, praising him, confirmed—'This is true. In the city of <s>Avantipurī</s>, <s>Ujjayinī</s>, she is the wife of a caravan-leader named <s>Anantakīrti</s>—truly named <s>Nitambavatī</s> (ample-hipped)—painted by me in wonder at her beauty.' He, immediately becoming infatuated and eager to see her, set out for <s>Ujjayinī</s>. Assuming the name <s>Bhārgava</s>, entering that household on the pretext of begging alms, he saw her. Having seen her, with <s>Kāma</s> (desire) greatly inflamed, he went out and begged the city elders for the guardianship of the cremation ground. And he obtained it. With the shrouds and other things obtained from corpses there, he attended upon a certain <s>Jain</s> nun called <s>Arhantikā</s>. Through her, he privately sent messages to <s>Nitambavatī</s>. But she, rebuking the nun, rejected the proposal. Learning through the nun's report that this woman of good family was of difficult virtue, he secretly instructed the messenger—'Approach the merchant's wife again. Tell her privately: A person like me, having perceived the defects of worldly existence, having taken to meditation with desire for liberation—how could such a one endeavor to corrupt the virtue of women of good families? This too was a test of you, endowed as you are with noble prosperity, superhuman beauty, and the prime of youth—whether or not that fickleness easily found in women has touched you. I am satisfied by your blameless disposition. Now I wish to see you after you have borne a child. But your husband, possessed by some planetary affliction, has become enfeebled by jaundice and incapable of conjugal union. And it is not possible to obtain a child from him without counteracting his ailment. Therefore, be gracious. Enter the garden alone, and secretly place your hand and foot in the hands of a certain <s>mantravādin</s> (spell-caster) brought by me; then, feigning loving anger, you should strike your husband on the chest with the hand consecrated by his spell. Thereupon he will attain nourishment of the finest bodily constituents and the vigor capable of producing excellent offspring. He will attend upon you like a queen. No apprehension need be entertained here.' When thus addressed, she will evidently consent. At night, bring me into the garden, and bring her in too—by that alone I shall be gratified by you.' She enticed her exactly so. That night, having gone to the garden, as <s>Nitambavatī</s> was brought in through the effort of the <s>Nirgranthikā</s> (Jain nun), he, as if touching her foot, snatched away one golden anklet, slightly scratched the root of her thigh with a knife, and quickly departed. She, overwhelmed with terror, blaming her own misconduct, almost wanting to kill the nun, washed that wound in the house-pond, applied a cloth bandage, and on the pretext of illness, spent three or four days in seclusion removing the other anklet as well. That rogue, thinking "I shall use this as leverage," approached <s>Anantakīrti</s> with that anklet. He, seeing it and saying "This is indeed my wife's anklet; how did you obtain it?" was persistently questioned by the rogue. But the rogue stood firm saying "I shall speak before the merchant guild." Then <s>Anantakīrti</s> sent word to his wife—"Send your pair of anklets." She, with shame and anxiety, sent the other one, saying "Today at night, when I entered the garden for relaxation, one of my anklets, loosely fastened, fell off. Though searched for even today, it was not found; here is the second one." With this matter and putting her forward, that merchant came to the assembly of merchants. The rogue, when questioned, reported respectfully—"It is well known to you that, by your command, I guard the cremation ground and live off that livelihood. Thieves, sometimes afraid of seeing me at night, might even burn corpses—so I sleep in the cremation ground at night. The next day, I saw a dark-complexioned woman forcibly dragging a half-burnt corpse from the funeral pyre. Out of greed for gain, suppressing my fear, I seized her; and a scratch was accidentally made at the root of her thigh by my blade. And this anklet was pulled from her foot. In just that much time, she fled at full speed. Such is the account of its acquisition. But you, sirs, are the authority." Upon deliberation, her being a <s>śākinī</s> (witch) was unanimously agreed upon by the citizens. Abandoned by her husband, in that very cremation ground, having lamented greatly, as she was about to hang herself with a noose, she was seized at night by that rogue. Having consoled her, he said—"Beautiful one, maddened by your appearance, I employed many stratagems through the nun to win you over; when these failed, this device was employed to make you exclusively mine for life. Therefore, be gracious to this servant who has no other refuge"—and falling at her feet again and again, employing hundreds of blandishments, he made her, who had no other recourse, subject to his will. Therefore it is said—"Wisdom is the means of accomplishing the difficult." Hearing this, the <s>Brahmarākṣasa</s> (Brahmin-demon) honored me. At that very moment, pearls thick as half-bloomed <s>puṃnāga</s> (Alexandrian laurel) buds fell from the sky along with drops of water. But I, looking upward wondering "What is this?" saw some <s>Rākṣasa</s> (demon) dragging a certain woman whose limbs were struggling. Thinking "How does this lawless demon abduct a woman even against her will?" I, with but feeble power of aerial movement and weaponless, was distressed. But that <s>Brahmarākṣasa</s> related to me, rebuking him—"Stop, stop, villain! Where are you carrying her off to?"—rose up and grappled with the <s>Rākṣasa</s>. But her, flung aside in his rage without regard, falling from the sky like a spray of blossoms from a celestial tree—I caught in both hands, facing upward with arms outstretched. Holding her as she trembled, with eyes closed, her body covered in goosebumps from the pleasure of contact with my body—I stood there, lowering that very woman gently. Meanwhile those two destroyed each other with the shattering of mountain peaks, with trees violently uprooted, and with blows of fists and feet. Then, setting her down on the exceedingly soft, sandy, flower-petal-strewn bank of a lake, gazing at her with longing, I recognized that princess, the sole beloved of my life—<s>Kandukāvatī</s>. For she, being consoled by me, looking at me sidelong and recognizing me, wept tenderly. And she said—"Lord, since seeing you my passion became unbearable; at that ball-festival, I was again consoled by my friend <s>Candrasenā</s> with stories about you alone. When I heard that you had been drowned in the middle of the ocean by my wicked brother <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s>," she continued, "deceiving my friends and attendants, wishing to abandon life, I went alone to the pleasure garden. There this vile <s>Rākṣasa</s> of <s>Kāmarūpa</s> (shape-shifting) form desired me. When his advances were rejected by me in my terror, he seized me as I struggled and ran off. Thus the matter stood. And I, by fate, have fallen into the hands of you, the lord of my life. Blessings upon you." Having heard this, I descended with her and boarded a ship. The ship, released and driven by a favorable wind, returned to that very city of <s>Dāmalipta</s>. Having disembarked, we effortlessly heard the lament of the tear-faced people—"<s>Tuṅgadhanvan</s>, the lord of <s>Suhma</s>, bereft of his son and daughter, with no other offspring, himself with his wife, has resolved upon fasting unto death on the bank of the spotless <s>Gaṅgā</s>. The devoted citizens, having no other protector, wish to die together with him." Then I, having related all that had transpired to that king, restored to him his two children. Pleased, he made me his son-in-law and lord of <s>Dāmālipta</s>. His son <s>Madanajīvā</s> was born to me.

children.text: iti śrīdaṇḍinaḥ kṛtau daśakumāracarite mitraguptacaritaṃ nāma ṣaṣṭha ucchvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, in the composition of the illustrious <s>Daṇḍin</s>, in the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s>, [ends] the sixth chapter (<s>ucchvāsa</s>) named 'The Adventures of <s>Mitragupta</s>.'

children.translated_text: Seventh chapter (<s>Saptamocchvāsa</s>).

children.text:
rājādhirājanandana, nagarandhragatasya te gatiṃ jñāsyannahaṃ ca gataḥ kadācitkaliṅgona /
kaliṅganagarasya nātyāsannasaṃsthitajanadāhasthānasaṃsaktasya kasyacitkāntāradharaṇijasyāstīrṇasarasakisalayasaṃstare tale nipadya nidrālīḍhadṛṣṭiraśayiṣi /
galati ca kālarātriśikhaṇḍajālakālāndhakāre, calitarakṣisi kṣaritanīhāre nijanilayanilīnaniḥ śeṣajane nitāntaśīte niśīthe ghanatarasālaśākhāntarālanirhrādini netraniṃsinīṃ nidrāṃ nigṛhṇat, karṇadeśaṃ gataṃ "kathaṃ khalenānena dagdhasiddhena riṃrasākāle nideśaṃ ditsatā jana eṣa rāgeṇānargalenārdita itthaṃ khalīkṛtaḥ /
kriyetāmyāṇakanarendrasya kenacidanantaśaktinā siddhyantarāya' iti kiṅkarasya kiṅkaryāścātikārataraṃ raṭitam /
tadākarṇya "ka eṣa siddhaḥ, kiṃ cānena kiṅkareṇa kariṣyate' iti didṛkṣākrāntahṛdayaḥ kiṅkaragatayā diśā kiñcidantaraṃ gatastaralataranarāsthiśakalaracitālaṅkārākrāntakāyam, dahanadagdhakāṣṭhaniṣṭhāṅgārarajaḥkṛtāṅgarāgam, taḍillatākārajaṭādharam, hiraṇyaretasyaraṇyacakrāndhakārarākṣase kṣaṇagṛhītanānendhanagrāsacañcadarciṣi dakṣiṇetareṇa kareṇa tilasiddhārthakādīnnirantaracaṭacaṭāyitānākirantaṃ kañcidadrākṣam /
tasyāgre sa kṛtāñjaliḥ kiṅkaraḥ "kiṃ karaṇīyam, dīyatāṃ nideśaḥ' ityatiṣṭhat /
ādiṣṭaścāyaṃ tenātinikṛṣṭāśayena-"gaccha, kaliṅgarājasya kardanasya kanyāṃ kanakalekhāṃ kanyāgṛhādihānaya' iti /
sa ca tathākārṣit /
tataścaināṃ trāsenāladhīyasāsrajarjareṇa ca kaṇṭhena raṇaraṇikāgṛhītena ca hṛdayena "hā tāta, hā janani' ti krandantīṃ kīrṇaglānaśekharasraji śīrṇanahane śirasijānāṃ saṃcaye nigṛhyāsinā śilāśitena śiraścikartiṣayāceṣṭata /
jhaṭiti cācchidya tasya hastāttāṃ śastrikāṃ tayā nikṛtya tasya tacchiraḥ sajaṭājālam, nikaṭasthasya kasyacijjīrṇasālasya skandharandhrenyadadhām /
tannidhyāya hṛṣṭataraḥ sa rākṣasaḥ kṣīṇādhirakathayat-"ārya, kadaryasyāsya kadarthanānna kadācinnidrāyāti netre /
tarjayati trāsayati ca akṛtye cājñāṃ dadāti /
tadatra kalyāṇarāśinā sādhīyaḥ kṛtam /
yadeṣa narakākaḥ kāraṇānāṃ nārakiṇāṃ rasajñānāya nītaḥ śītetaradīdhitidehajasya nagaram, tadatra dayānidheranantatejasaste 'yaṃ janaḥ kāñcidājñāṃ cikīrṣati /
ādiśa, alaṃ kālaharaṇena' ityanaṃsīt /
ādiśaṃ ca tam-"sakhe, saiṣā sajjanācaritā saraṇiḥ, yadaṇīyasikāraṇe 'naṇīyānādaraḥ saṃdṛśyate /
na cedidaṃ necchasi seyaṃ saṃnatāṅgayaṣṭirakleśārhāsatyanenākṛtyakāriṇātyarthaṃ kleśitā, tannayaināṃ nijanilayam /
nānyaditaḥ kiñcidasti cittārādhanaṃ naḥ' iti /
atha tadākarṇya karṇaśekharanilīnanīlanīrajāyitāṃ dhīratalatārakāṃ dṛśaṃ tiryakkiñcidañcitāṃ saṃcārayantī, salilacaraketanaśarāsanānatāṃ cillikālatāṃ lalāṭaraṅgasthalīnartakīṃ līlālasaṃ lālayantī, kaṇṭakitaraktagaṇḍalakhā, rāgalajjāntarālacāriṇī, caraṇāgreṇa tiraścīnanakhārciścandrikeṇa dharaṇitalaṃ sācīkṛtānanasarasijaṃ likhantī, dantacchadakisalayalaṅghinā harṣāsrasaliladhārāśīkarakaṇajālakleditasya stanataṭacandanasyārdratāṃ nirasyatāsyāntarālaniḥ-sṛtena tanīyasānilena hṛdayalakṣyadalanadakṣiṇaratisahacaraśarasyadāyitena taraṅgitadaśanacandrikāṇi kānicidetānyakṣarāṇi kalakaṇṭhīkalānyasṛjat-"ārya, kena kāraṇenainaṃ dāsajanaṃ kālahastādācchidyānantaraṃ rāgānilacālitaraṇaraṇikātaraṅgiṇyanaṅgasāgare kirasi /
yathā te caraṇasarasijarajaḥkaṇikā tathāhaṃ cintanīyā /
yadyasti dayā te 'trajane, ananyasādhāraṇaḥ karaṇīyaḥ sa eva caraṇārādhanakriyāyām /
yadi ca kanyāgārādhyāsanerahasyakṣaraṇādanartha āśaṅkyeta, naitadasti /
raktatarā hi nastatrasakhyaśceṭyaśca /
yatā na kaścidetajjñāsyati tathā yatiṣyante' iti /
sa cāhaṃ dehajenākarṇākṛṣṭasāyakāsanena cetasyatinirdayaṃ tāḍitastatkaṭākṣakālāyasanigaḍagāḍhasaṃyataḥ kiṅkarānananihitadṛṣṭiragādiṣam-"yatheyaṃ rathacaraṇajaghanā kathayati tathā cennācareyam, nayeta nakrakatenaḥ kṣaṇenaikenākīrtanīyāṃ daśām /
janaṃ cainaṃ saha nayānayā kanyayā kanyāgṛhaṃ hariṇanayanayā' iti /
nītaścāhaṃ niśācareṇa śāradajaladharajālakānti kanyakāniketanamṣa tatra ca kāñcitkālakalāṃ candrānanānideśāccandraśālaikadeśe taddarśanacalitadhṛtiratiṣṭham /
sā ca svacchandaṃ śayānāḥ karatalālasasaṃghaṭanāpanītanidrāḥ kāścidadhigatārthāḥ sakhīrakārṣīt /
athāgatya tāścaraṇanihitaśirasaḥ kṣaradasrakarālitekṣaṇā nijaśekharakesarāgrasaṃlagnapaṭcaraṇagaṇaraṇitasaṃśayitakalag iraḥ śanairakathayan-"ārya, yadatyādityatejasasta eṣā tayanalakṣyatāṃ gatā, tataḥ kṛtāntena gṛhītā /
dattā ceyaṃ cittajena garīyasā sākṣīkṛtya rāgānalam /
tadanenāścaryaratnena nalinākṣasya te ratnaśailaśilātalasthiraṃ rāgataralenālaṅkriyātāṃ hṛdayam /
asyāścaritārthaṃ stanataṭaṃ gāḍhāliṃṅganaiḥ sadṛśatarasya sahacarasya ca' iti /
tataḥ sakhījanenātidakṣiṇena dṛḍhatarīkṛtasnehanigalastayā saṃnatāṅgyā saṃgatyāraṃsi /
atha kadācidāyāsitajāyārahitacetasi, lālasālilaṅghanaglānaghanakesare, rājadaraṇyasthalīlalāṭālīlāyitatilake, lalitānaṅgarājāṅgīkṛtanirnidrakarṇikārakāñcanacchatre, dakṣiṇadahanasārathirayāhṛtasahakāracañcarīkakalike, kālāṇḍajakaṇṭharāgaraktaraktādharāratiraṇāgrasaṃnāhaśīlini, śālinakanyakāntaḥkaraṇasaṃkrāntarāgalaṅghitalajje, darduragiritaṭacandanāśleṣaśītalānilācāryadattanānālatānṛtyalīle kāle, kaliṅgarājaḥ sahāṅganājanena saha ca tanayayā sakalena ca nagarajanena daśa trīṇi ca dinādi dinakarakiraṇajālalaṅghanīye, raṇadalisaṅghalaṅghitanatalatāgrakisalayālīḍhasaikatataṭe, taralataraṅgaśīkarāsārasaṅgaśītale sāgaratīrakānane krījārasajātāsaktisasīt /
atha saṃtatagītasaṃgītasaṃgatāṅganāsahasraśṛṅgārahalānirargalānaṅgasaṃgharṣaharṣitaśca rāgatṛṣṇaikatantrastatra randhra āndhranāthana jayasiṃhenasalilataraṇasādhanānītenānenānekasaṃkhyenānīkena drāgāgatyāgṛhyata sakalatraḥ sā dyānīyata trāsataralākṣī dayitā naḥ saha sakhījanena kanakalekhā /
tadāhaṃ dāhenānaṅgadahanajanitenāntaritāhāracintaścintayandayitāṃ galitagātrakāntirityatarkayam-"gatā sā kaliṅgarājatanayā janayitrā janayitryā ca sahārihastam /
nirastadhairyastāṃ sa rājā niyataṃ saṃjighṛkṣet /
tadasahā ca sā satī gararasādinā sadyaḥ saṃtiṣṭheta /
tasyāṃ ca tādṛśīṃ daśāṃ gatāyāṃ janasyāsyānanyajena hanyeta śarīradhāraṇā /
sā kā syādgatiḥ' iti /
atrāntara āndhranagarādāgacchannagrajaḥ kaścidaikṣyata /
tena ceyaṃ kathā kathitā-"yathā kila jayasiṃhenānekanikāradatatasaṃgharṣaṇajighāṃsitaḥ sa kardanaḥ kanakalekhādarśanaidhitena rāgeṇārakṣyata /
sā ca dārikā yakṣeṇa kenacidadhiṣṭhitā na tiṣṭhatyagre narāntarasya /
āyasyati ca narendrasārthasaṃgrahaṇena tannirākariṣyannarendro na cāsti siddhiḥ' iti /
tena cāhaṃ darśatāśaḥ śaṅkaranṛtyaraṅgadeśajātasya jaratsālasyatkandharandrāntarjaṭājālaṃ niṣkṛṣya tena jaṭilatāṃ gataḥ kanthācīrasaṃcayāntaritasakalagātraḥ kāṃścicchiṣyānagrahīṣam /
tāṃścanānāścaryakriyātisaṃhitājjanādākṛṣṭānnacelādityāgānnityahṛṣṭānakāṣram /
ayāsiṣaṃ ca dinaiḥ kaiścidāndhranagaram /
tasya nātyāsanne salilarāśisadṛśasya kalahaṃsagaṇadalitanalinadalasaṃhatigalitākiñjalkaśakalaśārasya sārasaśreṇiśekharasaya sarasastīrakānane kṛtāniketanaḥ sthitaḥ śiṣyajanakathitacitraceṣṭākṛṣṭasakalanāgarajanābhisaṃdhānadakṣaḥ sandiśidiśītyakīrtye janena-"ya eṣa jaradaraṇyasthalīsarastīre sthaṇḍilaśāyī yatistasya kila sakalāni sarahasyāni saṣaḍaṅgāni ca chandāṃsirasanāgre saṃnihitāti, anyāni ca śāstrāṇi, yena yāni na jñāyante sa teṣāṃ tatsakāśādarthanirṇayaṃ kariṣyati /
asatyena nāsyāsyaṃ saṃsṛjyate /
saśarīraścaiṣa dayārāśiḥ /
etatsaṃgraheṇādya ciraṃ caritārthā dīkṣā /
taccaraṇarajaḥ kaṇaiḥ kaiścanaśirasi kīrṇairanekasyāneka ātaṅkaściraṃ cikitsakairasaṃhāryaḥ saṃhṛtaḥ tadaṅghikṣālanasalilasekairniṣkalaṅkaśirasāṃ naśyanti kṣaṇenaikenākhilanarendrayantralaṅghinaścaṇḍatārā grahāḥ /
na tasya śakyaṃ śakteriyattājñānam /
na cāsyāhaṅkārakaṇikā' iti /
sā ceyaṃ kathānekajanāsyasaṃcāriṇī tasya kanakalekhādhiṣṭhānadhanadājñākaranirākriyākriyātisaktacetaḥ kṣatrriyasyākarṣaṇāyāśakat sa cāharaharāgatyādareṇātigarīyasārcayannarthaiśca śiṣyānsaṃgṛhṇannidhigatakṣaṇaḥ kadācitkāṅkṣitārthasādhanāya śanaraiyāciṣṭa /
dhyānadhīraḥ sthānadarśitajñānasaṃnidhiścainaṃ nirīkṣya nicāyyākathayam-"tāt sthāna eṣa hi yatnaḥ /
tasya hi kanyāratnasya sakalakalyāṇalakṣaṇaikarāśerādhigatiḥ kṣīrasāgararaśanālaṅkṛtāyā gaṅgādinadīsahasrahārayāṣṭirājitāyā dharāṅganāyā evāsādanāya sādhanam /
na ca sa yakṣastadadhiṣṭhāyī kenacinnarendreṇa tasyā līlāñcitanīlanīrajadarśanāyā darśanaṃ sahate, tadatra sahyatāṃ trīṇyahāni, yairahaṃ yatiṣyer'thasyāsya sādhanāya' iti /
tathādiṣṭe ca hṛṣṭe kṣitīśe gate niśi niśi nirniśākarārciṣi nīrandhrāndhakārakaṇanikaranigīrṇadaśadiśi nidrānigaḍitanikhilajanadṛśi nirgataya jalatalanilīnagāhanīyaṃ nīrandhraṃ kṛcchrācchidrīkṛtāntarālaṃ tadekataḥ sarastaṭaṃ tīrthāsaṃnikṛṣṭaṃ kenacitkhananasādhanenākārṣam /
ghanaśileṣṭakācchannacchidrānanaṃ tattīradeśaṃ janairaśaṅkanīyaṃ niścitya, dinādisnā nanirṇiktagātraśca nakṣatrasaṃtānahārayaṣṭyagragrathitaratnam /
kṣaṇadāndhakāragandhahastidāraṇaikakesāriṇam, kanakaśailaśṛṅgaraṅgalāsyalīlānaṭam, gaganasāgaraghanataraṅgarājilaṅghanaikanakram, kāryākāryasākṣiṇam, sahasrārciṣaṃ sahasrākṣadigaṅganāṅgarāgarāgāyitakiraṇajālam, raktanīrajāñjalinārādhya nijaniketanaṃ nyaśiśriyam /
yāte ca dinatraye, astagiriśikharagairikataṭasādhāraṇacchaye /
acalarājakanyakākadarthanayāntarikṣākhyena śaṅkaraśarīreṇa saṃsṛṣṭāyāḥ saṃdhyāṅganāyāḥ raktacandanacarcitaikastanakalaśadarśanīye dinādhināthe, janādhināthaḥ sa āgatya janasyāsya dharaṇinyastacaraṇanakhakiraṇacchāditakirīṭaḥ kṛtāñjaliratiṣṭhat /
ādiṣṭaśca-"diṣṭyā dṛṣṭeṣṭasiddhiḥ /
iha jagati hi na nirīhaṃ dehinaṃ śriyaḥ saṃśrayante /
śreyāṃsi ca sakalānyanalasānāṃ haste nityasāṃnidhyāni /
yataste sādhīyasā saccaritenānākalitakalaṅkenārcitenātyādararacitenākṛṣṭacetasā janenānena sarastathā saṃskṛtam, yatheha te 'dya siddhiḥ syāt /
tadetasyāṃ nisi galādardāyāṃ gāhanīyam /
gāhanānantaraṃ ca salilatale satatagatīnantaḥsaṃcāriṇaḥ saṃnigṛhya yathāśakti śayyākāryā /
tataśca taṭaskhalitajalasthagitajalajakhaṇḍhacalitadaṇḍakaṇṭakāgradalitadeharājahaṃsatrāsajarjararasitasaṃdattakarṇasya janasya kṣaṇādākarṇanīyaṃ janiṣyate jalasaṃghātasya kiñcidāraṭitam /
śānte ca tatra salilaraṭite klinnagātraḥ kiñcidāraktadṛṣṭiryenākāreṇa niryāsyati nicāyya taṃ nikhilajananetrānandakāriṇaṃ na yakṣaḥ śakṣyatyagrataḥ sthitaye /
sthirataranihitasnehaśṛṅkhalānigaḍitaṃ ca kanyakāhṛdayaṃ kṣaṇenaikenāsahanīyadarśanāntarāyaṃ syāt /
asyāśca dharāṅganāyā nātyādṛtanirākṛtāricakraṃ cakraṃ karatalagataṃ cintanīyaṃ na tatra saṃśayaḥ /
taccedicchasyanekaśāstrajñānadhīradhiṣaṇairadhikṛtairitaraiśca hitaiṣigaṇairākalayya jālikaśataṃ cānāyya, antaraṅganaraśatairyatheṣṭadṛṣṭāntarālaṃ saraḥ kriyeta, rakṣā ca tīrātrriṃśaddaṇḍāntarāle sainikajanena sādaraṃ racanīyā /
kastatra tajjānāti yacchidreṇārayaścikīrṣanti' iti /
tattvasya hṛdayahāri jātam, tadadhikṛtaiśca tatra kṛtye randhradarśanāsahericchāṃ ca rājñā kanyakātirāgajanitāṃ nitāntaniścalāṃ niścityārtha eṣa na niṣiddhaḥ /
tathāsthitaśca tadāsādanadṛḍhatarāśayaśca sa ākhyāyata-"rājan, atra te janānte ciraṃ sthitam, na caikatra cirasthānaṃ naḥ śastam /
kṛtakṛtyaśceha na draṣṭāsi /
yasya te rāṣṭre grāsādyāsāditaṃ tasya te kiñcidanācarya kāryaṃ gatirāryagarhyā' iti /
tatraitaccirasthānasya kāraṇam /
taccādya siddham /
gaccha gṛhān /
yathārhajalena hṛdyagandhena snātaḥ sitasragaṅgarāgaḥ śaktisadṛśena dānenārādhitadharaṇitalataitilagaṇastilasnehasiktayaṣṭyagragrathitavartikāgniśikhāsahasragrastanaiśāndhakārarāśirāgatyārthasiddhaye yatethāḥ' iti /
sa kila kṛtajñatāṃ darśayan-"asiddhireṣā siddhiḥ, yadasaṃnidhirihāryāṇām /
kaṣṭā ceyaṃ niḥsaṅgatā, yā nirāgasaṃ dāsajanaṃ tyājayati /
na ca niṣedhanīyā garīyasāṃ giraḥ' iti snānāya gṛhānayāsīt /
ahaṃ ca nirgatya nirjane niśīthe sarastīrarandhranilīnaḥ sannīṣacchidradattakarṇaḥ sthitaḥ /
sthite cārdharātre kṛtayathādiṣṭakriyaḥ sthānasthānaracitarakṣaḥ sa rājā jālikajanānānīya nirākṛtāntaḥśalyaṃ śaṅkāhīnaḥ saraḥsalilaṃ salīlagatiragāhata /
gataṃ ca kīrṇakeśaṃ saṃhatakarṇanāsaṃ sarasastalaṃ hāstinaṃ nakralīlayā nīrātinilīnatayā taṃ tathā śayānaṃ kandharāyāṃ kanyatā vyagrahīṣam /
kharatarakāladaṇḍaghaṭṭanāticaṇḍaiśca karacaraṇaghātairnirdayadattanigrahaḥ kṣaṇenaikenājahātsa ceṣṭām /
tataścā kṛṣya taccharīraṃ chidre nidhāya nīrānnirayāsiṣam /
saṅgatānāṃ ca sainikānāṃ tadatyacitrīyatākārāntaragrahaṇam /
gajaskandhagataḥ sitacchatrādisakalarājacihnarājitaścaṇḍataradaṇḍidaṇḍatāḍanatrastajanadattāntarālayā rājavīthyā yātastāṃ niśāṃ rasanayananirastanidrāratiranaiṣam /
nīte ca janākṣilakṣyatāṃ lākṣārasadigdhadhiggajaśiraḥsadṛkṣe śakradigaṅganāratnādarśer'kacakre kṛtakaraṇīyaḥ kiraṇajālakarālaratnarājirājitarājārhāsanādhyāsī yathāsadṛśācāradarśinaḥ śaṅkāyantritāṅgānsaṃnidhiniṣādinaḥ sahāyānagāhiṣam-"dṛśyatāṃ śaktirārṣī, yattasya yaterajeyarayendriyāṇāṃ saṃskāreṇa nīrajasā nīrajasāṃnidhyaśālini saharṣālini sarasi sarasijadalasaṃnikāśacchāyasyādhikataradarśanayinyākārāntarasya siddhirāsīt /
adya sakalanāstikānāṃ jāyeta lajjānataṃ śiraḥ /
tadidānīṃ candraśekharanarakaśāsanasarasijāsanādīnāṃ tridaśeśānāṃ sthānānyādararacitanṛtyagītārādhanāni kriyantām /
hniyantāṃ ca gṛhāditaḥ kleśanirasanasahānyarthisārthairdhanāni' iti /
āścaryarasītirekahṛṣṭadṛṣṭayaste jaya jagadīśa, jayena sātiśayaṃ daśa diśaḥ sthagayannijena yaśasādirājayaśāṃsi' ityasakṛdāśāsyāracayanyathādiṣṭāḥ kriyāḥ /
sa cāhaṃ dayitāyāḥ sakhīṃ hṛdayasthānīyāṃ śaśāṅkasenāṃ kanyakāṃ kadācitkāryāntarāgatāṃ rahasyācakṣi-"kaccidayaṃ janaḥ kadācidāsīddṛṣṭaḥ' iti /
atha sā harṣakāṣṭhāṃ gatena hṛdayeneṣadālakṣya daśanadīdhitilatāṃ līlālasaṃ lāsayantī, lalitāñcitakaraśākhāntaritadantacchadakisalayā, harṣajalakledajarjaranirañjanekṣaṇā, racitāñjaliḥ "nitarāṃ jāne yadi na syādaindrajālikasya jālaṃ kiñcidetādṛśam /
kathaṃ caitat /
kathaya, iti snehaniryantraṇaṃ śanairagādīt /

ahaṃ cāsyai kārtsnyenākhyāya, tadānanasaṃkrāntena saṃdeśena saṃjanayyasahacaryā niratiśayaṃ hṛdayāhlādam, tataścaitayā dayitayā nirargalīkṛtātisatkṛtakaliṅganāthanyāyadattayā saṃgatyāndhrakaliṅgarājarājyaśāsī tasyāsyāriṇā lilaṅkhayiṣitasyāṅgarājasya sāhāyyakāyālaghīyasā sādhanenāgatyātra te sakhijanasaṃgatasya yādṛcchikadarśanānandarāśilaṅghitacetā jātaḥ' iti /
children.translated_text: And I, having told her everything in full, produced immeasurable delight in her heart through the message conveyed from his face; and thereafter, through union with this beloved who had been given to me by right by the honored lord of <s>Kaliṅga</s> with unrestricted and exceedingly generous hospitality, I became the ruler of the kingdoms of <s>Āndhra</s> and <s>Kaliṅga</s>. Having come here with no small force to aid the king of <s>Aṅga</s>, whose territory that enemy of hers sought to transgress, and having by chance encountered you, my friend, my heart has been overwhelmed by a flood of joy at seeing you,' thus he spoke.

children.translated_text: His lips illumined by the moonlight of a smile, <s>Rājavāhana</s>, together with his friends, applauded that skillful tale and said: 'Wonderful is this adventure of the great sage!

children.text: atraiva khalu phalitamatikaṣṭaṃ tapaḥ tiṣṭhatu tāvannarma /
children.translated_text: Here indeed his extremely arduous <s>tapas</s> (austerities) bore fruit. But let that stand — enough of jesting!

children.text: harṣaprakarṣaspṛśoḥ prajñāsattvayordṛṣṭamiha svarūpam' ityabhidhāya, punaḥ "avataratu bhavān' iti bahuśrute viśrute vikacarājīvasadṛśaṃ dṛśaṃ cikṣepa devo rājavāhanaḥ // Dkc_2,7 //
children.translated_text: The true nature of <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) and <s>sattva</s> (courage), which reach the height of joy, has been seen here.' Having spoken thus, he then said, 'Let Your Honor now begin,' and the lord <s>Rājavāhana</s> cast his gaze — resembling a blossoming lotus — upon the learned <s>Viśruta</s>.

O son of the king of kings, seeking to learn the whereabouts of you who had entered a tunnel in the city, I too once went to <s>Kaliṅga</s>. / Near the city of <s>Kaliṅga</s>, I lay down at the base of a certain forest tree in the wilderness, on a bed spread with fresh tender leaves, my eyes seized by sleep. / As the darkness of the black night's peacock-feathered veil was dissolving, as the dew was dissipating at the last watch, when all people had retreated into their own dwellings, in the exceedingly cold midnight, with the dense <s>sāla</s> tree branches rustling in the intervals, while I was suppressing sleep that was pressing upon my eyes, there reached my ears the excessively harsh cries of a male servant and a female servant: 'How has this wicked one, this accursed <s>siddha</s> (adept), at this unseemly hour, wishing to give commands, so tormented and deceived this person with his unrestrained passion! / Let someone of infinite power create an obstacle to the accomplishments of King <s>Yāṇaka</s>!' / Hearing that, with my heart seized by curiosity — 'Who is this <s>siddha</s>, and what will be done by this servant?' — I went some distance in the direction the servant had gone, and I saw someone whose body was covered with ornaments fashioned from fragments of human bones that were all the more unsteady, whose body-paint was made from the dust of charcoal from fire-burnt wood, who bore matted locks in the form of lightning creepers, and who, before a fire in the darkness of the forest circle of <s>Hiraṇyaretas</s> (the golden-seed, i.e., fire), with flames flickering as they momentarily seized fuel as their food-morsels, was with his left hand continuously scattering sesame seeds, white mustard, and other offerings with incessant crackling sounds. / Before him stood the servant with joined palms: 'What is to be done? Give the command.' / And he was commanded by that one of most vile intentions — 'Go, bring here from the maidens' quarters <s>Kanakalekhā</s>, the daughter of <s>Kardana</s>, king of <s>Kaliṅga</s>.' / And he did so. / Then, seizing her — who was crying 'Alas father! Alas mother!' with a throat choked and broken by tears from terror, with a heart gripped by trembling — with her garland of wilted flowers scattered, with the bindings of her hair undone and tresses disheveled, he endeavored to cut off her head with a stone-sharpened sword. / Swiftly snatching that blade from his hand, I used it to sever his head, matted locks and all, and placed it in a hollow of the trunk of some old nearby <s>sāla</s> tree. / Observing that, the <s>rākṣasa</s> (demon), greatly delighted and his troubles diminished, said — 'Noble sir, because of this miser's tormenting, my eyes never come to sleep. / He threatens and frightens, and gives commands in improper deeds. / Here a most excellent thing has been done by one who is a treasury of virtue. / Since this hell-crow has been led to the city of the son of the cool-rayed one (the Moon, i.e., to the realm of the dead) for the appreciation of the connoisseurs of torment among the hellish beings, therefore this servant wishes to carry out some command of yours, O ocean of compassion and infinite radiance. / Command, enough with the delay!' — thus he entreated. / And I commanded him — 'Friend, this is the path trodden by good people, that in matters concerning the helpless, no small regard is shown. / If you do not wish otherwise, this maiden of slender limbs, undeserving of suffering, has been extremely tormented by this evildoer who committed crimes; therefore take her back to her own dwelling. / No other reward for us pleases the heart.' / Then, hearing that, directing her gaze — which had become like a blue lotus nestled at the edge of her ear, with steady and enlarged pupils, cast slightly sideways — languidly playing with the creeper-vine of her brow that was bent like the bow of the water-born god (<s>Kāma</s>), a dancer on the stage of her forehead, with goosebumps on her reddened cheeks, moving between passion and modesty, with her face-lotus turned aside as she drew lines on the ground with the tip of her foot whose toenails cast moonlight-like rays, with a gentle breeze escaping from between her lips that transgressed the leaf-buds of her lip, dispelling the moisture of the sandal paste on her breast-slope that was wetted by a web of drops from the spray of tears of joy — a breeze skilled in piercing the target of the heart, given by the companion arrow of <s>Rati</s>'s lord (<s>Kāma</s>) — she released some syllables rippling with the moonlight of her teeth, resembling the notes of a female <s>kokila</s> bird — 'Noble sir, for what reason, having snatched this servant-girl from the hand of Death, do you now cast her into the ocean of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless Love-god), whose waves are the tinkling sounds stirred by the wind of passion? / I am to be regarded as but a particle of dust from your lotus-feet. / If you have compassion for this person here, that same person should be engaged exclusively in the service of your feet, shared with no other. / And if disgrace is feared from the breach of the secret of the maidens' quarters, that is not so. / For our friends and maidservants there are exceedingly devoted. / They will endeavor so that no one shall come to know of this.' / And I, struck exceedingly mercilessly in the heart by the one born of the body (<s>Kāma</s>), whose bow was drawn to the ear, tightly bound by the iron fetters of her sidelong glances dark as black iron, with my gaze fixed upon the servant's face, commanded — 'If this one of chariot-wheel-round hips speaks thus, and if I were not to act accordingly, the crocodile-fierce one would in a single moment lead to an unspeakable state. / Take this person along with this doe-eyed maiden to the maidens' quarters.' / And I was taken by the night-wanderer (<s>rākṣasa</s>) to the maiden's residence, which had the splendor of an autumn cloud-mass, and there, in a corner of the moonlight-terrace, at the direction of the moon-faced one (<s>Kanakalekhā</s>), I stood for some interval of time, my composure shaken by the sight of her. / And she, rousing some friends who lay sleeping at ease, their slumber removed by the clapping of her palms, made them aware of the matter. / Then, coming forward, those friends, with their heads placed at my feet, their eyes terrible with flowing tears, their garlands of hair-flowers causing the sound of tinkling that raised doubts of <s>kalahaṃsa</s> birds, softly spoke — 'Noble sir, since she who was beyond the reach even of your blazing radiance had gone beyond perception, she was therefore seized by Death (<s>Kṛtānta</s>). / And she has been given by the great god of Love (<s>Cittaja</s>), making the fire of passion the witness. / Therefore, with this wondrous jewel, let the heart of your lotus-eyed self, firm as the surface of the jewel-mountain, be adorned with the liquid of passion. / Her breast-slope is worthy of tight embraces from a most fitting companion, for the fulfillment of her desire.' / Then, through the exceedingly skillful company of her friends, with the fetters of affection firmly strengthened, I united with that slender-limbed one and began our love. / Then, at a time when the season had wearied wives and left hearts restless, when thick tresses were languishing from the transgression of longing, when the <s>tilaka</s> mark sported on the stage of the forehead like a royal forest clearing, when the beautiful golden parasol of the un-sleeping <s>karṇikāra</s> flower had been claimed by the beautiful love-god <s>Anaṅga</s>, when the buds of mango blossoms and bees had been carried off by the charioteer of the southern fire (the spring wind), when the red lower lip, colored with the hue of the <s>kālāṇḍaja</s> (cuckoo) bird's throat-passion, was readying its frontline for the battle of love-play, when passion transgressing modesty had entered the inner hearts of maidens of noble families, when the wind-teacher, cool from embracing the sandalwood on the slopes of <s>Dardura</s> mountain, gave the dance of various creepers as its lesson — at that time, the king of <s>Kaliṅga</s>, together with his womenfolk and his daughter and all the city's people, spent thirteen days in pleasure-gardens on the seashore, where the sun's rays were to be avoided, where the sandy banks were licked by the tips of the tender shoots of creepers swaying over the dancing-floors leapt over by buzzing swarms, and where it was cool from the contact with the spray of restless waves. / Then, while he was gratified by the unceasing amorous conflicts of a thousand women united through continuous songs and music, single-mindedly intent on the thirst of passion, <s>Jayasiṃha</s>, the lord of the <s>Āndhra</s>s, having found an opening, swiftly came with a countless army brought by means of water-crossing vessels and seized him together with all his family. / Our beloved <s>Kanakalekhā</s>, her eyes trembling with fear, was carried away along with her company of friends. / Then I, my body's luster fading from the burning born of the fire of <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love), deprived of food and lost in thoughts of my beloved, reasoned thus — 'The princess of <s>Kaliṅga</s> has gone into the hands of the enemy along with her father and mother. / That king, his composure lost, will surely seek to recover her. / And she, being a chaste woman (<s>satī</s>), unable to bear it, would quickly end her life with poison or the like. / And if she were to reach such a state, the life of this person would be destroyed by nothing other than that. / What then would be the course of action?' / In the meanwhile, an elder brother of someone was seen arriving from the <s>Āndhra</s> city. / And by him this story was told — 'It seems that <s>Kardana</s>, whom <s>Jayasiṃha</s> had wished to kill through many hostile confrontations, was protected by his passion kindled at the sight of <s>Kanakalekhā</s>. / And that maiden, possessed by some <s>Yakṣa</s> (spirit), does not remain in the presence of any other man. / And the king labors at collecting the royal retinue to remove that; still there is no success.' / Thereby inspired with the hope of seeing her, I went to an old <s>sāla</s> tree that stood in the area of <s>Śaṅkara</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) dance-ground, extracted the mass of matted locks from within its trunk-hollow, and having assumed the guise of a matted-hair ascetic with my entire body concealed under a collection of patched rags and bark garments, I gathered some disciples. / And those disciples, attracted from among the people by various wonderful acts and rituals, unwavering in their renunciation of cloth and other comforts, perpetually cheerful, I did not drive away. / And within a few days I traveled to the <s>Āndhra</s> city. / Having established my abode in the woodland on the shore of a lake not far from it — a lake resembling an ocean, whose surface was strewn with fragments of filaments scattered from lotus leaves torn apart by flocks of <s>kalahaṃsa</s> (white geese), crowned with rows of <s>sārasa</s> (cranes) — I stayed there, skilled in attracting all the city-folk through the wondrous deeds reported by my disciples, and the people unsolicited spread the word — 'This ascetic who sleeps on bare ground on the bank of the lake in the aged forest clearing — all the sacred texts with their secrets and six <s>Vedāṅga</s>s (auxiliary sciences of the <s>Veda</s>) are present at the tip of his tongue, as are other <s>śāstra</s>s (sciences); whoever does not know something will obtain the determination of that matter from him. / Falsehood does not touch his mouth. / And this embodied being is an ocean of compassion. / By the attainment of his company, our religious initiation has at last been fulfilled. / By a few particles of his foot-dust scattered on the head, many a chronic ailment incurable by physicians has been removed; by the sprinkling of the water that washed his feet, malignant planetary afflictions that defy all royal remedies vanish in a single instant for those with unblemished heads. / The extent of his power cannot be known. / And he has not a particle of ego.' / And this story, circulating on the lips of many people, was able to attract that <s>Kṣatriya</s> (warrior-king) whose mind was deeply absorbed in efforts to counteract the <s>Yakṣa</s>'s command that governed <s>Kanakalekhā</s>'s possession. / And he, coming day after day and worshipping with exceedingly great respect and also winning over the disciples with gifts, having found the right moment, gradually entreated for the accomplishment of his desired goal. / Steady in meditation, having displayed the presence of my knowledge as befitting my station, I gazed upon him, assessed him, and spoke — 'Son, here indeed is where the effort should be directed. / For the attainment of that jewel of a maiden, who is the sole repository of all auspicious marks, is the means for gaining the Earth-lady herself, adorned with the girdle of the milk-ocean, resplendent with the necklace of a thousand rivers like <s>Gaṅgā</s> and others. / But that <s>Yakṣa</s> who possesses her does not permit any king to behold her whose glance sports like a dark blue lotus; therefore let three days be endured, during which I shall endeavor for the accomplishment of this matter.' / And when thus directed, the delighted king departed, and on each night — when the moonbeams had vanished, when the ten directions were swallowed by the dense mass of impenetrable darkness, when all people's eyes were fettered by sleep — I went out and, by means of some digging implement, fashioned a passage on one side of the lake-bank, into the submerged depths that were to be waded through, with difficulty opening up the interior. / Having ascertained that that bank-area, with its opening concealed by thick bricks, would arouse no suspicion among people, I bathed and cleansed my body at the beginning of each day, and with a jewel strung at the tip of a garland-staff made of a string of stars (lights), I worshipped the thousand-rayed one (<s>Sūrya</s>, the Sun) — the sole lion for tearing apart the darkness-elephant of the night, the dancer performing on the stage of the golden mountain-peak, the sole crocodile for crossing the waves dense as the ocean of the sky, the witness of right and wrong, whose web of rays was praised as the body-paint of the courtesans of the realm of the thousand-eyed one (<s>Indra</s>) — with offerings of red lotuses held in joined palms, and then retired to my own dwelling. / When the three days had passed, at the time when the sun's disc shared the reddish hue of the sunset mountain's peak, when only one breast-pitcher of the twilight-lady was visible, painted with red sandal — she who was united with the body of <s>Śaṅkara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) called the sky (the space between, i.e., the atmosphere) through his tormenting of the mountain-king's daughter (<s>Pārvatī</s>) — the lord of men came and stood with joined palms, the rays of the toenails of his feet placed on the ground covering his crown. / And he was told — 'By good fortune, the desired accomplishment has been achieved. / Indeed in this world, prosperity does not resort to the effortless embodied being. / And all auspicious things are always at hand for the diligent. / Through your most excellent conduct, of spotless character, worshipped with excessive devotion, the people whose hearts are attracted have so prepared the lake that today your success shall come to pass here. / Therefore, when this night is waning, it must be entered by wading. / And immediately after wading, holding the breath of the currents that move constantly beneath the water's surface, a bed must be made as best one can. / Then, in a moment, there will arise some stirring of the water-mass that will reach the ears of the people — an alarming sound caused by the stumbling at the bank, the agitation of water-creatures concealed in the water, the moving of thorny reeds whose tips tear open the skin, and the frightened honking of royal geese. / And when that water-sound has subsided, he who emerges with wet body and slightly reddened eyes — in whatever form — upon discerning him, the <s>Yakṣa</s> will not be able to stand before that one who brings delight to the eyes of all people. / And the maiden's heart, bound with the firmly fixed chain of affection, will in a single instant become unable to bear any obstacle to seeing him. / And the sovereignty over this Earth-lady, with the hostile circle neither too honored nor rejected, should be contemplated as within the grasp of his hand — there is no doubt in this. / Therefore, if you desire it, having consulted with others — advisors steady in the knowledge of many <s>śāstra</s>s and other well-wishers — and having brought a hundred fishermen, and with hundreds of trusted men making the lake visible at desired intervals, and guards being carefully posted at thirty <s>daṇḍa</s> (staff-lengths) intervals along the banks by the military personnel.' / 'Who there would know what the enemies intend through what breach?' / That captivated his heart, and the officials there, having ascertained through the task both the inability to find any breach by the enemies and the king's absolutely firm desire born of excessive passion for the maiden, did not oppose this plan. / And when matters stood thus, he whose resolve to attain her was most firm was told — 'O king, this person has stayed long among your people, and prolonged stay in one place is not advisable for us. / And having accomplished the purpose here, you shall not see me again. / For one who has obtained sustenance and other things in your kingdom, to depart without doing something for you — that course would be censured by the noble.' / Here is the reason for this long stay. / And that is now accomplished. / Go home. / Having bathed with proper water and pleasant fragrance, wearing white garlands and body-paint, having propitiated the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>s on the earth's surface with gifts befitting your power, with the darkness of night consumed by the thousands of flame-tips of wicks strung on the tips of staffs anointed with sesame oil, come and strive for the accomplishment of your purpose.' / He, displaying his gratitude, said — 'This success is itself a failure, in that the noble ones will no longer be present. / And this separation is painful, which makes the innocent servant-people give up. / But the words of the venerable are not to be opposed.' And he went home for his bath. / And I, going out in the deserted midnight, concealed myself at the opening in the lake-bank, and stood with my ear placed at the narrow opening. / When midnight arrived, the king, having performed the prescribed rituals, with guards posted at their proper stations, having brought the fishermen, free of the inner thorn of doubt, without any suspicion, entered the lake's waters with graceful gait. / And when he had gone to the bottom of the lake, with hair spread out, holding his ears and nose shut, I seized him by the neck in the manner of a crocodile, through my complete concealment beneath the water, as he lay there thus. / And with exceedingly fierce blows of hands and feet, harsh as the strikes of the black rod of Death, the restraint imposed upon him was merciless, and in a single instant he ceased all movement. / Then, dragging his body and depositing it in the opening, I emerged from the water. / And among the assembled soldiers, the seizing of one form within another — that was not at all wondered at. / Mounted on an elephant's back, resplendent with the white parasol and all other royal insignia, I proceeded through the royal highway where the people, terrified by the blows of the rod of the most severe punisher, gave way, and I spent that night in the pleasure of love-sport with her whose sleep was banished by the delight of passion-filled eyes. / And when the day was brought to the attention of the people, the sun's orb resembling the head of the red-lacquer-smeared directional elephant and like the jewel-mirror of the courtesan of <s>Indra</s>'s quarter, having accomplished my duties, seated on a royal throne resplendent with rows of radiant jewels whose webs of rays were fierce, I addressed the attendants sitting nearby, their limbs restrained by suspicion, displaying conduct befitting their stations — 'Behold the power of the sages (<s>ṛṣi</s>s), for by the purified, passionless consecration of the senses of that striving ascetic, there was success in taking on another form in that lake, which was auspicious with its joyful presence, free of impurity, resembling lotus petals in its complexion, and granting superior vision. / Today let the heads of all atheists (<s>nāstika</s>s) bow in shame. / Therefore, now let the abodes of the lords of the gods — <s>Candraśekhara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), <s>Narakaśāsana</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), <s>Sarasijāsana</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), and other divine lords — be honored with devotedly arranged dance and song worship. / And let wealth be brought from the homes and other places, capable of removing the distress of the multitudes of supplicants.' / With eyes delighted by the excess of the <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) of wonder, they blessed — 'Victory to you, O lord of the world; with your victory, may your own fame, exceedingly covering the ten directions, outshine the glory of all paramount sovereigns!' — and they repeatedly offered such blessings and carried out the commanded rituals. / And I, at some point when an opportunity arose through another matter, secretly told <s>Śaśāṅkasenā</s>, a maiden who was the heart-trusted friend of my beloved — 'Has this person ever been seen before?' / Then she, her heart having reached the pinnacle of joy, faintly revealing the creeper of her teeth's radiance, languidly making it dance, with the tender shoots of her lip-petals screened by her gracefully curved finger-branches, her eyes with their collyrium loosened and blurred by tears of joy, with palms joined, said — 'I know full well — unless this be some magician's illusion, something of this sort. / But how can this be? / Tell me' — and she spoke slowly, her affection beyond restraint. /

children.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter), called the adventures of <s>Mantragupta</s>, in the <s>Daśakumāracarita</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Daṇḍin</s>.
