atha so 'pyācacakṣe-"deva, mayāpi paribhramatā vindhyāṭavyāṃ ko 'pi kumāraḥ kṣudhā tṛṣā ca kliśyannakleśārhaḥ kvacitkūpābhyāśe 'ṣṭavarṣadeśīyo dṛṣṭaḥ /
sa ca trāsagadgadamagadat-"mahābhāga, kliṣṭasya me kriyatāmārya, sāhāyyakam /
asya me prāṇāpahāriṇīṃ pipāsāṃ pratikartumudakamudañcanniha kūpe ko 'pi niṣkalo mamaikaśaraṇabhūtaḥ patitaḥ /
tamalamasmi nāhamuddhartum, /
iti athāhamabhyetya vratatyā kayāpi vṛddhamuttārya, taṃ ca bālaṃ vaṃśanālīmukoddhṛtābhiradbhiḥ phalaiśca pañcapaiḥ śarakṣepocchritasya lakucavṛkṣasya śikharātpāṣāṇapātitaiḥ prātyānītaprāṇavṛttimāpādya, tarutalaniṣaṇṇastaṃ jarantamabravam-"tāta, ka eṣa bālaḥ, ko vā bhavānan, kathaṃ ceyamāpadāpannā' iti /
so 'śrugadgadamagadat-"śrūyatāṃ mahābhāga vidarbho nāma janapadaḥ tasminbhojavaṃśabhūṣaṇam, aṃśāvatāra iva dharmasya, atisattvaḥ, satyavādī, vadānyaḥ, vinītaḥ, ninetā prajānām, rañjitabhṛtyaḥ, kīrtimān, udagraḥ, buddhimūrtibhyāmutthānaśīlaḥ, śāstrapramāṇakaḥ, śakyabhavyakalpārambhī, saṃbhāvayitā budān prabhāvayitā sevakān, udbhāvayitā bandhūn, nyagbhāvayitā śatrūn, asaṃbaddhapralāpeṣvadattakarṇaḥ, kadācidapyavitṛṣṇo guṇeṣu, atinadīṣṇaḥ kalāsu, nediṣṭo dharmārthasaṃhitāsu, svalpe 'pi sukṛte sutarāṃ pratyupakartā, pratyavekṣitā kośavāhanayoḥ, yatnena parīkṣitā sarvādhyakṣāṇām, ṣāḍguṇyopayoganipuṇaḥ manumārgeṇa praṇetā cāturvarṇyasya, puṇyaślokaḥ, puṇyavarmā nāmāsīt /
sa puṇyaiḥ karmabhiḥ prāṇya puruṣāyuṣam, punarapuṇyena prājānāmagaṇyatāmareṣu /
tadanantaramanantavarmā nāma tadāyatiravanimadhyatiṣṭhat /
sa sarvaguṇaiḥ samṛddho 'pi daivāddaṇḍhanītyāṃ nātyādṛto 'bhūt /
tamekadā rahasi vasurakṣito nāma mantrivṛddhaḥ piturasya bahumataḥ pragalbhavāgabhāṣata-"tāta, sarvaivātmasaṃpadabhijanātprabhṛtyanyūnaivātrabhavati lakṣyate /
buddhiśca nisargapaṭvī, kalāsu nṛtyagītādiṣu citreṣu ca kāvyavistareṣu prāptavistarā tavetarebhyaḥ prativiśiṣyate /
tathāpyasāvapratipadyātmasaṃskāramarthaśāstreṣu, anagnisaṃśodhitena hemajātirnātibhāti buddhiḥ /
buddhihīno hi bhūbhṛdatyucchrito 'pi parairadhyāruhyamāṇamātmānaṃ na cetayate /
na ca śaktaḥ sādhyaṃ sādhanaṃ vā vibhjya vartitum /
ayathāvṛttaśca karmasu pratihanyamānaḥ svaiḥ paraiśca paribhūyate /
na cāvajñātasyājñā prabhavati prajānāṃ yogakṣemārādhanāya /
atikrāntaśāsanāśca prajā yatkiñcanavādinyo yatākathañcidvartinyaḥ sarvāḥ sthitīḥ saṃkireyuḥ nirmaryādaśca loko lokādito 'mutaśca svāminamātmānaṃ ca bhraṃśayeta /
āgamadīpadṛṣṭena khalvadhvanā sukhena vartate lokayātrā /
divyaṃ hi cakṣurbhūtabhavadbhaviṣyatsu vyavahitaviprakṛṣṭādiṣu ca viṣayeṣu śāstraṃ nāmāpratihatavṛtti /
tena hīnaḥ satorapyāyataviśālayorlocanayorandha eva janturarthadarśaneṣvasāmarthyāt' ato vihāya bāhmavidyāsvabhiṣaṅgamāgamaya daṇḍanītiṃ kulavidyām /
tadarthānuṣṭhānana cāvarjitaśaktisiddhiraskhalitaśāsanaḥ śādhi ciramudadhimekhalāmurvīm iti /
etadākarṇya sthāna eva gurubhiranuśiṣṭham /
tathā kriyate' ityantaḥpuramaviśat /
tāṃ ca vārtāṃ pārthivena pramadāsaṃnidhau prasaṅgenodīritāmupaniśamya samīpopaviṣṭaścittānuvṛttikuśalaḥ prasādavitto gītanṛtyavādyādiṣvabāhmo bāhmanārīparāyaṇaḥ paṭurayantritamukho bahubhaṅgiviśāradaḥ paramarmānveṣaṇaparaḥ parihāsayitā parivādaruciḥ paiśunyapaṇḍhitaḥ sacivamaṇḍalādapyutkocahārī sakaladurnayopādhyāyaḥ kāmatantrakarṇadhāraḥ kumārasevako vihārabhadro nāma smitapūrvaṃ vyajñapayat-"deva, daivānugraheṇa yadi kaścidbhājanaṃ bhavati vibhūteḥ, tamakasmāduccāvacairupapralobhanaiḥ kadarthayantaḥ svārthaṃ sādhayanti śiraḥ, baddhvā da--bhiḥ, ajinenācchādya, navanītenopalipya, anaśanaṃ ca śāyayitvā, sarvasvaṃ svīkariṣyanti /
tebhyo 'pi ghoratarāḥ pāṣaṇḍhinaḥ putradāraśarīrajīvitānyapi mocayanti /
yadi kaścitpaṭujātīyo nāsyai mṛgatṛṣṇikāyai hastagataṃ tyaktumicchet /
tamanye parivāryāhuḥ--"ekāmapi kākiṇīṃ kārṣāpaṇalakṣamāpādayema, śastrādṛte sarvaśatrun ghātayem, ekaśarīriṇamapi martyaṃ cakravartinaṃ vidadhīmahi, yadyasmaduddiṣṭena mārgeṇācaryate' iti /
sa punarimānpratyāha-"ko 'sau mārgaḥ' iti /
punarime bruvate-"nanu catasro rājavidyāstrayī vārtānvīkṣikī daṇḍanītiriti /
tāsu tisrastrayīvārtānvīkṣikyo mahatyo mandaphalāśca, tāstāvadāsatām /
adhīṣva tāvadṛṇḍanītim /
iyamidānīmācāryaviṣṇuguptena mauryārthe ṣaḍūbhiḥ ślokasahasraiḥ saṃkṣiptā /
saiveyamadhītya samyaganuṣṭhīyamānā yathoktakarmakṣamā' iti /
sa "tathā' ityadhīte /
śṛṇoti ca /
tatraiva jarāṃ gacchati /
tattu kila śāstraṃ śāstrāntarānubandhi /
sarvameva vāṅmayamaviditvā na tattvato 'dhigaṃsyate /
bhavatu kālena bahunālpena vā tadarthādhigatiḥ /
adhigataśāstreṇa cādāveva putradāramapi na viśvāsyam /
ātmakṛkṣerapi kṛte taṇḍulairiyadbhiriyānodanaḥ saṃpadyate /
iyata odanasya pākāyetāvadindhanaṃ paryāptamiti mānonmānapūrvakaṃ deyam /
utthitena ca rājñā kṣālitākṣālite mukhe muṣṭimardhamuṣṭiṃ vābhyantarīkṛtya kṛtsnamāyavyayajātamahnaḥ prathame 'ṣṭame vā bhāge śrotavyam /
śṛṇvata evāsya dviguṇamapaharanti te 'dhyakṣadhūrtāścatvāriṃśataṃ cākyopadiṣṭānāharaṇopāyānsahasradhātmabuddhyaiva te vikalpayitāraḥ /
dvitīye 'nyonyaṃ vivadamānānāṃ janānāmākrośāddahyamānakarṇaḥ kaṣṭaṃ jīvatiḥ tatrāri prāḍvivākādayaḥ svecchayā jayaparaujayā vidadhānāḥ pāpenākīrtyā ca bhartāramātmanaścārthairyojayanti /
tṛtīye snātuṃ ca labhate /
bhuktasya yāvadandhaḥpariṇaāmastāvadasya viṣabhayaṃ na śāmyatyeva /
caturthe hiraṇyapratihāya hastaṃ prasārayannevottiṣṭhati /
pañcame mantracintayā mahāntamāyāsamanubhavati /
children.translated_text: In the fifth [watch], he endures great exertion through deliberation on counsel (<s>mantra</s>).

children.text: tatrāpi mantriṇo madhyasthā ivānyonyaṃ mithaḥ saṃbhūya doṣaguṇau dūtacārahavākyāni śakyāśakyatāṃ deśakālakāryāvasthāśca svecchayā viparivartayantaḥ, svaparimitramaṇḍalānyupajīvanti /
children.translated_text: Therein too, the ministers, as if impartial, secretly combining with one another, manipulating at will the [assessment of] faults and merits, the words of envoys, spies, and messengers, [the evaluation of] what is possible and impossible, and the circumstances of place, time, task, and situation — they exploit the circles of allies of one's own [king] and of the enemy.

children.text: bāhmābhyantarāṃśca kopān gūḍhamutpādya prakāśaṃ praśamayanta iva svāminamavaśamavagṛhṇanti /
children.translated_text: And, covertly instigating both external and internal discontents while appearing to pacify them openly, they [in fact] subjugate the master against his will.

children.text: ṣaṣṭhe svairavihāro mantro vā sevyaḥ //
children.translated_text: In the sixth [watch], leisure recreation or counsel (<s>mantra</s>) is to be attended to. //

Then he too began to narrate: 'O lord, as I too was wandering through the forests of the <s>Vindhya</s> mountains, I saw somewhere near a well a boy of about eight years, suffering from hunger and thirst though undeserving of such suffering.
He spoke, his voice stammering with fear: "O noble one, please help me, wretched as I am!
Some person, while drawing water from this well to relieve my life-threatening thirst, has fallen in helplessly — he who was my sole refuge.
I am unable to pull him out."
Thereupon I approached and, by some contrivance, pulled out the old man; and I restored the boy to life by giving him water drawn up through a bamboo tube and fruits of the <s>lakuca</s> tree knocked down with stones from its top, which stood at an arrow-shot's height, reviving his failing life-breath. Then, seated beneath the tree, I asked the old man: "Father, who is this boy, and who are you, sir, and how has this calamity befallen you?"
He spoke, his voice choked with tears: "Hear me, noble one. There is a country called <s>Vidarbha</s>. In it, an ornament of the <s>Bhoja</s> dynasty, as if an incarnation of <s>Dharma</s> himself, exceedingly courageous, truthful in speech, generous, modest, a leader of his people, one who had won the devotion of his servants, renowned, lofty-minded, diligent in both intellect and bodily form, taking the <s>śāstras</s> (sacred sciences) as his authority, undertaking only what was feasible and fitting, one who honored the wise, empowered his servants, elevated his kinsmen, and humbled his enemies, who lent no ear to incoherent prattle, who was never without thirst for virtues, supremely skilled in the arts, most closely devoted to works on <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) and <s>artha</s> (prosperity), exceedingly grateful even for the smallest favor, one who personally inspected his treasury and army, who carefully examined all his superintendents, expert in the application of the <s>ṣāḍguṇya</s> (six measures of foreign policy), who guided the four <s>varṇas</s> (social orders) along the path of <s>Manu</s>, of celebrated fame — his name was <s>Puṇyavarmā</s>.
Having lived a full human lifespan through his meritorious deeds, <s>Puṇyavarmā</s> then, by ill fortune, came to be counted among the gods.
After him, one named <s>Anantavarmā</s>, his heir, took charge of the earth.
Though he was endowed with all virtues, by fate he did not pay sufficient regard to <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (the science of governance).
One day, an aged minister named <s>Vasurakṣita</s>, who had been highly esteemed by his father, spoke to him boldly in private: 'My son, all your personal accomplishments, from noble birth onward, are seen to be in no way deficient.
Your intellect, naturally sharp, and your proficiency in the arts — dance, song, and the like — and in the extensive domain of poetry, surpass those of others.
Yet, unless that intellect undergoes self-refinement through the <s>arthaśāstras</s> (sciences of statecraft), it does not truly shine — just as gold that has not been purified by fire does not fully gleam.
For a king devoid of wisdom, however exalted, does not perceive that he is being mounted upon by others.
Nor is he able to distinguish between ends and means and act accordingly.
And one who acts improperly in affairs is thwarted and despised by both his own people and his enemies.
Moreover, the commands of one who is disrespected have no power to secure the welfare of his subjects.
And subjects who have transgressed the bounds of authority, speaking whatever they please and living however they wish, would throw all established orders into confusion; and a world without boundaries would cause both the master and themselves to fall from this world and the next.
The journey of worldly life proceeds easily along the path illuminated by the lamp of sacred tradition.
For the <s>śāstra</s> (science) is indeed a divine eye whose operation is unobstructed in matters past, present, and future, as well as in things hidden and remote.
One who lacks it, even though possessing large and wide eyes, is truly blind in discerning the meaning of things, due to his incapacity.' Therefore, setting aside your attachment to other branches of learning, master <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (the science of governance) — the hereditary science of your family.
And through the practical application of its teachings, having secured power that brooks no resistance and maintaining unshaken authority, rule this earth girdled by the ocean for a long time.'
Hearing this, he said, 'It shall be done just as I have been instructed here by my elders,' and entered the inner palace.
But a certain courtier named <s>Vihārabhadra</s> — who sat nearby and had overheard that conversation when the king casually repeated it in the presence of his women — skilled in pandering to one's inclinations, possessed of ingratiating ways, an outsider to the sacred arts of song, dance, and music yet wholly devoted to other men's wives, sharp-tongued, unrestrained of mouth, expert in manifold stratagems, intent on probing others' vulnerabilities, a mocker, one who relished slander, learned in calumny, one who extracted bribes even from the circle of ministers, a professor of every kind of wickedness, the helmsman of the ship of sensual pleasure, a servant of the prince — this <s>Vihārabhadra</s>, with a preliminary smile, submitted: 'O lord, if by divine grace someone becomes a vessel of prosperity, why do these headshakers torment him with all manner of enticements high and low? They bind his head with ropes, cover him with animal hides, smear him with fresh butter, make him fast — and then appropriate everything he has!
Even more terrible than these are the heretical ascetics, who make one renounce even sons, wife, body, and life itself.
If some sharp-witted fellow refuses to let go of what is already in his hand for this mirage, then others surround him and say: "We can turn even a single <s>kākiṇī</s> (small copper coin) into a hundred thousand <s>kārṣāpaṇas</s> (silver coins); we can destroy all enemies without weapons; we can make even a single mortal into a <s>cakravartin</s> (universal sovereign) — if only you follow the path we prescribe!"
He then asks them: "What is that path?"
They reply: "Why, there are four royal sciences: the <s>Trayī</s> (the three Vedas), <s>Vārtā</s> (economics/agriculture), <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic/philosophy), and <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> (the science of governance).
Of these, the first three — the Vedas, economics, and philosophy — are vast but yield meager results. Let them be for now.
Study <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> at least!
It has now been condensed by the teacher <s>Viṣṇugupta</s> (Kauṭilya) for the sake of the <s>Maurya</s> dynasty into six thousand verses.
This very science, once studied and properly applied, is capable of accomplishing everything it promises."
So he says, "Very well," and studies it.
And he listens.
And right there he grows old.
For that science, you see, is intertwined with every other science.
Without knowing the entirety of literature, one cannot truly grasp it.
But let us grant that, in much time or little, one attains understanding of its meaning.
Even for one who has mastered the science, from the very start one must not trust even one's own sons and wife.
Even for cooking done for oneself, the exact amount of rice grains needed to produce a given quantity of cooked rice must be calculated, and the precise amount of fuel sufficient for cooking that much rice must be given only after prior measurement and weighing.
Moreover, when the king rises, whether or not his face has been washed, he must first take in hand a fistful — or half a fistful — and then listen to the entire account of the day's income and expenditure in the first eighth part of the day.
And even as he listens, those scoundrels among the superintendents steal double from him; and the forty methods of embezzlement taught by <s>Kauṭilya</s> they multiply a thousandfold by their own ingenuity.
In the second portion of the day, his ears burning from the mutual quarreling and abuse of litigants, he lives in misery. There, the chief judges and others, dispensing victory and defeat at their own whim, yoke their master — and themselves — with sin and infamy through their wealth.
In the third portion, he gets to bathe.
After eating, until the food is digested, his fear of poisoning simply does not subside.
In the fourth portion, he rises, stretching out his hand to receive gold offerings.'

so 'syaitāvānsvairavihārakālo yasya tisrastripādottarā nāḍīkāḥ /
saptame caturaṅgabalapratyavekṣaṇaprayāsaḥ /
aṣṭame 'sya senāpatisakhasya vikramacintākleśaḥ /
punarupāsyaiva saṃdhyām, prathame rātribhāge gūḍhapuruṣā draṣṭavyāḥ /
tanmukhena cātinṛśaṃsāḥ śastrāgnirasapraṇidhayo 'nuṣṭheyāḥ /
dvitīye bhojanānantaraṃ śrotriya iva svādhyāyamārabheta /
tṛtīye tūryaghoṣeṇa saṃviṣṭaścaturthapañcamau śayīta kila /
kathamivāsyājasracintāyāsavihvalamanaso varākasya nidrāsukhamupanamet /
punaḥ ṣaṣṭhe śāstracintākāryacintārambhaḥ /
saptame tu mantragraho dūtābhipreṣaṇāni ca /
dūtāśca nāmobhayatra priyākhyānalabdhānarthānvītaśulkabādhavartmani vāṇijyayā vardhayantaḥ, kāryamavidyāmānamapi leśenotpādyānavarataṃ bhramanti /
aṣṭame purohitādayo 'bhyetadyainamāhuḥ-"adya dṛṣṭo duḥsvapnaḥ /
duḥsthā grahāḥ śakunāni cāśubhāni /
śāntayaḥ kriyantām /
sarvamastu sauvarṇameva homasādhanam /
evaṃ sati karma guṇavadbhavati /
brahmakalpā ime brāhmāṇāḥ /
kṛtamebhiḥ svastyayanaṃ kalyāṇataraṃ bhavati /
te cāmī kaṣṭadryā bahvapatyā yajvāno vīryavantaścādyāpyaprāptapratigrahāḥ /
dattaṃ caibhyaḥ svargyamāyuṣyamariṣṭanāśanaṃ ca bhavati' iti bahu bahu dāpayitvā tanmukhena svayamupāṃśu bhakṣayanti /
tadevamaharniśamavihitasukhaleśamāyāsabahulamaviralakadarthanaṃ ca nayato 'nayajñasyāstāṃ cakravārtitā svamaṇḍalamātramapi durārakṣyaṃ bhavet /
śāstrajñasamājñāto hi yaddadāti, yanmānayati, yatpriyaṃ bravīti, tatsarvamatisaṃdhātumityaviśvāsaḥ /
aviśvāsatā hi janmabhūmiralakṣmyāḥ /
yāvatā ca nayena vinā na lokayātrā sa loka eva siddhaḥ nātra śāstreṇārthaḥ stanandhayo 'pi hi taistairupāyaiḥ stanapānaṃ jananyā lipsate tadapāsyātiyantraṇāmanubhūyantāṃ yatheṣṭamindriyasukhāni /
ya'pyupadiśanti "evamindriyāṇi jetavyāni, evamariṣaḍvargastyājyaḥ, sāmādirupāyavargaḥ sveṣu pareṣu cājasraṃ prayojyaḥ, saṃdhivigrahacintayaiva neyaḥ kālaḥ, svalpo 'pi sukhasyāvakāśo na deyaḥ' iti, tairapyebhirmantribakairyuṣmattścauryārjitaṃ dhanaṃ dāsīgṛheṣveva bhujyate /
ke caite varākāḥ /
ye 'pi mantrakarkaśāstantrakartāraḥ śukrāṅgirasaviśālākṣabāhudantiputraparāśaraprabhṛtayastaiḥ-kimariṣaḍvargo jitaḥ, kṛtaṃ vā taiḥ śāstrānuṣṭhānam /
tairapi hi prārabdheṣu kāryeṣu dṛṣṭe siddhyasiddhī /
paṭhantaścāpaṭhadbhiratisaṃdhīyamānā bahavaḥ /
nanvidamupapannaṃ devasya, yaduta sarvalokasya vandyā jātiḥ, ayātayāmaṃ vayaḥ, darśanīyaṃ vapuḥ, aparimāṇā vibhūtiḥ /
tatsarvaṃ sarvāviśvāsahetunā sukhopabhogapratibandhinā bahumārgavikalpanātsarvakāryeṣvamuktasaṃśayena tantrāvāpena mā kṛthā vṛkṣā /
santi hi te dantināṃ daśasahasrāṇi, hayānāṃ lakṣatrayam, anantaṃ ca pādātam /
api ca pūrṇānyeva haimaratnaiḥ kośagṛhāṇi /
sarvaścaiṣa jīvalokaḥ samagramapi yugasahasraṃ bhuñjāno na te koṣṭhāgārāṇi recayiṣyati /
kimidamaparyāptaṃ yadanyāyārjitāyāsaḥ kriyate /
jīvitaṃ hi nāma janmavatāṃ catuḥpañcānyahāni /
tatrāpi bhogayogyamalpālpaṃ vayaḥ-khaṇḍam /
apaṇḍitāḥ punararjayanta eva dhvaṃsante /
nārjitasya vastuno lavamapyāsvādayitumīhante /
kiṃ bahunā rājyabhāraṃ bhārakṣameṣvantaraṅgeṣu bhaktimatsu samarpya, apsaraḥpratirūpābhirantaḥpurikābhī ramamāṇo gītasaṃgītapānagoṣṭhīśca yathartu badhnanyathārhaṃ kuru śarīralābham' iti pañcāṅgīspṛṣṭabhūmirañjalicumbitacūḍaściramaśeta /
prāhasīcca prītiphullalocano 'ntaḥpurapramadājanaḥ /
jananāthaśca sasmitam "uttiṣṭha, nanu hitopadeśādguravo bhavantaḥ /
kimiti gurutvaviparītamanuṣṭhitam' iti tamutthāpya krīḍīnirbharamatiṣṭhat /
athaiṣu dineṣu bhūyobhūyaḥ prastuter'the preryamāṇo mantrivṛddhena, vacasābhyupepya manasaivācittajña ityavajñātavān /
athaivaṃ mantriṇo manasyabhūt--"aho me mohādbāliśyam /
aruciter'the codayannarthīvākṣigato 'hamasya hāsyo jātaḥ /
spaṣṭamasya ceṣṭānāmāyathāpūrvyam /
tathā hi /
na māṃ snigdhaṃ paśyati, na smitapūrvaṃ bhāṣate, na rahasyāni vivṛṇoti, na haste spṛśati, na vyasaneṣvanukampate, notsaveṣvanugṛhṇāti, na vilobhanavastu preṣayati, na matsukṛtāni pragaṇayati, na me ga-havārtāṃ pṛcchati, na matpakṣānpratyavekṣate, na māmāsannakāryeṣvabhyantarīkaroti, na māmantaḥpuraṃ praveśayati /
api ca māmanarheṣu karmasu niyuṅkte, madāsanamanyairavaṣṭabhyamānamanujānāti, madvairiṣu viśrambhaṃ darśayati, maduktasyottaraṃ na dadāti, matsamānadoṣānvigarhati, marmaṇi māmupahasati, svamatamapi mayā varṇyamānaṃ pratikṣipati, mahārhāṇi vastūni matprahitāni nābhinandati, nayajñānāṃ skhalitāni matsamakṣaṃ mūrkhairuddhoṣayati, satyamāhacāṇakyaḥ-"cittajñānānuvartino 'narthā apa priyāḥ syuḥ /
dakṣiṇā apa tadbhāvabahiṣkṛtā dveṣyā bhaveyuḥ' iti /
tathāpi kā gatiḥ /
avinīto 'pi na parityājyaḥ pitṛpitāmahānuyātairasmādṛśairayamadhipatiḥ /
aparityajanto 'pi kamupakāramaśrūyamāṇavācaḥ kurmaḥ /
sarvathā nayajñasya vasantabhānoraśmakendrasya haste rājyamidaṃ patitam /
api nāmāpado bhāvinyaḥ prakṛtisthamenamāpādayeyuḥ /
anartheṣu sulabhavyalīkeṣu kvacidutpanno 'pi dveṣaḥ sadvṛttamasmairocayet /
bhavatu bhavitā tāvadanarthaḥ /
stambhitapiśunajihvo yathākathañcidabhraṣṭapadastiṣṭheyam' iti /
evaṃ gate mantriṇi, rājani ca kāmavṛtte, candrapālito nāmāśvakendrāmātyasyendrapālitasya sūnuḥ, asadvṛttaḥ pitṛnirvāsito nāma bhūtvā, bahubhiścāraṇagaṇairbahvībhiranalpakauśalābhiḥ śilpakāriṇībhiranekacchannakiṅkaraiśca parivṛto 'byetya vividhābhiḥ krīḍābhirvihārabhadramātmasādakarot /
amunā caiva saṃkrameṇa rājanyāspadamalabhata /
labdharandhraśca sa yadyadvayyasanamārabhate tattathetyavarṇayat--"deva, yathā mṛgayā hyaupakārikī na tathānyat /
atra hi vyāyāmotkarṣādāpatsūpakartā dīrghādhvalaṅghanakṣamo jaṅghājavaḥ, kaphāpacayādārogyaikamūlamāśayāgnidīptiḥ, medopakarṣādaṅgānāṃ sthairyakārkaśyātilāghavādīni, śītoṣṇavātavarṣakṣutpipāsāsahatvam, sattvānāmavasthāntareṣu cittaceṣṭitajñānam, hariṇagavalagavayādivadhena sasyalopapratikriyā, vṛkavyāghnādighātena sthalapathaśalyaśodhanam, śailāṭavīpradeśānāṃ vividhakarmakṣamāṇāmālocanam, āṭavikavargaviśrambhaṇam, utsāhaśaktisaṃdhukṣaṇena pratyanīkavitrāsanamiti bahutamā guṇāḥ /
dyūte 'pi dravyarāśestṛṇavattyāgādanupamānamāśayaudāryam, jayaparājayānavasthānāddharṣavivādayoraviveyatvam, pauruṣaikanimittasyāmarṣasya vṛddhiḥ, akṣahastabhūmyādigocarāṇāmatyantadurupalakṣyāṇāṃ kūṭakarmaṇāmupalakṣaṇādanantabuddhinaipuṇyam, ekaviṣayopasaṃhārāccittasyāticitramaikāgryam, adhyavasāyasahacareṣu sāhaseṣvatiratiḥ, atikarkaśapuruṣapratisaṃsargādananyadharṣaṇīyatā, mānāvadhāraṇam, akṛpaṇaṃ ca śarīrayāpanamiti /
uttamāṅganopabhoge 'pyarahthadharmayoḥ saphalīkaraṇam, phuṣkalaḥ puruṣābhimānaḥ bhāvajñānakauśalam, alobhakliṣṭamāceṣṭitam, akhilāsu kalāsu vaicakṣaṇyam, alabdhopalabdhilabdhānurakṣaṇarakṣitopabhogabhuktānusaṃdhānaruṣṭānunayādi ṣvajasramabhyupāyaracanayā buddhivācoḥ pāṭavam, utkṛṣṭaśarīrasaṃskārātsubhagaveṣatayā lokasaṃbhāvanīyatā, paraṃ suhṛtpriyatvam, garīyasī parijanavyapekṣā, smitapūrvābhibhāṣitvam, udriktasattvatā, dākṣiṇyānuvartanam /
apatyotpādanenobhayalokaśreyaskaratvamiti /
pāne 'pi nānāvidharāgabhaṅgapaṭīyasāmāsavānāmāsevanātspṛhaṇīyavayovyavasthāpanam, ahaṅkāraprakarṣādaśeṣaduḥ-khatiraskaraṇam, aṅgajarāgadīpanādaṅganopabhogaśaktisaṃdhukṣaṇam, aparādhapramārjanānmanaḥśalyonmārjanam, aṅgajarāgadīpanādaṅganopabhogaśaktisaṃdhukṣaṇam, aparādhapramārjanānmanaḥśalyonmārjanam, aśrāvyaśaṃsibhiranargalapralāpairviśvāsopabṛṃhaṇam, matsarānanubandhādānandaikatānatā, śabdādīnāmindriyārthānāṃ sātatyenānubhavaḥ, saṃvibhāgaśīlatayā suhṛdvargasaṃvargaṇam, anupamānamaṅgalāvaṇyam, anuttarāṇi vilasitāniṃ, bhayārtiharaṇācca sāṅgramikatvamiti /
vākpāruṣyaṃ daṇḍo dāruṇo dūṣaṇāni cārthānāmeva yathāvakāśamaupakārikāṇi /
nahi muniriva narapatirupaśamaratirabhibhavitumarikulamalam, abalambituṃ ca lokatantram' iti /
asāvapi gurupadeśamivātyādareṇa tasya matamanvavartata /
tacchīlānusāriṇyaśca prakṛtayo viśṛṅkhalamasevanta vyasanāni /
sarvaśca samānadoṣatayā na kasyacicchidrānveṣaṇāyāyatiṣṭa /
samānabhartṛprakṛtayastantrādhyakṣāḥ svāni karmaphalānyabhakṣayan /
tataḥ kramādāyadvārāṇi vyaśīryanta /
vyayamukhāni viṭavidheyatayā vibhoraharaharvyavardhanta /
sāmantapaurajānapadamukhyāśca samānaśīlatayopārūḍhaviśrambheṇa rājñā sajānayaḥ pānagoṣṭhīṣvabhyantarīkṛtāḥ svaṃsvamācāramatyācāriṣuḥ /
tadaṅgānāsu cānekāpadeśapūrvamapācarannarendraḥ /
tadantaḥpureṣu cāmī bhinnavṛtteṣu mandratrāsā bahusukhairavartanta /
sarvaśca kulāṅganājanaḥ sulabhabhaṅgibhāṣaṇarato bhagnacāritrayantraṇastṛṇāyāpi na gaṇayitvā bhartṝndhātṛṇamantraṇānyaśṛṇot /
tanmūlāśca kalahāḥ sāmarṣāṇāmudabhavan /
ahanyanta durbalā balibhiḥ /
apahṛtāni dhanavatāṃ dhanāni taskarādibhiḥ /
apahṛtaparibhūtayaḥ prahatāśca pātakapathāḥ /
hatabāndhavā hṛtavittā badhabandhāturāśca muktakaṇṭhamākrośannaśrukaṇṭhyaḥ prajāḥ /
daṇḍaścāyathāpraṇīto bhayakrodhāvajanayat /
kṛśakuṭumbeṣu lobhaḥ padamadhattaḥ vimānitāśca tejasvino 'mānenādahyanta /
teṣu teṣu cākṛtyeṣu prāsaranparoṣajāpāḥ /
tadā ca mṛgayuveṣamṛgabāhulyavarṇanenādridroṇīranapasāramārgāḥ suṣkatṛṇavaṃśagulmāḥ praveśya dvārato 'gnivisargaiḥ, vyāghrādivadhe protsāhya tanmukhapātanaiḥ, iṣṭakūpatṛṣṇotpādanenātidūrahāritānāṃ prāṇahāribhiḥ kṣutpipāsābhivardhanaiḥ, tṛṇagulmagūḍhataṭapradarapātahetubhirviṣamamārgapradhāvanaiḥ, viṣamukhībhiḥ kṣurikābhiścaraṇakaṇṭakoddharaṇaiḥ viṣvagvisaravicchinnānuyātṛtayaikākīkṛtānāṃ yatheṣṭaghātanaiḥ, mṛgadehāparāddhairnāmeṣumokṣaṇaiḥ, sapaṇabandhamadhiruhyādriśṛṅgāṇi duradhirohāṇyananyalakṣyaiḥ prabhraṃśanaiḥ, āṭavikacchadmanā vipineṣu viralasainikānāṃ pratirodhanaiḥ, akṣadyūtapakṣiyuddhayātrotsavādisaṃkuleṣu balabadanupraveśanaiḥ, itareṣāṃ hiṃsotpādanaiḥ, gūḍhotpāditavyalīkebhyo 'priyāṇi prakāśaṃ labdhvā sākṣiṣu tadvikhyāpyākīrtiguptihetubhiḥ parākramaiḥ, parakalatreṣu suhṛttevanābhiyojya jārānbhartṝnumayaṃ vā prahṛtya tatsāhasopanyāsaiḥ, yogyanārīhāritānāṃ saṃketeṣu prāgupanilīya paścādabhidutyākīrtanīyaiḥ pramāpaṇaiḥ, upapralobhya bilapraveśeṣu nidhānakhananeṣu mantrasādhaneṣu ca vighnavyājasādhyairvyāpādanaiḥ, mattagajādhirohaṇāya preya pratyapāyanivartanaiḥ, vyālahastinaṃ koṣayitvā lakṣyīkṛtamukyamaṇḍaleṣvapakramaṇaiḥ, yogyāṅganābhiraharniśamabhiramayya rājayakṣmotpādanaiḥ, vastrābharaṇamālyāṅgarāgādiṣu rasavidhānakauśalaiḥ, cikitsāmukhenāmayopabarhaṇairanyaiścābhyupāyeraśmakendraprayuktāstīkṣṇarasadādayaḥ prakṣapitapravīramanantavarmakaṭakaṃ jarjaramakurvan /
atha vasantabhānurbhānuvarmāṇaṃ nāma vānavāsyaṃ protsāhyānantavarmaṇā vyagrāhayat /
tatparāmṛṣṭarāṣṭraparyantaścānantavarmā tamabhiyoktuṃ balasamutthānamakarot /
sarvasāmantebhyaścāśmakendraḥ prāgupetyāsya priyataro 'bhūt /
apare 'pi sāmāntāḥ sasagaṃsata /
gatvā cābhyarṇe narmadārodhasi nyaviśana /
tasmiṃścāvasare mahāsāmantasya kuntalapateravantidevasyātmanāṭakīyāṃ kṣmātalorvaśīṃ nāma candrapālitādibhiratipraśastanṛtyakauśalāmāhūyāntavarmā nṛtyamadrākṣīt /
ātiraktaśca bhuktavānimāṃ madhumattām /
aśmakendrastu kuntalapatimekānte samabhyadhatta-"pramatta eṣa rājā kalatrāṇi naḥ parāmṛśati /
kiyatyavajñā soḍhavyā /
mama śatamasti hastinām, pañcaśatāni ca te /
tadāvāṃ saṃbūya muraleśaṃ vīrasenamṛcīkeśamekavīraṃ koṅkaṇapatiṃ kumāraguptaṃ sāsikyanāthaṃ ca nāgapālamupajapāva /
te cāvaśyamasyāvinayamasahamānā asmanmatenaivopāvarteran /
ayaṃ ca vānavāsyaḥ priyaṃ me mitram /
amunainaṃ durvinītamagrato vyatipaktaṃ pṛṣṭataḥ prāharema /
kośavāhanaṃ ca vibhajya gṛhṇīmaḥ' iti /
hṛṣṭena cāmunābhyupete, viṃśatiṃ vaśarāṃśukānām, pañcaviṃśatiṃ kāñjanakuṅkumapalānām, prābhṛtīkṛtyāptamukhena taiḥ sāmantaiḥ saṃmantrya tānapi svamatāvasthāpayat /
uttaredyusteṣāṃ sāmantānāṃ vānavāsyasya ca anantavarmā nayadveṣādāmipatvamagamat /
vasantabhānuśca tatkośavāhanamavaśīrṇamātmādhiṣṭitameva kṛtvā yathāprayāsaṃ yathābalaṃ ca vibhajya gṛhṇīta /
yuṣmadanujñayā yenakenacidaṃśenāhaṃ tuṣyāmi' iti śāṭhyātsarvānuvarttī, tenaivāmiṣeṇa nimittīkṛtenotpāditakalahaḥ sarvasāmantānadhvaṃsayat /
tadīyaṃ ca sarvasvaṃ svayamevāgrasat /
vānavāmyaṃ kenacidaṃśenānugṛhya pratyāvṛtya sarvamanantavarmarājyamātmasādakarot /
asmiṃścāntera mantrivṛddho vasurakṣitaḥ kaiścinmaulaiḥ saṃbhūya bālamenaṃ bhāskaravarmāṇam, asyaiva jyāyasīṃ baginīṃ trayodaśavarṣāṃ mañjuvādinīm, anayośca mātaraṃ mahādevīṃ vasuṃdharāmādāyāpasarpannāpado 'syā bhāvitayā dāhajvareṇa dehamajahāt /
asmādṛśairmitraistu nītvā māhiṣmatīṃ bhartṛdvaimāturāya bhrātre mitravarmaṇe sāpatyā devī darśitābhūt /
tāṃ cāryāmanāryo 'sāvanyathābhyamanyata /
nirbhartsitaśca tayā "sutamiyamakhaṇḍacāritrā rājyarhiṃ cikīrṣati' iti nairghṛṇyāttamenaṃ bālamajighāṃsīt /
idaṃ tu jñātvā devyāhamājñaptaḥ-"tāta, nālījaṅgaḥ, jīvatānenārbhakeṇa yatra kvacidavadhāya jīva /
jīveyaṃ cedahamapyenamanusariṣyāmi /
jñāpaya māṃ kṣemapravṛttaḥ vyagāhiṣi /
pādacāriṇaṃ cainamāśvāsayituṃ ghoṣe kvacidahāni kānicidviśramayya, tatrāpi rājapuruṣasaṃpātabhīto duradhvamapāsaram /
tatrāsya dāruṇapipāsāpīḍitasya vāri dātukāmaḥ kūpe 'sminnapabhraśya patitastvayaivamanugṛhītaḥ /
svamevāsyātaḥ śaraṇamedhi viśaraṇasya rājasūnoḥ' ityañjalimabadhnāt /
"kimīyā jātyāsya mātā' ityanuyukte mayāmunoktam-"ityañjalimabadhnāt /
"kimīyā jātyāsya mātā' ityanuyukte mayāmunoktam-"pāṭaliputrasya vaṇijo vaiśravaṇasya duhitari sāgaradattāyāṃ kosalendrātkusumadhanvano 'sya mātā jātā' iti /
"yadyevametanmāturmatpituścaiko mātāmahaḥ' iti sasnehaṃ tamahaṃ sasvaje /
vṛddhenoktam-"sindhudattaputrāṇāṃ katamaste pitā' iti /
"suśrutaḥ' ityukte so 'tyahṛṣyat /
ahaṃ tu "tapanayāvaliptamaśmakanayenaivonmūlya bālamenaṃ pitrye pade pratiṣṭhāpayeyam' iti pratijñāya kathamasyaināṃ kṣudhaṃ kṣapayeyam' ityacintayam /
tāvadāpatitau ca kasyāpi vyādhasya trīnipūnatītya dvau mṛgau sa ca vyādhaḥ /
tasya hastādavaśiṣṭamiṣudvayaṃ kodaṇḍaṃ cākṣiṣyāvadhiṣam /
ekaśca sapatrākṛto 'nyaśca niṣpatrākṛto 'patat /
taṃ caikaṃ mṛgaṃ dattvā mṛgayave, anyasyāpalomatvacaḥ klomāpāhye, niṣkulākṛtya vikṛtyorvaṅghrigrīvādīni śūlākṛtya dāvāṅgāraṣuṣa taptenāmiṣeṇa tayorātmanaśca kṣudhamatārṣam /
etasminkarmaṇi matsauṣṭhavenātihṛṣṭaṃ kirātamasmi pṛṣṭavān-"api jānāsi māhiṣmatīvṛttāntam' iti /
asāvācaṣṭa-" tatra vyāghratvaco dṛtaści vikrīyādaivāgataḥ kiṃ na jānāmi /
pracaṇḍavarmā nāma caṇḍavarmānujo mitravarmaduhitaraṃ mañjuvādinīṃ vilipsurabhyetīti tenotsavottarā purī' iti /
atha karṇe jīrṇamabravam-"dhūrto mitravarmā duhitari samyakpratipattyā mātaraṃ viśvāsya tanmukhena pratyākṛṣya bālakaṃ jighāṃsati /
tatpratigatyaṃ kuśalamasya madvārtā ca devyai raho nivedya punaḥ kumāraḥ śārdūlabhakṣita iti prakāśamākrośanaṃ kāryam /
sa durmatirantaḥprīto bahirduḥkhaṃ darśayandevīmanuneṣyati /
punastayā tvanmukhena sa vācyaḥ-"yadapekṣayā tvanmatamatyakramiṣaṃ so 'pi bālaḥ pāpena me paralokamagāt /
adya tu tvadādeśakāriṇyevāham' iti /
sa tayoktaḥ prītiṃ pratipadyābhipatsyati /
punaranena vatsanābhanāmnā mahāviṣeṇa saṃnīya toyaṃ tatra mālāṃ majjayitvā tayā sa vakṣasi mukhe ca hantavyaḥ /
"sa evāyamasiprahāraḥ pāpīyasastava bhavatu yadyasmi pativratā' /
punaranenāgadena saṃgamite 'mbhasi tāṃ mālāṃ majjayitvā svaduhitre deyā /
mṛte tu tasmiṃstasyāṃ ca nirvikārāyāṃ satyām, satītyevaināṃ prakṛtayo 'nuvartiṣyante /
punaḥ pracaṇḍavarmaṇe saṃdeśyam-"anāyakamidaṃ rājyam /
anenaiva saha vālikeyaṃ svīkartavyā' iti /
tāvadāvāṃ kāpālikavepacchannau devyaiva dīyamānabhikṣau puro vahirupaśmaśānaṃ vatsyāvaḥ /
punarāryaprāyānpauravṛddhānāptāṃśca mantrivṛddhānekānte bravītu devī-"svapne 'dya me devyā vindhyavāsinyā kṛtaḥ prasādaḥ /
adya caturthe 'hani pracaṇḍavarmā mariṣyati /
pañcame 'hani revātaṭavartini madbhavane parīkṣya vaijanyam, janeṣu nirgateṣu kapāṭamuddhāṭya tvatsutena saha ko 'pi dvijakumāro niryāsyati /
sa rājyamidamanupālya bālaṃ te pratiṣṭhāpayiṣyati /
sa khalu bālo mayā vyāghrīrūpayā tiraskṛtya sthāpitaḥ /
sā ceyaṃ vatsā mañjuvādinī tasya dvijātidārakasya dāratvenaiva kalpitā' iti /
tadetadatirahasyaṃ yuṣmāsveva guptaṃ tiṣṭhatu yāvadetadupapatsyate' iti /
sa sāṃpratamatiprītaḥ prayātor'thaścayāyaṃ yathācintitamanuṣṭhito 'bhūt /
pratidiśaṃ ca lokavādaḥ prāsarpat-"aho māhātmyaṃ pativratānām /
asiprahāra eva hi sa mālāprahārastasmai jātaḥ /
na śakyamupadhiyuktametatkarmeti vaktum /
yatastadeva dattaṃ dāma duhitre stanamaṇḍanameva tasyai jātaṃ na mṛtyuḥ /
yo 'syāḥ pativratāyāḥ śāsanamativartate sa bhasmaiva bhavet' iti /
atha mahāvrativeṣeṇa māṃ ca putraṃ ca bhikṣāyai praviṣṭau dṛṣṭvā prasnutastanī pratyutthāya harṣākulamabravīt-"bhagavan, ayamañjaliḥ anātho 'yaṃ jano 'nugṛhyatām /
asati mamaikaḥ svapnaḥ sa kiṃ satyo na vā' ti /
mayoktam-"phalamasyādyaiva drakṣyasi' iti /
"yadyevaṃ bahu bhāgadheyamasyā vo dāsyāḥ /
sa khalvasyāḥ sānāthyaśaṃsī svapnaḥ' iti maddarśanarāgabaddhasādhvasāṃ mañjuvādinīṃ praṇamayya, bhūyo 'pi sā harṣagarbhamabrūta-"taccenmithyā so 'yaṃ yuṣmadīyo bālakapālī śvo mayā niroddhavyaḥ' iti /
mayāpi sasmitaṃ mañjuvādinīrāgalīnadṛṣṭilīḍhadhairyeṇa "evamastu' iti labdhabhaikṣaḥ, nālījaṅghamākārya nirgamya tataśca taṃ cānuyāntaṃ śanairapṛccham-"kvāsāvalyāyuḥ prathitaḥ pracaṇḍavarmā' iti /
so 'brūta-"rājyamidaṃ mametyapāstaśaṅko rājāsthānamaṇḍapa eva tiṣṭhatyupāsyamānaḥ kuśīlavaiḥ' iti /
"yadyevamudyāne tiṣṭha' iti taṃ jarantamādiśya tatprakāraikapārśvaikvacicchūnyamaṭhikāyāṃ mātrāḥ samavatārya, tadrakṣaṇaniyuktarājaputraḥ, kṛtakuśīlavaveṣalīlaḥ pracaṇḍavarmāṇametyānvarañjayam /
anurañjitātape tu samaye, janasamājajñānopayogīni saṃhṛtya nṛtyagītanānāruditādihastacaṅkramaṇamūrdhvapādālātapādapīṭhavṛścikamakaralaṅghanādīni mastyodvartanādīni ca karaṇāni, punarādāyādāyāsannavartināṃ kṣurikāḥ tābhirupāhitavarṣmā citraduṣkarāṇi karaṇāni śyenapātotkrośapātādīni darśayan, viṃśaticāpāntarālāvasthitasya pracaṇḍavarmaṇaśchurikayaikayā pratyurasaṃ prahṛtya, "jīvyādvarṣasahasraṃ vasantabhānuḥ' ityabhigarjan, madgātramarukartumudyatāseḥ kasyāpi cārabhaṭasya pīvarāṃsabāhuśikharamākramya, tāvataiva taṃ vicetākurvan, sākulaṃ ca lokamuccakṣūkurvan, dvipuruṣocchritaṃ prākāramatyalaṅghayam /
avaplutya copavane "madanupātināmeṣa panthā dṛśyate' iti bruvāṇa eva nālījaṅghasamīkṛtasaikataspṛṣṭapādanyāsayā tamālavīthyā cānuprākāraṃ pracā pratipradhāvitaḥ; punaravācocciteṣṭakacitatvādalakṣyapātena pradrutya, laṅghitaprākāravaprakhātavalayaḥ, tasyāṃ śanyamaṭhikāyāṃ tūrṇameva praviśya, pratimuktapūrvaveṣaḥ saha kumāreṇa matkarmatumularājadvāraduḥkhalabdhavartamā śmaśānoddeśamabhyagām /
prāgeva tasmindurgāgṛhe prātimādhiṣṭhāna eva mayā kṛtaṃ bhagrapārśvasthairyasthūlaprastarasthagitabāhmadvāraṃ bilam /
atha galati madhyarātre varṣavaropanītamahārharatnabhūṣaṇapaṭṭanivasanau tadbilamāvāṃ praviśya tūṣṇīmatiṣṭhāva /
devī tu pūrvedyureva yathārhamagnisaṃskāraṃ mālavāya dattvā pracaṇḍavarmaṇe caṇḍavarmaṇe ca tāmavasthāmaśmakendropadhikṛtāmeva saṃdiśya, uttaredyuḥ pratyuṣasyeva pūrvasaṃketitapaurāmātyasāmantavṛddhaiḥ sahābhyatya bhagavatīmarcayitvā samarcanapratyakṣaṃ parīkṣitakukṣivaijanyaṃ tadbhavanaṃ pidhāya dattadṛṣṭiḥ saha janena sthitvā, paṭīyāṃsaṃ paṭahaśabdamakārayat /
aṇutararandhrapraviṣṭena tena nādenāhaṃ dattasaṃjñaḥ śirasaivotkṣipya sapratimaṃ lohapādapīṭhamaṃsalapuruṣaprayatnaduścalamubhayakaravidhṛtamekapāśvramekato niveśya niragamam /
niragamayaṃ ca kumāram /
atha yathāpūrvamarcayitvā durgāmuddhāṭitakapāṭaḥ pratyakṣībhūya pratyayahṛṣṭadṛṣṭi /
spaṣṭaromāñcamudyatāñjalirūḍhavismayaṃ ca praṇipatantīḥ prakṛtīrabhyadhām-"itthaṃ devī vindhyavāsinī manmukhena yuṣmānājñāpayati-mayā sakṛṣayā śārdūlarūpaiṇa tiraskṛtyādya vo dattamenamadyaprabhṛti matputratayā mandamātṛpakṣa iti parigṛhṇantu bhavantaḥ /
api ca durghaṭakūṭakoṭighaṭanāpāṭavaprakaṭaśāṭhyaniṣṭhurāśmakaghaṭaghaṭṭanātmānaṃ māṃ manyadhvamasya rakṣitāram /
rakṣānirveśaścāsya svaseyaṃ subhrūrabhyanujñātā mahyamāryayā' iti /
śrutvaitat "aho bhāgyavānbhojavaṃśaḥ, yasya tvamāryādatto nāthaḥ' ityaprīyanta prakṛtayaḥ /
sā tu vācāmagocarāṃ harṣāvasthāmaspṛśanme śvaśrūḥ /
tadahareva ca yathāvadagrāhayanmañjuvādinīpāṇipallavam /
prapannāyāṃ ca yāminyāṃ samyageva bilapratyapūrayam /
alabdharandhraśca loko naṣṭamuṣṭicintādikathanairabhyupāyāntaraprayuktairdvivyāṃśatāmeva mama samarthayamānaḥ, madājñāṃ nātyavartata /
rājaputrasyāryāputra iti prabhāvahetuḥ prasiddhirāsīt /

acintayaṃ ca-"rājyaṃ nāma śaktitrayāyattama, śaktayaśca mantraprabhāvotsāhāḥ parasparānugṛhītāḥ kṛtyeṣu kramante /
mantreṇa hi viniścayor'thānām, prabhāveṇa prārambhaḥ, utsāhena nirvahaṇam /
ataḥ pañcāṅgamantramūlaḥ, dvirūpaprabhāvaskandhaḥ, caturgaṇotsāhaviṭapaḥ, dvisaptatiprakṛtipatraḥ, ṣaḍguṇakisalayaḥ, śaktisiddhipuṣpaphalaśca, nayavanaspatirneturupakaroti /
sa cāyamanekādhikaraṇatvādasahāyena durupajīvyaḥ /

atha nālījaṅghaṃ rahasyaśikṣayam-"tāta, āryamāryaketumekānte brūhi-"ko māyāpuruṣo ya imāṃ rājyalakṣmīmanubhavati, sa cāyamasmadbālo bhujaṅgenāmunā parigṛhītaḥ /
kimudgīryeta grasyeta vā' iti /
sa yadvadiṣyati "tadasmi bodhyaḥ' iti /
so 'nyadaivaṃ māmāvedayat-"muhurupāsya prābhṛtaiḥ pravartya citrāḥ kathāḥ, saṃvāhya pāṇipādam, ati visrambhadattakṣaṇaṃ tamaprākṣaṃ tvadupadiṣṭena nayena /
sāpyevamakathayat-"bhadra, maivaṃ vādīḥ /
abijanasya śuddhidarśanam, asādhāraṇaṃ buddhinaipuṇam, atimānuṣaṃ prāṇabalam, aparimāṇamaudāryam, atyāścaryamastrakauśalam, analpaṃ śilpajñānam, anugrahārdraṃ cetaḥ, tejaścāpyaviṣahyamabhyamitrīṇam /
ityasminneva saṃnipātino guṇāḥ ye 'nyatraikaikaśo 'pi durlabhāḥ /
dviṣatāmeṣa cirabilvadrumaḥ, prahvāṇāṃ tu candanataruḥ, tamuddhṛtya nītijñaṃmanyamaśmakamimaṃ ca rājaputraṃ pitrye pade pratiṣṭhitameva viddhi /
nātra saṃśayaḥ kāryaḥ' iti /
taccāpi śrutvā bhūyobhūyaścopadābhirviśodhya taṃ me matisahāyamakaravam /
tatsakhaśca satyaśaucayuktānamātyānvividhavyañjanāṃśca gūḍhapuruṣānudapādayam /
tebhyaścopalabhya lubdhasamṛddhamatyutsiktamavidheyaprāyaṃ ca prakṛtimaṇḍalamalubdhatāmabhikhyāpayan, dhārmikatvamudbhāvayana, nāstikānkadarthayan, kaṇṭakānviśodhayan, amitropadhīnapaghnan, cāturvarṇyaṃ ca svadharmakarmasu sthāpayan, abhisamāhareyamarthānarthamūlā hi daṇḍaviśiṣṭakarmārambhā na cānyadasti pāpiṣṭhaṃ tatra daurbalyāt, ityākalayya yogānanvatiṣṭham /
vyacintayaṃ ca--sarvo 'pyatiśūraḥ sevakavargo mayi tathānurakto yathājñayā jīvitamapi tṛṇāya manyate /
rājyadvitayasainyasāmagryā ca nāhamaśmakeśādvasantabhānornyūno nītyāviṣṭaśca /
ato vasantabhānu parājitya vidarbhādhipateranantavarmaṇastanayaṃ bhāskaravarmāṇaṃ pitrye pade sthāpayitumalamasmi /
ayaṃ ca rājasūnurbhavānyā putratvena parikaspitaḥ /
ahaṃ cāsya sāhāyye niyukta iti sarvatra kiṃvadantī saṃjātāsti /
adyāpi caitanmatkapaṭakṛtyaṃ na kenāpi viditam, /
atrasthāścāsminbhāskaravarmaṇi rājatanaye "ayamasmatsvāmino 'nantavarmaṇaḥ putro bhavānyāḥ prasādādetadrājyamavāpsyati' iti baddhāśā vartante /
aśmakeśasainyaṃ ca rājasūnorbhavānīsāhāyyaṃ viditvā "davyāḥ śakteḥ puro na balavatī mānavī śaktiḥ' ityasmābhirvigrahe calacittamivopalakṣyate /
atratyāśca maulāḥ prakṛtayaḥ prathamameva rājasutābhyudayābhilāṣiṇya idānīṃ ca punarmayā dānamānādyāvajarnana viśvāsitā viśeṣeṇa rājaputramevābhikāṅkṣanti /
aśmakendrāntaraṅgāśca bhṛtyā madīyairviśvāsyatamaiḥ puruṣaiḥ prabhūtāṃ prītimutpādya madājñayā rahasītyupajaptāḥ--"yūyamasmanmitrāṇi, ato 'smākaṃ śubhodarkaṃ vaco vācyamava /
atra bhavānyā rājasūnoḥsāhāyyakāya viśrutaṃ viśrutaṃ māṃ niyujya taddhastenāśmakendrasya vasantabhānostatpakṣesthitvā ye cānena saha yostyanti teṣāmapyantakātithibhavanaṃ vihitam /
yāvadaśmakendreṇa sa janyavṛttirna jātastāvadenamanantavarmatanayaṃ bhāskaravarmāṇamanusariṣyatha /
sa vītabhayo bhūyasīṃ pravṛttamāsādya saparijanaḥ sukhana nivatsyati na cedbhavānītriśūlavaśyo bhaviṣyati /
bhavānyā ca mametyājñaptamasti yadekavaraṃ sarveṣāṃ kathaya /
ato mayā yuṣmābhiḥ saṃhamaitrīmavabudhya sarvebhyo gaditam' ityākarṇya te 'śmakendrāntaraṅgabhṛtyā rājasūnorbhavānīvaraṃ viditvā pūrvameva bhinnamanasa āsan /
viśeṣataśca madīyamiti vacanaṃ śrutvā te sarve 'pi madvaśe samabhavan /
ena sarvamapi vṛttāntabhavabudhyāśmakeśena vyacinti--"yadrājasūnormaulāḥ prajāstāḥ sarvā apyenameva prabhumabhilaṣanti /
madīyaśca bāhma ābhyantaro bhṛtyavargo bhinmanā iba lakṣyate /
evaṃ yadyahaṃ kṣamāmavalambya gṛha eva sthāsyāmi tata utpannopajāpaṃ svarājyamapi paritrātu na śakṣyāmi /
ato yāvatā bhinnacittena madavabodhakaṃ prakaṭayantā madbalena saha mithovacanaṃ na saṃjātaṃ tāvataiva tena sākaṃ vigrahaṃ racayāmi ityevaṃ vihite so 'vaśyaṃ madagre na kṣaṇamavasthāsyate' iti niścityānyāyena pararājyakramaṇapāpapreritaḥ sasainyo mṛtyumukhamivāsmatsainyamabhyayāt /
tamabhyāyāntaṃ viditvā rājaputraḥ puro 'bhavat /
ato 'śmakendrameva turagādhirūḍho yāntamabhyasaram /
tāvat sarvā eva tatsenā "yadayametāvato 'parimitasyāsmatsainyasyoparyeka evābhyāgacchati tatra bhavānīvara evāsādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ nānyat' iti niścityālekhyālikhitā ivāvasthitāḥ /
tato mayābhigamya saṃgarāya samāhūto vasantabhānuḥ sametya māmasiprahāreṇa dṛḍhamabhyahan /
ahaṃ ca śikṣāviśeṣaviphalitatadasiprahāraḥ pratiprahāreṇa taṃ prahṛtyāvakṛttamaśmakendraśiro 'vanau vinipātya tatsainikānavadam--"ataḥ paramapi ye yuyutsavo bhavanti te sametya mayā yudhyantām /
na cedrājatanayacaraṇapraṇāmaṃ vidhāya tadīyāḥ santaḥ svasvavṛttyupabhogapūrvakaṃ nijānnijānadhikārānniḥśaṅkaṃ paripālayantaḥ sukhenāvatiṣṭhantu' iti /
madvacanaśravaṇānantaraṃ sarve 'pyaśmakendrasevakāḥ khakhavāhanātsahasāvatīrya rājasūnumānasya tadvaśavartinaḥ samabhavan /
tato 'haṃ tadaśmakendrarājyaṃ rājasūnusādvidhāya tadrakṣaṇārthaṃ maulāntvānadhikāriṇo niyujyātmībhūtenāśmakendrasainyena ca sākaṃ vidarbhānabhyetya rājadhānyāṃ taṃ rājatanayaṃ bhāskaravarmāṇamabhiṣicya pitrye pade nyaveśayam /
ekadā ca mātrā vasundharayā sahāvasthitaṃ taṃ rājānaṃ vapyajijñapam--"mayaikasya kāryasyārambhaścikīrṣito 'sti /
sa yāvanna siddhyati tānavanmayā na kutrāpyekatrāvasthātuṃ śakyam /
ata iyaṃ madbhāryā tvadbhaginī mañjuvādinī kiyantyahāni yuṣmadantikameva tiṣṭhatu /
ahaṃ ca yāvadiṣṭajanopalambhaṃ kiyantamapyanehasaṃ bhuvaṃ vibhramyaṃ tamāsādya punaratra sameṣyāmi' ityākarṇya mātrānumatena rājñāhamagādi-"yadetadasmākametadarājyopalambhalakṣaṇasyaitāvatobhyudayasyāsādhāraṇo heturbhavāneva /
bhavantaṃ vinā kṣaṇamapyasmābhiriyaṃ rājyadhūrna nirvāhyā /
ataḥ kimevaṃ vakti bhavān' ityākarṇya mayā pratyavādi-"yuṣmābhirayaṃ cintālavo 'pi na citte cintanīyaḥ /
yuṣmadgṛhe yaḥ sacivaratnamāryaketurasti sar idṛgvidhānāmanekeṣāṃ rājyānāṃ dhuramudvoḍhuṃ śaktaḥ /
children.translated_text: In your household there is a jewel among ministers, <s>Āryaketu</s>, who is capable of bearing the burden of many such kingdoms;

children.text: tatastaṃ tatra niyujyāhaṃ gamiṣyāmi' ityādivacanasaṃdohaiḥ pralobhito 'pi sajananīko nṛpo 'nekairāgrahairmāṃ kiyantamapi kālaṃ prayāṇopakramāt nyavartayat /
children.translated_text: Then, although enticed by numerous such persuasive words as 'Having appointed him there, I shall depart,' the king, together with my mother, through many insistences, kept delaying my departure for a considerable time.

children.text: utkalādhipateḥ pracaṇḍavarmaṇo rājyaṃ mahyaṃ prādān /
children.translated_text: He gave me the kingdom of <s>Pracaṇḍavarman</s>, the lord of <s>Utkala</s>.

children.text: ahaṃ ca tadrājyamātmasātkṛtvā rājānamāmantrya yāvattvadanveṣaṇāya prayāṇopakramaṃ karomi tāvadevāṅganāthena siṃhavarmaṇā svasāhāyyāyākārito 'tra samāgataḥ pūrvapuṇyaparipākātsvāminā samagaṃsi' iti //
children.translated_text: And having made that kingdom my own and taken leave of the king, just as I was making preparations to set out in search of you, I was summoned here by <s>Siṃhavarman</s>, the lord of <s>Aṅga</s>, for his assistance, and having arrived here, by the ripening of past merit, I have been reunited with my master.

His time for leisurely recreation is only three and three-quarter <s>nāḍikās</s> (time units). In the seventh (division of the day), there is the toil of inspecting the <s>caturaṅgabala</s> (four-fold army). In the eighth, he has the burden of deliberating on military strategy with his friend the <s>senāpati</s> (general). Then, having worshipped at the evening <s>saṃdhyā</s> (twilight prayer), in the first watch of the night, the <s>gūḍhapuruṣas</s> (secret agents) are to be seen. Through them, the most ruthless schemes involving weapons, fire, and poison are to be carried out. In the second watch, after eating, he should begin <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study) like a learned <s>śrotriya</s> (Vedic scholar). In the third watch, having retired to the sound of musical instruments, he should supposedly sleep through the fourth and fifth watches. But how could the pleasure of sleep come to this wretched one whose mind is agitated by constant worry and exertion? Then again in the sixth watch, there is the commencement of deliberation on <s>śāstra</s> (treatises) and state affairs. In the seventh, there is consultation on secret counsel and the dispatching of envoys. And these envoys, profiting on both sides through commerce on roads beset by transit tolls, reporting favorable news while concealing failures, manufacturing business even where none exists by the slightest pretext, wander about ceaselessly. In the eighth watch, the <s>purohita</s> (royal priest) and others approach him and say: 'Today a bad dream was seen. The planets are unfavorable and the omens inauspicious. Let pacificatory rites be performed. Let all the sacrificial materials be of gold alone. Only then will the ritual be efficacious. These <s>brāhmaṇas</s> are equal to <s>Brahmā</s> himself. If the benedictory rite is performed by them, it will be most auspicious. And these men are poor, have many children, are performers of sacrifices and valiant, yet even now they have not received gifts. Whatever is given to them brings heaven, long life, and the destruction of calamities' — thus having extracted vast amounts through such pretexts, they themselves secretly consume it all. Thus, for one ignorant of statecraft who passes day and night without a moment's pleasure, overwhelmed with exertion and unceasing harassment — let alone universal sovereignty, even his own small territory becomes difficult to protect. For whatever one instructed by those who know the <s>śāstras</s> (treatises) gives, whomever he honors, whatever kind words he speaks — all of it is suspected of being deception, and so there is distrust. And distrust is indeed the birthplace of misfortune. Moreover, since worldly affairs cannot proceed without statecraft, the world itself is already accomplished in it — there is no need for <s>śāstra</s> (formal treatises) here, for even an infant obtains breast-milk from its mother by various stratagems. So cast all that aside and experience sensory pleasures as you wish, free from excessive constraint. As for those who teach: 'The senses must be conquered thus, the group of six enemies must be abandoned thus, the means beginning with <s>sāma</s> (conciliation) must be constantly applied to one's own people and to others, time must be spent solely in deliberation on <s>saṃdhi</s> (alliance) and <s>vigraha</s> (war), not even a small opportunity for pleasure should be given' — even by these minister-cranes, the wealth stolen from you is enjoyed in the houses of their servant-girls. And who are these wretches? Even those who composed harsh treatises on statecraft — <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Āṅgirasa</s>, <s>Viśālākṣa</s>, <s>Bāhudantiputra</s>, <s>Parāśara</s>, and others — did they conquer the group of six enemies? Was <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) fulfilled? Was unsurpassed bliss attained? Even for them, in the enterprises they undertook, both success and failure were observed. And many who studied the texts were outwitted by those who had not studied them. Is this not fitting for Your Majesty, that your lineage is honored by all the world, your youth is unspent, your body is handsome, and your wealth is immeasurable? So let not all this be rendered fruitless by the cause of universal distrust — which obstructs the enjoyment of pleasures, which through the multiplication of many alternative strategies leaves one with unresolved doubt in all affairs — by that net of statecraft. For you have ten thousand elephants, three hundred thousand horses, and infinite infantry. Moreover, the treasure-houses are full of gold and gems. Even if the entire living world were to enjoy them for a full thousand <s>yugas</s> (ages), they would not empty your granaries. What is the point of this insufficiency for which the trouble of unjust acquisition is undertaken? For the life of mortals is but four or five days. Even within that, the portion of age fit for enjoyment is very small. The foolish simply keep acquiring and then perish. They do not desire to taste even a particle of what they have acquired. In short, entrust the burden of the kingdom to capable, devoted inner-circle members, and, taking delight with harem ladies who rival <s>Apsarases</s> (celestial nymphs), spending time in song, relaxation, and play, enjoy the rewards of sovereignty.' The harem ladies spoke with eyes blooming with delight. And the king said with a smile: 'Rise, are you not my elders by virtue of giving beneficial counsel? Why have you acted contrary to the dignity of elders?' Having raised him up, he indulged freely in play. Then, during those days, though repeatedly urged by the aged minister regarding the matter at hand, the king verbally agreed but in his mind dismissed him as one ignorant of his thoughts. Then the minister thought thus: 'Alas, my folly born of delusion! By urging him in a matter that displeases him, I have become, like a petitioner, a laughingstock in his eyes. The deviation from his former conduct is evident. For he does not look at me with affection, does not speak with a smile, does not reveal secrets, does not touch my hand, does not show compassion in my misfortunes, does not participate in my celebrations, and is generally displeased even with what I say that is agreeable to him. Moreover, he assigns me to unworthy tasks, permits others to usurp my seat, shows trust in my enemies, and even when hearing my words spoken about the hostile faction, disregards them. Even my servants, knowing the master's disposition, should become hostile, excluded from his favor.' Still, what recourse is there? Even though undisciplined, this lord should not be abandoned by ones like us who have followed his father and grandfather. Yet even without abandoning him, what benefit can we render when our words go unheard? In any case, this kingdom has fallen into the hands of <s>Vasantabhānu</s>, the king of <s>Aśmaka</s>, who is skilled in statecraft. If only future calamities might restore him to his natural state! For hatred, which easily arises in misfortunes where deceit is readily available, might make him appreciate good conduct. Let the calamity come, then. With the tongues of slanderers restrained, let me somehow maintain my position without falling.' Thus, with the minister standing aside and the king indulging his desires, one named <s>Candrapālita</s>, the son of <s>Indrapālita</s>, the minister of the lord of <s>Aśvaka</s>, who was of bad conduct and had been banished by his father, approached. And through this very intermediary, he obtained a place near the king. Having found an opening, whatever vice the king undertook, he praised it — 'Your Majesty, nothing is as beneficial as the hunt. For through the excellence of physical exercise, one develops speed of legs capable of traversing long distances, which helps in times of calamity; from the reduction of <s>kapha</s> (phlegm), there comes the kindling of digestive fire, which is the sole root of health; from the melting of fat, a lightness of limbs conducive to all actions arises; from the observation of the behavior of deer and such, the ways of the enemy are understood; and from the enjoyment of forests, rivers, mountains, and such, love for the countryside grows, bringing knowledge of one's own territory that is useful for choosing battle and camp sites. In gambling too, there is an incomparable magnanimity of spirit from discarding heaps of wealth like grass, fearlessness from the uncertainty of victory and defeat in contests of audacity and dispute, and the earning of wealth depending solely on prowess. In the enjoyment of fine women too, there is the fruition of both <s>artha</s> (wealth) and <s>dharma</s> (duty), abundant manly pride, skill in understanding emotions, conduct untainted by greed, and the generation of offspring that secures welfare in both worlds. In drinking too, there is the preservation of enviable youthfulness through the consumption of various wines expert in dispelling diverse passions, the disregard of all sorrows through the intensification of ego, the production of wit in convivial assemblies, and the stimulation of the pleasure of romantic sport. Harsh speech, severe punishment, and defamations are each beneficial in their proper place as matters of wealth. For a king is not like a sage whose delight is in tranquility — he cannot subdue the enemy's forces nor sustain the governance of the people.' The king too followed his opinion with excessive reverence, as if it were a guru's teaching. And the subjects, following his character, indulged in vices without restraint. And because everyone shared the same faults, no one stood ready to search out another's weaknesses. The superintendents of departments, having the same master and the same disposition, consumed the fruits of their own offices. Consequently, the sources of revenue gradually crumbled. The avenues of expenditure, owing to the king's subservience to libertines, increased day by day. And the chief feudatories, citizens, and rural notables, drawn into drinking parties with intimate familiarity by the king who shared their habits, exposed their own conduct along with their wives. And the king violated their women under various pretexts. And in the inner quarters of those whose codes of conduct were broken, they lived with little fear and much pleasure. All women of good families, delighting in the easy talk of flattery, with the restraints of good conduct broken, not caring even a straw for their husbands, listened to the counsels of go-betweens. And quarrels rooted in these arose among the resentful. The weak were beaten by the strong. The wealth of the wealthy was stolen by thieves and the like. The plundered, humiliated, and beaten took to the path of crime. The people, having lost their kinsmen, robbed of their wealth, afflicted by captivity and bondage, cried out at the top of their voices with tear-choked throats. And punishment, administered improperly, generated fear and anger. Greed took root among those with meager households, and the proud burned with the fire of dishonor. And in those various misdeeds, whispers born of resentment spread. Then, on a hunt, by describing the abundance of game, he lured the king into mountain valleys with no escape routes, thick with dry grass and bamboo thickets, and setting fires at the entrances, and through tigers and such, he had him killed. Then <s>Vasantabhānu</s>, having incited one named <s>Bhānuvarman</s> of <s>Vanavāsī</s>, seized him through <s>Anantavarman</s>. And <s>Anantavarman</s>, whose kingdom's borders had been encroached upon, made preparations to mobilize his army to attack him. The lord of <s>Aśmaka</s> approached him first among all the feudatories and became dearer to him. The other feudatories also came together. And having marched, they encamped nearby on the banks of the <s>Narmadā</s>. During this time, <s>Candrapālita</s> and others highly praised a dancing girl named <s>Kṣmātalorvśī</s> of the great feudatory lord of <s>Kuntala</s>, <s>Avanideva</s>. And the king, excessively infatuated, enjoyed this intoxicating woman. The lord of <s>Aśmaka</s>, meanwhile, approached the lord of <s>Kuntala</s> privately and said: 'This heedless king molests our wives. How much contempt is to be endured? I have a hundred elephants, and you have five hundred. So let us two, joining together, secretly incite <s>Muraleśa</s>, <s>Vīrasena</s>, <s>Ṛcīkeśa</s>, <s>Ekavīra</s>, the lord of <s>Koṅkaṇa</s>, <s>Kumāragupta</s>, and the lord of <s>Sāsikya</s>, <s>Nāgapāla</s>. They too, unable to tolerate his insolence, will surely come over to our side. And this prince of <s>Vanavāsī</s> is my dear friend. Using him, we shall attack this ill-mannered one from the front and strike him from behind. And we shall divide and seize his treasury and army.' When this was eagerly agreed to by him, twenty bundles of fine cloth, twenty-five loads of gold and saffron were sent as gifts through a trusted messenger, and those feudatories were secured through conciliation and gifts. The next day, <s>Anantavarman</s>, out of hatred for statecraft, became hostage to those feudatories and the prince of <s>Vanavāsī</s>. And <s>Vasantabhānu</s>, having made the disintegrating treasury and army his own, said: 'Divide and take according to your effort and your strength. With your permission, I shall be satisfied with whatever share.' Thus, through his cunning subservience to all, having created a quarrel using that very bait, with all the feudatories turning against <s>Anantavarman</s>, he himself swallowed all of his possessions. Having bestowed a certain portion on the prince of <s>Vanavāsī</s>, he returned and made the entire kingdom of <s>Anantavarman</s> his own. During this interval, the aged minister <s>Vasurakṣita</s>, joining with certain hereditary nobles, fled to <s>Traipurī</s> with this young <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>, the son of that very king's elder sister, taking him from the clutches of danger. But by friends like us, the queen along with her offspring was taken to <s>Māhiṣmatī</s> and presented to her maternal half-brother <s>Mitravarman</s>. But that ignoble one regarded the noble lady otherwise than was proper. And when she rebuked him, he, out of cruelty, wished to kill this child, thinking 'This woman of unblemished character wants to make her son a claimant to the kingdom.' Learning of this, the queen commanded me: 'Dear <s>Nālījaṅgha</s>, let this infant live. Take him and leave him anywhere and live yourself. If I survive, I too shall follow him. Inform me when you have safely departed.' And to give rest to this child who was traveling on foot, I stopped for some days in a cowherd settlement, but fearing the arrival of royal agents even there, I departed by a difficult road. There, wishing to give water to this child who was tormented by terrible thirst, I slipped and fell into this well, and was rescued by you. Be the refuge of this shelterless prince.' Thus he joined his palms in supplication. When I asked, 'What is the caste of his mother?', he said: 'Born to <s>Sāgaradattā</s>, the daughter of a merchant named <s>Vaiśravaṇa</s> of <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>, from the king of <s>Kosala</s>...' 'If that is so, then his maternal grandfather and my father's are one and the same,' and I embraced him with affection. The old man said: 'Which of the sons of <s>Sindhudatta</s> is your father?' When I said '<s>Suśruta</s>,' he was overjoyed. Then I vowed: 'I shall uproot this <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, puffed up with arrogance, using statecraft itself, and establish this child in his ancestral seat' — and how could I have disregarded this vow, with tears and an embrace? Just then, two deer and a hunter arrived, having crossed three pools belonging to some hunter. From his hand I snatched the remaining two arrows and the bow and killed him. One deer I made to appear feathered with arrows, and the other I made to appear without arrows and it fell. Giving one deer to the hunter, I skinned the other's hide and soft parts, stripped it bare, distorted its limbs, feet, and neck, impaled it on a stake, and roasted it on forest fire embers. And I ate. Greatly delighted by my skill in this task, I asked the forest-dweller: 'Do you know the news from <s>Māhiṣmatī</s>?' He replied: 'I sell tiger skins and leather bags there — why would I not know? One named <s>Pracaṇḍavarman</s>, the younger brother of <s>Caṇḍavarman</s>, is approaching to obtain the hand of <s>Mitravarman</s>'s daughter <s>Mañjuvādinī</s>, so the city is festive.' Then I whispered into his ear: 'The wicked <s>Mitravarman</s>, having won the mother's trust through proper treatment of the daughter, will through her lure back and kill the child. So we must go there immediately. Inform her of my news in secret, and also convey my skill to the queen. Then publicly wail that the prince has been devoured by a tiger. That evil-minded one, inwardly delighted but outwardly showing grief, will console the queen. Then through you she should tell him: "The child for whose sake I transgressed your wishes has also gone to the next world through my misfortune. Now I am entirely obedient to your commands." Told this by her, he will be pleased and will approach her. Then, mixing water with this great poison called <s>vatsanābha</s> and soaking a garland in it, she should strike him on the chest and face with it, saying: "May this very sword-blow fall upon you, O sinner, if I am a faithful wife." Then, soaking that garland in water mixed with this antidote and giving it to her own daughter — when he dies and she remains unharmed, the people, believing her to be a true <s>satī</s> (faithful wife), will follow her. Then a message should be sent to <s>Pracaṇḍavarman</s>: "This kingdom is without a leader. He should take this girl along with this kingdom." Meanwhile, the two of us, disguised as <s>Kāpālika</s> (skull-bearing ascetics), receiving alms given by the queen herself, shall dwell before the city near a cremation ground. Then let the queen tell the noble city elders and trusted aged ministers privately: "Today in a dream, the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s> has granted me a boon. On the fourth day from now, <s>Pracaṇḍavarman</s> will die. On the fifth day, in my house on the bank of the <s>Revā</s>, after testing for an auspicious sign, when the people have left, opening the door, some twice-born one along with your son will appear." He will protect this kingdom and establish your child. That child has been concealed by me in the form of a tigress. And this girl <s>Mañjuvādinī</s> has been destined as the wife of that twice-born youth,' she should say. 'Let this most secret matter remain guarded among you alone until it comes to pass.' And at that time, the plan that was conceived with great delight proceeded exactly as planned. In every direction, popular rumor spread: 'Oh, the greatness of faithful wives! For that garland-blow became a sword-blow to him. It cannot be said that this act involved deception, for the very same garland given to the daughter became merely an ornament for her breast, not death. Whoever transgresses the command of this faithful wife shall surely turn to ashes.' Then, seeing me and the boy entering for alms in the guise of great ascetics, the queen, her breasts flowing with milk, rose and spoke in a voice trembling with joy: 'Venerable one, I had a dream. Is it true or not?' I said: 'You will see its fruit this very day.' 'If so, great is the fortune of this servant of yours. That dream indeed portended her finding a protector.' Having made <s>Mañjuvādinī</s>, whose bashfulness was bound with the redness of love at seeing me, bow down, she again spoke with tears of joy: 'Venerable sir, this girl is given to you. Command me.' And I, smiling, with my composure melted by <s>Mañjuvādinī</s>'s gaze steeped in love, having received alms saying 'So be it,' summoned <s>Nālījaṅgha</s> and departed. And from there, in the evening, I entered the temple of <s>Durgā</s>. He reported: 'This one, thinking the kingdom is his, stands without apprehension in the very assembly hall, attended by performers.' 'If so, wait in the garden,' I instructed the old man, and having brought down the mothers into an empty cell beside one wall of that enclosure, I assigned <s>Nālījaṅgha</s> to guard them. When the evening sun had set, having gathered skills useful for understanding assemblies of people — dancing, singing, various cries, hand-gestures, walking, standing on the head, torch-juggling, footstool-balancing, and other entertainer's tricks — I leapt down into the pleasure garden and, saying 'This is the path that my followers can see,' with footsteps placed on the sand smoothed by <s>Nālījaṅgha</s>, like a <s>tamāla</s> tree come to life, I entered the assembly hall. Already, in that very <s>Durgā</s> temple, at the base of the idol itself, I had made a hole concealed by a thick slab of stone placed beside the pedestal, blocking the second entrance. Then, as midnight waned, the two of us, wearing magnificent jewel ornaments and silk garments brought by the rainy season's bounty, entered that hole and stood silently. The queen, the day before, having duly given the funeral rites to the <s>Mālava</s> lord, had sent word to <s>Pracaṇḍavarman</s> and <s>Caṇḍavarman</s> about the situation contrived through the stratagem of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord. Alerted by the sound entering through the tiniest crack, I, lifting with my head alone the iron footstool along with the idol — a task normally requiring the effort of many men — difficult to move, emerged. And I brought out the prince. Then, having worshipped <s>Durgā</s> as before, with the doors thrown open, appearing in person with eyes delighted by proof, with goosebumps clearly visible, with palms raised in salutation, and bowing with amazement, I addressed the assembled nobles: 'Thus has the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s> through me commanded you — so says the queen.' Moreover, consider me, who am skilled in the performance of myriads of difficult and intricate deceptions, whose brazen cunning is evident in the harsh shattering of the <s>Aśmaka</s> pot — consider me to be his protector. And as the price of protection, this beautiful-browed sister of his has been sanctioned for me by the noble queen.' Hearing this, the nobles were delighted: 'Oh, how fortunate is the <s>Bhoja</s> dynasty, whose lord is <s>Āryādatta</s>!' And my mother-in-law experienced a state of joy beyond the reach of words. That very day she duly gave me the hand of <s>Mañjuvādinī</s> in marriage. And when night fell, I properly filled in the hole. And the people, finding no opening, convinced themselves of my divine nature through tales of miraculous feats and other stratagems, and obeyed my commands. The fame of the prince as the son of the noble queen became the cause of his authority. And on an auspicious day, having brought before him the well-formed boy, having him instructed in statecraft by the <s>purohita</s> (priest), I administered the royal affairs. And I reflected: 'Kingship depends on three powers, and these powers — counsel, authority, and energy — mutually supporting each other, advance in their tasks. For through counsel comes the determination of affairs, through authority the commencement, and through energy the completion. Therefore, this tree of kingship, rooted in the five-limbed counsel, trunked in the two forms of authority, branched with the four classes of energy, leafed with the seventy-two elements of the state, with sprouts of the six policies — this tree of power must be nurtured. And this, being subject to many departments, is difficult to manage alone. There is one named <s>Āryaketu</s>, a minister of <s>Mitravarman</s>, who, being of <s>Kosala</s> lineage, is related to the prince on the maternal side and endowed with ministerial qualities — I shall secure him by the very device of showing disregard for his counsel.' Then I instructed <s>Nālījaṅgha</s> secretly: 'Dear one, tell the noble <s>Āryaketu</s> privately: "Who is this impostor who enjoys this royal fortune? He is nothing but an agent of the lord of <s>Aśmaka</s>. What will he extract or devour?" Whatever he says, I must be informed.' The next day, he reported to me thus: 'Having attended upon him frequently, engaged him with gifts, told him various stories, massaged his hands and feet, and at a moment granted in great confidence...' She too spoke thus: 'Dear one, do not speak so. The purity of his noble birth is evident, his intellectual acumen is extraordinary, his physical prowess is superhuman, his generosity is immeasurable, and his skill in weapons is astounding. In him alone converge qualities that are individually rare elsewhere. He is a long-standing <s>bilva</s> tree to his enemies, but a sandalwood tree to the humble. If he were to be removed and this <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, who merely thinks himself skilled in statecraft, and this prince were to be established in their ancestral seats — there is no doubt about this.' Having heard that too, and having further tested him through repeated trials, I made him my ally in counsel. And through his companionship, I appointed ministers endowed with truth and purity, and secret agents of various guises. Learning from them that the circle of subjects was greedy, prosperous, excessively arrogant, and mostly disobedient, I proclaimed my own freedom from greed, displayed my righteousness, and reflected: 'My entire retinue of even the bravest warriors is so devoted to me that at my command they would consider even life itself as trivial as grass. And with the military resources of two kingdoms, I am not inferior to <s>Vasantabhānu</s>, the lord of <s>Aśmaka</s>, and I am versed in statecraft. Therefore, I am capable of defeating <s>Vasantabhānu</s> and establishing <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>, the son of <s>Anantavarman</s> the lord of <s>Vidarbha</s>, in his ancestral seat. And this prince has been claimed as a son by the goddess <s>Bhavānī</s>. And the popular belief has spread everywhere that I have been appointed to assist him. Even now, no one has discovered that this is my stratagem. And the people here, regarding this prince <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>, say: "This is the son of our lord <s>Anantavarman</s>; by the grace of <s>Bhavānī</s> he shall obtain this kingdom" — this has been confirmed through ritual display. And the army of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, knowing the divine assistance of <s>Bhavānī</s> for the prince, will think "the power of destiny is greater than human power" and will hesitate in battle. And the hereditary nobles and subjects here, who from the very beginning desired the prosperity of the prince, and who have now been further won over by me through gifts, honors, and other means of securing trust — all these will be allied with me. And the inner-circle servants of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, having been cultivated with great affection by my most trusted agents, have been secretly whispered to at my command: "You are the lord of <s>Aśmaka</s>'s own people. It is widely known that <s>Bhavānī</s> has appointed me to assist the prince. After the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord is defeated at my hands, what will become of those who, standing in his faction, have gone over to <s>Vasantabhānu</s>? As long as the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord has not yet engaged in battle, you should follow this son of <s>Anantavarman</s>, <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>. Freed from fear, having obtained abundant livelihood, he will live happily with his retinue. If not, he will fall under the trident of <s>Bhavānī</s>. And <s>Bhavānī</s> has commanded me to tell this one boon to all. Therefore, having understood my friendship with you, I have told this to all of you." Hearing this, those inner-circle servants of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, knowing the boon of <s>Bhavānī</s> for the prince, accepted it as settled. And especially upon hearing the words "my own" — they all came under my control. The lord of <s>Aśmaka</s> too, learning all these developments, reflected: "The hereditary subjects of the prince — all of them desire him alone as their master. And my own external and internal retinue of servants appears to be of divided mind. If, under such circumstances, I remain patient and stay at home, I shall not be able to protect even my own kingdom once insurrection has arisen. Therefore, before my divided-hearted servants reveal their awareness of my situation and before secret communication occurs between them and his forces, I should engage in battle with him." Learning that he was marching against us, the prince went forward. Thereupon, I rode on horseback and charged toward the advancing <s>Aśmaka</s> lord himself. At that, his entire army thought: 'Since this one comes alone against our immense and boundless force, surely the boon of <s>Bhavānī</s> alone is the extraordinary cause — what power have we against the divine?' — and they became paralyzed in every limb. Then, having approached and challenged <s>Vasantabhānu</s> to single combat, he met me and struck me hard with a sword-blow. But I, having rendered his sword-blow ineffective through superior skill, struck him with a counter-blow, severed the head of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord, and casting it upon the ground, said to his soldiers: 'Those who still wish to fight beyond this, let them come together and fight with me. Otherwise, let them pay obeisance at the feet of the prince and, as his loyal subjects, fearlessly protect their respective offices while enjoying the fruits of their own livelihoods in peace.' Immediately upon hearing my words, all the servants of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord swiftly dismounted from their horses, honored the prince, and came under his command. Then I, having established the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord's kingdom for the prince, appointing hereditary nobles as administrators for its protection, and together with the army of the <s>Aśmaka</s> lord that had become my own, marched to <s>Vidarbha</s>, and in the royal capital, having consecrated that prince <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>, I established him in his ancestral seat. And one day, I informed the king who was seated with his mother <s>Vasundharā</s>: 'I wish to undertake the commencement of a certain task. Until it is accomplished, I cannot stay in one place anywhere. Therefore, let this wife of mine, your sister <s>Mañjuvādinī</s>, stay in your presence for some days. And I, wandering over however much of the earth is necessary until I find the persons I seek, having found them, shall return here again.' Hearing this, with the mother's approval, the king said to me: 'It is you alone who are the extraordinary cause of all this prosperity of ours, namely the acquisition of this kingdom. Without you, we cannot bear the yoke of this kingdom even for a moment. Why then does my lord speak thus?' Hearing this, I replied: 'You should not entertain even a particle of this worry in your mind.
